concepts.name: Will · Skill · Opportunity
concepts.line: Every action needs at least two of three: wanting it, being able, and an open door.

concepts.name: The 2/3 Rule
concepts.line: Find the one missing pillar and push there — not everywhere.

concepts.name: The Capable Bystander
concepts.line: Skill and access without fire: no productivity hack fixes a missing why.

concepts.name: The Dreaming Sprinter
concepts.line: Desire plus an open door is the best place to learn anything.

concepts.name: The Competent Prisoner
concepts.line: When will and skill are full, the fight is structural, not personal.

concepts.name: Self-Efficacy
concepts.line: Believed skill, not actual skill, decides whether you even try.

concepts.name: The Map Is Not the Territory
concepts.line: Everything you know is a simplified map. Useful, never complete.

concepts.name: You See What You Aim At
concepts.line: Your goals decide what your eyes even notice.

concepts.name: Reframing
concepts.line: Same event, different frame, different body, different action.

concepts.name: Stress Mindset
concepts.line: Believing stress can fuel you changes what it does to you.

concepts.name: Pragmatic Truth
concepts.line: Judge an idea by what happens when you live by it.

concepts.name: Perceive → Appraise → Recalibrate
concepts.line: Run your mind like a good controller: predict, compare, adjust, repeat.

concepts.name: Fast & Slow Thinking
concepts.line: A quick hare and a careful owl share your skull. Know who's driving.

concepts.name: Anchoring
concepts.line: The first number you hear quietly drags every estimate after it.

concepts.name: Availability Bias
concepts.line: What's easy to remember feels more likely than it is.

concepts.name: Confirmation Bias
concepts.line: You hunt for evidence you're right. Try hunting for the opposite.

concepts.name: Loss Aversion
concepts.line: Losing $50 hurts about twice as much as winning $50 feels good.

concepts.name: Inversion
concepts.line: To get what you want, first list how to guarantee failure — then avoid it.

concepts.name: Second-Order Thinking
concepts.line: Ask 'and then what?' — twice.

concepts.name: Base Rates
concepts.line: Before the vivid story, ask: how often does this happen in general?

concepts.name: Feedback Loops
concepts.line: Reinforcing loops snowball; balancing loops hold steady. Spot which one you're in.

concepts.name: Delays
concepts.line: When results lag actions, people overcorrect. Patience is a systems skill.

concepts.name: Leverage Points
concepts.line: Small push, right place, big change. Usually the goal or the rules — not the numbers.

concepts.name: Fixes That Fail
concepts.line: The quick fix that relieves today often feeds tomorrow's problem.

concepts.name: Shifting the Burden
concepts.line: Relying on a crutch weakens the muscle that would have solved it.

concepts.name: The Habit Loop
concepts.line: Cue → craving → response → reward. Change any link, change the habit.

concepts.name: Identity-Based Habits
concepts.line: Every action is a vote for the person you're becoming.

concepts.name: 1% Compounding
concepts.line: 1% better daily is ~37× in a year. 1% worse is near zero.

concepts.name: The Two-Minute Rule
concepts.line: Make the start so small you can't say no.

concepts.name: Environment Design
concepts.line: Willpower is a weak lever. Rearrange the room instead.

concepts.name: Never Miss Twice
concepts.line: Missing once is an accident. Missing twice is the start of a new habit.

concepts.name: Name It to Tame It
concepts.line: 'Bad' is vague. 'Embarrassed and tired' is workable.

concepts.name: The Pause
concepts.line: Between trigger and reaction there's a gap. Widen it by three breaths.

concepts.name: Self-Compassion
concepts.line: Talk to yourself like you'd talk to a friend who's struggling.

concepts.name: Procrastination Is a Feeling Problem
concepts.line: We don't avoid tasks. We avoid the feeling the task gives us.

concepts.name: Emotional Contagion
concepts.line: Moods spread like weather fronts through rooms and group chats.

concepts.name: Start With Why
concepts.line: People commit to why you do it before what you do.

concepts.name: Meaning Through Responsibility
concepts.line: Pick up the heaviest load you can carry. Meaning is in the carrying.

concepts.name: Order & Chaos
concepts.line: Too much order is a cage; too much chaos is a flood. Live on the border.

concepts.name: Aim at Something
concepts.line: A worthy aim reorganizes what you see, do and endure.

concepts.name: Flow
concepts.line: Challenge slightly above skill + clear goals = time disappears.

concepts.name: Growth Mindset
concepts.line: Treating ability as trainable changes how you handle hard things.

concepts.name: The Power of 'Yet'
concepts.line: 'I can't do this' → 'I can't do this yet.' One word, new door.

concepts.name: Grit
concepts.line: Passion plus perseverance for long-term goals predicts more than talent alone.

concepts.name: Deliberate Practice
concepts.line: Practice at the edge of your ability, with feedback, on one weakness.

concepts.name: Mistakes as Data
concepts.line: A mistake is the most precise feedback you'll get today.

concepts.name: The Cookie Jar of Wins
concepts.line: Keep proof of what you've survived. Reach in when it gets hard.

concepts.name: Quitting Wisely
concepts.line: Grit isn't never quitting. It's quitting the right things on purpose.

concepts.name: Three Kinds of Conversation
concepts.line: Every talk is practical, emotional or social. Match the kind, or miss each other.

concepts.name: Looping for Understanding
concepts.line: Repeat back what you heard, ask if you got it right. People soften when proven heard.

concepts.name: Introvert / Extrovert Energy
concepts.line: It's not shy vs. loud — it's where you recharge.

concepts.name: Shared Stories
concepts.line: Money, nations, rules: humans cooperate at scale by believing the same stories.

concepts.name: Steelmanning
concepts.line: State the other side so well they'd say 'yes, exactly' — then disagree.

concepts.name: Asking for Help Is Brave
concepts.line: The bravest thing you can say is often 'help'.

concepts.name: Deep Work
concepts.line: Undistracted focus on hard things is rare — and therefore valuable.

concepts.name: Attention Residue
concepts.line: Each switch leaves part of your mind behind on the last task.

concepts.name: Sleep Saves Your Learning
concepts.line: Sleep is when the brain files today's learning. Skip it, lose it.

concepts.name: The Scroll Loop
concepts.line: Variable rewards keep thumbs moving long after joy has left.

concepts.name: Boredom Is a Signal
concepts.line: Boredom isn't empty — it's your mind asking for a better goal.

concepts.name: One-Way vs Two-Way Doors
concepts.line: Most decisions are reversible. Decide those fast; slow down only for the one-way doors.

concepts.name: Regret Minimization
concepts.line: Picture yourself at 80. Which choice would you regret not making?

concepts.name: The Pre-Mortem
concepts.line: Imagine it failed. Now explain why — before it happens.

concepts.name: Expected Value
concepts.line: Odds × payoff. Good decisions can have bad outcomes — judge the decision.

concepts.name: Opportunity Cost
concepts.line: The real price of a yes is the best thing you said no to.

concepts.name: Circle of Competence
concepts.line: Know the edge of what you know — that's where mistakes live.

concepts.name: Dichotomy of Control
concepts.line: Some things are up to you, some aren't. Spend energy only on the first.

concepts.name: Circle of Influence
concepts.line: Proactive people work inside what they can influence; it grows.

concepts.name: The Golden Mean
concepts.line: Courage sits between cowardice and recklessness. Virtue is calibrated.

concepts.name: Knowing You Don't Know
concepts.line: The wisest person in Athens was the one who knew what he didn't know.

concepts.name: Amor Fati
concepts.line: Don't just accept what happened. Use it as fuel.

concepts.name: This Too Shall Pass
concepts.line: Feelings and fortunes are weather, not climate.

concepts.name: Begin With the End in Mind
concepts.line: Write your own eulogy, then live backwards from it.

concepts.name: If-Then Plans
concepts.line: "When X happens, I'll do Y" hands the decision to the moment, so you don't need willpower then.

concepts.name: The Spotlight Effect
concepts.line: You feel watched; most people are too busy with their own spotlight to notice your stumble.

concepts.name: The Happiness Treadmill
concepts.line: Every new thing you get soon feels normal, so 'more' never stays exciting for long.

concepts.name: Blaming People, Not Situations
concepts.line: When others slip, we blame their character; when we slip, we blame the situation.

concepts.name: Still-Water Watching
concepts.line: Quiet observers spot the slow loops and delayed effects a loud room talks right past.

concepts.name: The Nightly Reset
concepts.line: A short evening ritual closes the day's loops so sleep can file skills and wash out bad moods.

concepts.name: Three Good Things
concepts.line: Writing down three good things each night trains your eyes to notice what's already going right.

concepts.name: The Stockdale Paradox
concepts.line: Face the brutal facts and keep faith you'll prevail. Blind optimists break; realists endure.

concepts.name: Real-World Risky Play
concepts.line: Climbing, scraping, and making up games outdoors builds courage and friends no screen can.

concepts.name: Psychological Safety
concepts.line: Teams learn fastest when anyone can admit a mistake or ask a question without being punished.

concepts.name: Small Promises, Big Trust
concepts.line: Trust is built in tiny deposits: kept promises and fairly shared credit, one at a time.

concepts.name: Open Loops Nag
concepts.line: Unfinished tasks keep tugging at your mind; writing the next step down lets your brain let go.

concepts.name: The Sunk Cost Trap
concepts.line: What you've already spent is gone; only future costs and gains should decide what's next.

concepts.name: Memento Mori
concepts.line: Remembering your time is limited makes today's choices clearer and small grudges smaller.

concepts.name: Creative & Truthful Courage
concepts.line: Speak your truth with kindness, measure progress against yourself.

concepts.name: The Self-Reflection Loop
concepts.line: Learn from experience, adjust your course, and grow.

cards.hook: Pick one thing you keep meaning to do. Let's see what makes it easier.
cards.title: Will, Skill, Opportunity

game.prompt: Pick your thing: revise for a test, a side hustle, an instrument, getting fitter, or something else. Answer every line for that one goal.

questions.q: I actually want this.
I could do a rough version today.
Nothing outside me is stopping me.

W.name: Fired Up, Building Up
W.text: Today the want is strong, but skill and access score low. Don't wait for both: build the cheaper one first, usually a small skill.

S.name: Skilled, Looking for a Why
S.text: Today your answers show skill, but little want and no open door. Ask whether this goal is truly yours, or borrowed from someone else.

O.name: The Open Door
O.text: Today the door looks open, but want and know-how score low. Check whether anything behind that door sparks your curiosity.

SW.name: Ready, Door Closed (for now)
SW.text: Today you want it and can do it, but the door scores shut. That's structural, not a flaw in you. Find another door, or build one with others.

OW.name: Eager, Door Open
OW.text: Want plus an open door today: a great place to learn anything. Your next move is practice, in small, honest reps with feedback.

OS.name: Ready, Waiting for a Why
OS.text: Everything scores high today except the fire. No productivity trick fixes a missing why. Look for the reason that would make this matter to you.

OSW.name: Full Agency
OSW.text: All three pillars score high today. The only thing left is to start. Put the first 10 minutes in your calendar.

results.name: The Starting Line
results.text: No pillar scored strong today, which is common, especially after a hard stretch. It's a starting point, not a verdict. Raise the easiest one this week (often a tiny skill rep) and play again in 7 days.

mid.name: The Half-Lit Path
mid.text: Today all three pillars sit in the middle. Pick the cheapest one to raise by a notch this week (often a 10-minute skill rep) and play again in 7 days.

cards.insight: Action needs a want, an ability and an open door; Blumberg and Pringle argued in 1982 that research kept forgetting the third. Most stuck goals miss one, and pushing harder on the strong ones may not fix the weak one.
cards.model: Stuck? Don't push everywhere. Find the missing pillar: Will, Skill or Opportunity.
cards.try_today: Write your goal at the top of a page, then one line each for W, S and O. Circle the weakest and take one step on it.

source.work: Blumberg & Pringle, The missing opportunity in organizational research (Academy of Management Review, 1982); adapted as the original QUMNI WSO framework, drawing on Self-Determination Theory and self-efficacy research

cards.try_team: Each person writes one stuck goal and scores Will, Skill and Opportunity 1-5. In pairs, the helper may only offer help on the lowest score.

cards.hook: A gifted kid grows up with no instruments. What happens to the gift?
cards.title: Talent needs a door

game.prompt: Picture a child with a gift for music and a hunger to play, born in a place with no instruments, no teachers and no time off work. Does her talent show up anyway?
choices: Yes, real talent always finds a way
Probably not, or only in pieces
game.reveal: Usually not, or only in pieces. If you said yes, that's the story we're all told: we hear about those who made it, not the many with grit and no door. Gifts are spread widely; open doors are not.

cards.insight: Stories where grit beats everything hide the many who had grit and no door. Seeing the missing pillar is kinder, and more accurate, than blaming people for not trying.
cards.model: Talent and drive are necessary, not sufficient. Someone has to open, or build, the door.
cards.try_today: Think of one person whose skill you admire but who lacks a door. Send them one lead, intro or resource today.

source.work: Gray, Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751); Giddens, The Constitution of Society (1984); QUMNI WSO Framework

cards.try_team: Each person names one door someone once opened for them (a teacher, a lift, a loan, an intro). Then list doors your group could open for someone else.

from_source.quote: Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, / And waste its sweetness on the desert air.
from_source.cite: Thomas Gray, Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751), stanza 14
from_source.next_read: Stanzas 12-15, from 'Perhaps in this neglected spot is laid' to 'Some mute inglorious Milton'

cards.hook: You have one hour to help a stuck friend. Where do you spend it?
cards.title: Push the missing pillar

steps.scenario: Ana loves baking and is great at it. She wants to sell cakes at the local summer fair, but she has no stall. You help by…

options.text: Sending her an advanced baking class
options.feedback: Kind, but her skill is already strong. More of what she has won't get her a stall.

options.text: Giving her a pep talk about following her dream
options.feedback: Her will is already on fire. Encouragement is nice, but it isn't what's missing.

options.text: Asking the fair organiser you know if she can share a table
options.feedback: Yes. Will and Skill are lit; Opportunity is missing. One door does more than ten pep talks.

steps.scenario: Leo has free time, a phone and a language app already set up. He keeps saying he 'should' learn Spanish but never opens it. You…

options.text: Ask what he'd actually do with Spanish, and why it matters to him
options.feedback: Yes. Skill can be learned and the door is open; the gap is Will. A real reason does more than a schedule.

options.text: Make him a strict study timetable
options.feedback: Structure helps once he wants it. Right now it would be a plan for something he doesn't care about yet.

options.text: Pay for the premium version of the app
options.feedback: He already has the door. A bigger door won't make him walk through it.

cards.insight: A QUMNI rule of thumb, not a research finding: two pillars are often enough to take a first step, and help on the third pays off most. People tend to push the pillar that's already strong because it feels comfortable.
cards.model: Push the one weak pillar, not all three. Small help in the right spot beats big help elsewhere.
cards.try_today: Ask someone stuck: 'Is it wanting, knowing how, or access?' Then offer help only on the answer they give.

source.work: QUMNI 2/3 rule: an untested rule of thumb inspired by Blumberg & Pringle (Academy of Management Review, 1982), whose own model says all three pillars interact

cards.try_team: Each person shares one stuck goal. The group may only ask: 'Is it wanting, knowing how, or access?' Then offer one help aimed at that answer.

cards.hook: Two of three pillars often get you moving. Can you spot who's close?
cards.title: Spot the 2 out of 3

game.prompt: Does this person have at least two pillars lit?

items.text: Mia wants to run a 5K, has never run, and there's a park next door.
items.why: Will + Opportunity. Skill can be built on the way: start with walk-run intervals.

items.text: Sam plays piano well and has one at home, but stopped enjoying it after his exams.
items.why: Skill + Opportunity, but Will is missing, the hardest to borrow. Rest, then find his own reason.

items.text: Jo dreams of acting, has never tried, and no theatre is nearby.
items.why: Only Will. Build one more pillar first, like an online class or a local reading group.

items.text: Raj can fix bikes, loves it, and a neighbour just asked for help.
items.why: All three. Full agency: he only needs to say yes.

items.text: Lee has a free gym pass but no interest and no idea how to train.
items.why: Only Opportunity. An open door alone doesn't move anyone.

cards.insight: A QUMNI rule of thumb, not a research finding: with two pillars lit, a first step is often possible and the third can grow on the way. Will is the exception: without a reason that's yours, the others rarely carry you.
cards.model: Two pillars often make motion possible; if the missing one is Will, start there.
cards.try_today: List three goals. Count the lit pillars for each. Start the one with the most lit today.

source.work: QUMNI 2/3 rule: an untested rule of thumb inspired by Blumberg & Pringle (Academy of Management Review, 1982), whose own model says all three pillars interact

cards.try_team: Write five goals from the group on slips of paper. Sort them together by how many pillars are lit, then plan the first step of one 'two-lit' goal.

cards.hook: Stuck on a goal? Maybe the reason isn't yours yet.
cards.title: The Capable Bystander

questions.q: When I picture finishing this goal, I feel…

options.label: Like I've finally pleased someone else
Like I did something that matters to me

questions.q: If nobody would ever know I quit, I would…
The reason for this goal mostly came from…
When I describe it to a friend, I say…

zones.label: Borrowed goal
zones.text: Today this goal sounds borrowed. That isn't a character flaw. Find your own reason inside it, or consider letting it go.

zones.label: Flickering fire
zones.text: Today your answers mix 'want' and 'should'. Link the goal to one person or value you truly care about and see if the want grows.

zones.label: Real fire
zones.text: Today your answers show real want. If you're still stuck, look at Skill or Opportunity instead of blaming motivation.

cards.insight: With skill and access in place, the missing piece is often a reason that's yours. Goals that fit your values tend to last longer. If nothing has felt worth wanting for weeks, talk to someone.
cards.model: No productivity hack fixes a missing why. Find your reason, or free yourself from the goal.
cards.try_today: Write: 'This matters to me because…' If nothing comes, that's information, not failure. Can it be dropped, changed or tied to what you love?

source.work: Deci & Ryan, Self-Determination Theory (1985); Ryan & Deci, American Psychologist (2000); applied in the QUMNI WSO framework

cards.try_team: Each person says one goal as 'I have to…', then tries 'I get to… because…'. Goals nobody can rephrase may need a new reason, or a rethink.

cards.hook: Practised for hours. Why aren't you better? Order a real session.
cards.title: Practice That Actually Works

game.prompt: Put a good practice session in order
items: Pick one small sub-skill
Practice just beyond your comfort zone
Get fast, honest feedback
Adjust and try again
game.explain: This is the core loop of deliberate practice: narrow focus, a stretch, feedback, then correction. Repeating what you can already do feels good but teaches little.

cards.insight: Hours alone don't build skill; focused practice with feedback does more. The '10,000-hour rule' is a myth Ericsson himself rejected, and practice explains only part of skill differences.
cards.model: Skill grows at the edge: one sub-skill, a stretch, feedback, adjust, repeat.
cards.try_today: Choose one tiny part of a skill you want. Do 5 focused minutes on only that, then ask someone for one piece of feedback.

source.work: Ericsson & Pool, Peak (2016); Macnamara et al., Psychological Science (2014); applied in the QUMNI WSO framework

cards.try_team: Everyone picks one tiny sub-skill (a chord, a serve, five new words). Practise 3 minutes, then swap and give each other one piece of feedback.

from_source.quote: …it is from playing the lyre that both good and bad lyre-players are produced.
from_source.cite: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
from_source.next_read: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapters 1-2: how skills and virtues are built by practice

cards.hook: Reading your notes again feels like learning. Is it lying to you?
cards.title: Pull it out, don't pour it in

steps.scenario: In a week you need to know new material: words in a language, a certification topic, or how a new system works. You've got one hour. Which plan sticks best?

options.text: Read the notes four times, slowly and carefully
options.feedback: It feels great because it gets familiar. But in tests a week later, rereading lost to self-quizzing by a lot.

options.text: Read once, then close the notes and write what you remember, three times
options.feedback: Yes. Pulling it out of memory is what makes it stick. It feels harder, and that's the point.

options.text: Highlight the key parts, then reread the highlights
options.feedback: Very popular, but big reviews found highlighting adds little on its own. Turn highlights into questions instead.

steps.scenario: Your friend tries self-quizzing and says: 'This feels awful, I keep forgetting. Rereading felt better.' You say…

options.text: 'Then go back to rereading, it's less stressful'
options.feedback: Kind, but the smooth feeling is the trap: easy now, forgotten later.

options.text: 'Struggling to remember is the workout. That's how it sticks.'
options.feedback: Yes. Effortful recall feels like failing while it's building memory. Gaps you find are gifts.

options.text: 'Maybe you're just not good at memorising'
options.feedback: Meant gently, but forgetting during practice is normal for everyone, not a sign of low talent.

cards.insight: In a classic study, students who reread a text recalled about 40% a week later; those who tested themselves recalled about 61%. Yet the rereaders felt more sure they'd remember.
cards.model: Easy-feeling study often isn't learning. Pull it out of your head; don't just pour it back in.
cards.try_today: Pick something you're learning. Close the book and write or say all you remember for 3 minutes. Then check the gaps.
cards.try_team: End a meeting, lesson or onboarding session with a 2-minute brain dump: everyone writes the 3 things they remember, no notes, then compares.

source.work: Roediger & Karpicke, Test-enhanced learning (Psychological Science, 2006); Dunlosky et al., Improving students' learning (Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2013)

cards.hook: You're trying harder and harder. What if the wall isn't you?
cards.title: Ready, Door Closed

game.prompt: Where's the blocker: something you can grow, or something in the way?

items.text: The qualification you earned abroad isn't recognised where you live now.
items.why: A rule, not a flaw. Look for bridging courses or paths that don't need it.

items.text: You keep skipping guitar practice since you stopped caring about the songs.
items.why: That's Will, and it's allowed to change. Pick songs you love, or take a guilt-free break.

items.text: You can only study after 11pm because you look after family every evening.
items.why: Time is Opportunity. Shrink the task or swap for a better slot, not more willpower.

items.text: You don't know how to edit videos for the channel you want to start.
items.why: That's Skill, and it's learnable fast with free tutorials and feedback.

items.text: The club you want to join only takes people who know a member.
items.why: A gate. Build doors: show up at open events, ask for an intro.

cards.insight: When will and skill are full, more effort on yourself can turn into self-blame. Some walls are rules, money, time or gatekeepers. That's not an excuse; it says change the setup.
cards.model: If you want it and can do it but still can't, the fight is structural. Change the setup, not yourself.
cards.try_today: Name one outside blocker on a goal. Write two other doors around it: another route, person, or place.

source.work: Giddens, The Constitution of Society (1984); Bourdieu, The Forms of Capital (1986); applied in the QUMNI WSO framework

cards.try_team: List the walls your team, class or family keeps hitting. Mark each 'something we can build' or 'in the setup'. Pick one setup wall and name who could move it.

cards.hook: Rich kids vs poorer kids: how much likelier to become inventors?
cards.title: The lost Einsteins

game.question: In the US, kids from the richest 1% of families vs kids from the poorer half: how many times more likely are they to become inventors?
game.explain: About 10 times. Differences in maths scores at age 8 explained less than a third of that gap: even among kids with top maths scores, the richer ones were still far more likely to invent. Exposure mattered: kids who grew up around inventors were more likely to invent, often in the very same field.

cards.insight: Talent is spread widely; doors are not. In this US data, growing up near people doing the work was one of the strongest doors. The study is observational, but the pattern is large.
cards.model: Ability is often not the bottleneck; access is. Seeing someone up close do the work is a door.
cards.try_today: Find one person who does something you'd love to do. Ask them one question: 'How did you get started?'
cards.try_team: Invite someone with an unusual job or hobby to talk for 5 minutes to your class, team or family. Ask: 'Who first showed you this?'

source.work: Bell, Chetty, Jaravel, Petkova & Van Reenen, Who Becomes an Inventor in America? The Importance of Exposure to Innovation (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2019)

cards.hook: A friend says 'I'm just not a speaker.' What actually helps?
cards.title: Belief built by doing

steps.scenario: Your friend dreads speaking up in class or at family dinners and says 'I'm just not that kind of person.' You…

options.text: Tell them they're amazing and will be fine
options.feedback: Warm, and encouragement does help a bit. But words fade fast when the moment comes.

options.text: Suggest they say one prepared sentence the next time the group meets
options.feedback: Yes. A small success they create themselves is the strongest source of 'I can'. Then make the next step a bit bigger.

options.text: Send them a video of a famous speaker
options.feedback: Watching others helps most when the model is similar to them. A star can feel out of reach.

options.text: Say some people just aren't speakers
options.feedback: Meant kindly, but it locks the belief in place. Belief in what you can do changes with experience.

cards.insight: Bandura found that whether you even try depends on believing you can, not only on real skill. The strongest builder of that belief is a small success of your own.
cards.model: Believed skill decides if you try. Build belief with small wins you earn, not with pep talks alone.
cards.try_today: Pick something you think you're 'bad at'. Do the smallest possible version of it once today and notice that you did it.

source.work: Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change (1977)

cards.try_team: Each person names one thing they're 'not a ___ person' about and commits to its tiniest version this week. Next time, everyone reports back.

from_source.quote: …we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.
from_source.cite: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
from_source.next_read: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapter 1

cards.hook: Where does your 'I can do this' actually come from?
cards.title: Your four sources of belief

questions.q: I can remember recent times I did something hard and it worked.
I often finish small things I start.
I know someone like me who has done what I want to do.
I've watched someone at my level learn this and get better.
People I trust tell me they think I can do it.
Someone has given me specific, honest feedback that I'm improving.
When I'm nervous, I read it as my body getting ready, not as a sign I'll fail.
Butterflies before a challenge usually help me more than they hurt.

advice.0: Your own wins scored lowest today? Set a goal so small you can't fail, finish it, and write it down. Stack a few this week.
advice.1: Role models scored lowest today? Find one person a step or two ahead of you, not a superstar, and learn how they started.
advice.2: Support scored lowest today? Tell one supportive person your goal and ask them to check in with you in a week.
advice.3: Reading your body scored lowest today? Before a hard task, notice the racing heart and tell yourself: 'This is my body getting ready, not a sign I'll fail.'

cards.insight: Bandura named four sources of 'I can': your own wins, seeing people like you succeed, encouragement, and how you read your body. Own wins count most; the others fill gaps.
cards.model: Belief in yourself is built from four sources. Find your weakest and feed it.
cards.try_today: Write down three things you did well in the past month. Read the list right before your next hard task.

source.work: Bandura, Self-Efficacy: The Exercise of Control (1997); Jamieson et al., arousal reappraisal studies (2010)

cards.try_team: Go round the group: each person names one recent small win they saw someone else in the room achieve. Everyone leaves with wins they didn't notice.

cards.hook: Same students, same leaflet. One extra sentence. Guess the gap.
cards.title: The one-sentence plan

game.question: Students wrote one line: 'During the next week, I will exercise on [day] at [time] at [place].' What % of them exercised that week?
game.explain: 91%. Students who only read a motivating leaflet: 35%. Those who did nothing: 38%. One small UK study (Milne, Orbell & Sheeran, 2002), so treat 91% as a best case, not a promise.

cards.insight: Wanting wasn't the gap: the leaflet alone changed nothing. Deciding when and where did. Across 94 tests the effect is medium to large; big real-world trials find smaller gains.
cards.model: Motivation says 'I should'. A plan with a time and place says 'Tuesday, 7pm, the park'.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you keep putting off. Write: 'On [day] at [time] in [place], I will [first step].' Put it where you'll see it.

source.work: Milne, Orbell & Sheeran, Combining motivational and volitional interventions (British Journal of Health Psychology, 2002); Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006) meta-analysis

cards.try_team: Everyone writes one goal as 'On [day] at [time] in [place], I will…'. Swap with a partner, who checks: could a stranger tell exactly when it happens?

cards.hook: Your plan sounds great. Will it survive a rainy Tuesday?
cards.title: Write a plan that fires

steps.scenario: Maya, 16, means to revise after school but ends up scrolling. Which plan is most likely to work?

options.text: "This week I'll take revision more seriously."
options.feedback: Not quite. A sincere goal, but it never says when, so the moment passes and the phone wins.

options.text: "When I put my school bag down at home, I'll open my notes for 10 minutes before my phone."
options.feedback: Yes. A clear cue (bag down) plus a small, specific action. The decision is already made when the moment arrives.

options.text: "I'll revise for three hours every night."
options.feedback: Not quite. Big and brave, but there's no trigger, and the size makes it easy to put off.

steps.scenario: Sam, a manager, keeps meaning to praise good work but forgets by the end of the day. Pick the plan.

options.text: "I'll try to be more appreciative."
options.feedback: Not quite. Good intent, but no moment to hook onto. Busy days swallow vague plans.

options.text: "If a meeting ends, then before I leave the room I'll thank one person for one specific thing."
options.feedback: Yes. Meetings happen anyway, so the cue is built in, and 'one specific thing' is small enough to do.

steps.scenario: Rosa, 68, plans a daily walk after lunch. What should she add to protect it?

options.text: "If it rains, then I'll walk laps of the covered market instead."
options.feedback: Yes. Planning for the obstacle in advance is the second half of the trick: the backup is ready before the excuse.

options.text: "If I miss a day, I'll walk twice as far tomorrow."
options.feedback: Not quite. Doubling up turns one missed day into a bigger hurdle. A backup for the same day works better.

options.text: "Nothing will stop me."
options.feedback: Not quite. Lovely spirit, but rain will come. Plans that expect obstacles tend to beat plans that deny them.

cards.insight: The best plans name a cue you can't miss and a step small enough to do. Plan for the likely obstacle too. Then the moment makes the decision, not your mood.
cards.model: If [moment], then [small action]. Then add: if [obstacle], then [backup].
cards.try_today: Write one 'If [moment], then [action]' for a goal, plus one 'If [obstacle], then [backup]'. Read both aloud once.

source.work: Gollwitzer, Implementation intentions (American Psychologist, 1999); Gollwitzer & Sheeran, meta-analysis (Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 2006)

cards.try_team: Each person shares one goal and its likeliest obstacle. The group helps write one 'If [obstacle], then [backup]' plan for each person in 5 minutes.

cards.hook: When did you last think about one hard thing for 60 minutes straight?
cards.title: Deep Work

questions.q: When a hard task gets uncomfortable, I usually…

options.label: Switch to something easier for a bit
Take a short pause, then go back in

questions.q: When I study or work on something hard, my notifications are…

options.label: All on, I like being reachable
Off until I choose to look

questions.q: The thing that matters most to me right now (a subject, a project, a hobby) gets done…

options.label: In the gaps between other things
Whenever I find a quiet moment
In a block I protect on purpose

questions.q: At the end of a busy day I often feel…

options.label: Exhausted, but unsure what I made
Tired, and I can point to progress

zones.label: Mostly shallow today
zones.text: Today's answers lean toward reacting. That's normal in a ping-everywhere world, not a flaw. One protected block a day would change more than any app.

zones.label: Mixed today
zones.text: Your answers show deep focus sometimes, more by luck than design. Choose the time, the place and the one task in advance and it gets far more reliable.

zones.label: Deep-leaning today
zones.text: Your answers say you already guard your focus. Next step: stretch the block by 10 minutes, or bring a harder problem into it.

cards.insight: Newport argues that focus on hard things is getting rarer, so it's worth more. It's a skill, not a personality type: schedule it, then sit through the first uncomfortable minutes.
cards.model: Busy is not the same as productive. Protect one block for the work that actually moves things.
cards.try_today: Pick one task, set a 25-minute timer, put your phone in another room, and work until it rings.

source.work: Deep Work (2016)

cards.try_team: Hold a 45-minute quiet hour together: phones in a basket, questions wait. Afterwards each person names one thing they finished.

from_source.quote: the faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will.
from_source.cite: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), Vol. 1, Ch. XI 'Attention'
from_source.next_read: The Principles of Psychology, Vol. 1, Ch. XI 'Attention' (read the whole chapter; the passage closes the section 'The Varieties of Attention', in the middle of the chapter)

cards.hook: Half your to-do list could be done half-asleep. Which half?
cards.title: Deep vs. Shallow Tasks

game.prompt: Does this need your full brain?

items.text: Replying 'sounds good!' in a group chat
items.why: Easy to do while distracted, and easy for anyone to do.

items.text: Writing the first draft of a tough essay
items.why: Needs you to hold many ideas at once. Interruptions wreck it.

items.text: Learning a new chord on the guitar
items.why: New skills need focused attention on the exact part you get wrong.

items.text: Booking a dentist appointment
items.why: Necessary, but low-thought. Batch it with other small chores.

items.text: Planning how to fix a money problem
items.why: Hard trade-offs need quiet thinking, not 30-second bursts.

items.text: Rearranging the apps on your phone
items.why: Feels productive, uses little brain. A classic stand-in for hard work.

cards.insight: Shallow tasks need doing, but anyone can do them tired. Deep tasks make something new and need your fresh hours. Most of us spend our best energy on the shallow pile first.
cards.model: Give your freshest hour to the deep pile. Batch the shallow pile for when you're tired.
cards.try_today: Write tomorrow's list in two columns, deep and shallow, and do one deep item before you open any messages.

source.work: Deep Work (2016)

cards.try_team: Everyone sorts this week's tasks into deep and shallow. Protect one deep slot each, then clear the shallow ones together in one 20-minute sweep.

from_source.quote: My experience is what I agree to attend to. Only those items which I notice shape my mind
from_source.cite: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), Vol. 1, Ch. XI 'Attention'
from_source.next_read: The Principles of Psychology, Vol. 1, Ch. XI 'Attention', opening pages

cards.hook: How long do you stay on one screen before switching? Guess.
cards.title: Attention Residue

game.question: In Gloria Mark's recent workplace studies, how many seconds did people stay on one screen, on average, before switching?
game.explain: About 47 seconds on average in her studies from 2016 onward, down from about 2.5 minutes in 2004 (Mark, Attention Span, 2023). Sophie Leroy separately found that after a switch, part of your mind stays stuck on the task you just left.

cards.insight: Leroy calls it attention residue: after a switch, part of your mind stays on the last task. So quick 'just checking' glances aren't free. A note on where you stopped helps you let go.
cards.model: Every switch leaves a bit of you behind. Fewer switches means more of you shows up.
cards.try_today: Before you switch tasks, write one line: where you stopped and the next step. Then switch.

source.work: Leroy, Why is it so hard to do my work? (2009); Mark, Attention Span (2023)

cards.try_team: Start your next meeting, lesson or family task with 60 seconds of silence: everyone writes where they left their last task. Then phones face-down.

cards.hook: It's 1 a.m. before a big day. Do you push on or close the laptop?
cards.title: Sleep Saves Your Learning

steps.scenario: Big exam or presentation at 9 a.m. You've prepared all evening. It's 1 a.m. and you feel you've only half got it. You…

options.text: Do one quick review of the key points, then sleep
options.feedback: Smart. A short review before sleep, then real sleep, gives your brain both the material and the time to store it.

options.text: Stay up all night to cover everything
options.feedback: Understandable panic. But without sleep, recall and focus usually drop, so extra hours can cost more than they add.

options.text: Sleep, then cram at 6 a.m.
options.feedback: Better than no sleep. But you're tired at 9 a.m., and you've lost some of the sleep that seems to help memory.

steps.scenario: You're learning a new skill this month: a language, a sport, an instrument. The best plan is…

options.text: Practice once a week for three hours
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but one long session is harder to hold on to than the same time spread across many days.

options.text: Practice 20 minutes most days, sleeping well between
options.feedback: Yes. Spreading practice out is one of the best-tested ways to learn, and the nights of sleep in between seem to help too.

options.text: Practice late at night to save time
options.feedback: Fine sometimes, but if it eats into sleep, you may lose the gains you just made.

cards.insight: Many studies link sleep to holding on to what you learned, though the effect is smaller and patchier than popular books suggest (Walker's included).
cards.model: Learning = practice + sleep. Cutting sleep to cram more rarely pays off.
cards.try_today: Set an alarm 30 minutes before your bedtime tonight that means: screens down, lights low.

source.work: Stickgold, Sleep-dependent memory consolidation, Nature (2005); Walker, Why We Sleep (2017)

cards.try_team: Agree a team rule: no messages about tomorrow's deadline after 10 p.m. Try it for one release or project cycle and compare how the mornings go.

cards.hook: You opened the app for 'one second.' Can you trace what happened?
cards.title: The Scroll Loop

game.prompt: Put the scroll loop in order
items: A small itch: boredom, worry, an awkward pause
Thumb reaches for the phone, almost on its own
Unpredictable feed: dull, dull, then something great
A short hit of relief or novelty
The itch is still there, so you keep going
game.explain: The feed works like a slot machine: you never know when the next good post comes, so you keep pulling. The relief is real but brief, and it doesn't fix the itch that started it.

cards.insight: Feeds reward you at random, the hardest kind of reward to stop chasing. You're not weak; the design is strong. Haidt links heavy phone use to harm in teens; researchers still debate how much.
cards.model: If the reward is random, the habit is sticky. Break the loop at the itch, not the thumb.
cards.try_today: Next time you reach for your phone, pause and name the itch in one word (bored, tense, lonely). Then decide.

source.work: Ferster & Skinner, Schedules of Reinforcement (1957); Haidt, The Anxious Generation (2024)

cards.try_team: Each person names the itch that starts their scroll (bored, tense, lonely). Then everyone picks one swap for it, like a walk or texting a friend.

cards.hook: Two pigeons. One gets food every peck, one at random. Who quits last?
cards.title: Why Random Rewards Hook Us

game.prompt: Two pigeons learn to peck a button for food. Pigeon A gets food every single peck. Pigeon B gets food at random, unpredictable pecks. Then the food stops completely. Which pigeon keeps pecking longer?
game.reveal: Pigeon B, by a lot. If you picked A, that's the natural guess: more food should mean a stronger habit. But random rewards are much harder to give up (Ferster & Skinner). Feeds and slot machines pay out at random too.

cards.insight: When rewards are predictable, you notice fast when they stop. When they're random, every empty pull feels like 'maybe next time.' That's why refresh-for-something-new apps are hard to put down.
cards.model: Random rewards build the stickiest habits. Make the good stuff predictable and the feed boring.
cards.try_today: Turn off notifications for one app that pings you at random, and check it at two set times instead.

source.work: Schedules of Reinforcement (1957)

cards.try_team: Agree two set times a day to check the family, class or team chat, instead of answering every ping. Try it for a week and compare notes.

cards.hook: Alone with your thoughts for 15 minutes, or a mild shock? Guess.
cards.title: Boredom Is a Signal

game.question: In a 2014 study, people sat alone with nothing to do for 15 minutes, with a button that gave a mild electric shock. What % of men shocked themselves at least once?
game.explain: 2 in 3 men chose to ZAP THEMSELVES rather than just sit with their thoughts for 15 minutes (women: 1 in 4), even though they'd said they'd pay to avoid that shock. Small study (Wilson et al., Science, 2014), but… oof.

cards.insight: That urge to grab your phone the second you're bored? Same thing. Researchers see boredom as a signal that what you're doing doesn't engage you. Listened to, it can point to a better goal.
cards.model: Boredom is a question, not a void: 'What would actually be worth my attention right now?'
cards.try_today: Next time you feel bored, wait two minutes before grabbing your phone and ask: what would I like to be doing?

source.work: Out of My Skull (2020); Wilson et al., Science (2014)

cards.try_team: Set a 3-minute timer: no phones, no talking, just sit. When it rings, each person shares one idea or wish that popped up while bored.

from_source.quote: all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
from_source.cite: Blaise Pascal, Pensées (1670), §139, trans. W. F. Trotter
from_source.next_read: Pensées, Section II, §139 to §143 (on diversion), Trotter translation

cards.hook: Your phone buzzes mid-revision. "Just a sec" costs way more than that.
cards.title: Leave Tasks Cleanly

steps.scenario: You're halfway through something that needs thought: revision, a TikTok edit, a hard level in a game. Your phone buzzes with the group chat. You…

options.text: Check it now, then come back
options.feedback: Very normal. The catch: the task you left keeps tugging at you while you read, and the chat tugs once you're back. Both get less of you.

options.text: Finish the sentence or step, jot the next move, then check
options.feedback: Yes. Leroy and Glomb found a quick 'ready-to-resume' note helps people let go of the unfinished task, so the next one gets more of their mind.

options.text: Ignore it, but keep wondering who it was
options.feedback: Half a win: the phone stayed down. But the wondering is residue too. Next time, put the phone out of sight before you start.

steps.scenario: You have one hour for two things: writing something hard (an essay, a letter) and catching up on messages. Which plan leaves the least residue?

options.text: Switch every few minutes so nothing piles up
options.feedback: It feels efficient, but each switch leaves a trail. Twenty switches, twenty trails.

options.text: 40 minutes on the hard thing, then 20 on messages
options.feedback: Yes. One switch, at a clean stopping point. The messages will still be there in 40 minutes.

options.text: Both at once, with the chat open in a corner
options.feedback: Most of us feel we can multitask. Mostly we switch fast and pay a small cost each time.

cards.insight: Leroy found people do worse on a new task when the last one is left unfinished. A short note on where you stopped helps your mind let go. A few clean switches beat many quick ones.
cards.model: Close the loop before you switch: finish the bit, note the next step, then move.
cards.try_today: Check your messages at three set times today instead of whenever they buzz.
cards.try_team: Agree a 'clean switch' rule for a week: before interrupting someone, ask 'good stopping point?' If not, wait two minutes.

source.work: Leroy, Why is it so hard to do my work? (2009); Leroy & Glomb, Tasks interrupted, Organization Science (2018)

cards.hook: Rats ran a maze all day. At night, their brains did something eerie.
cards.title: Your Brain Replays the Day

game.prompt: Scientists record 'place cells' in rats: brain cells that fire at certain spots along a maze route. The rats run the maze, then fall asleep. What do those cells do during sleep?
choices: Go quiet: the brain is resting
Replay the maze route, in order
game.reveal: They replay the route, in the same order, often many times faster than the real run. If you guessed 'quiet', that's the common view: sleep looks like switching off. It isn't (Wilson & McNaughton, 1994; Lee & Wilson, 2002).

cards.insight: Human studies suggest something similar: memories get reactivated and strengthened in deep sleep. The replay evidence is mostly from rats, but it's a big reason sleep after learning matters.
cards.model: Sleep isn't switching off. It's when your brain rehearses what you learned today.
cards.try_today: Tonight, spend two minutes before bed recalling one thing you learned today. Then put the screen away and sleep.
cards.try_team: End the day as a family or class: each person says one thing they learned. Recall it again at breakfast and see what stuck.

source.work: Wilson & McNaughton, Science (1994); Lee & Wilson, Neuron (2002); Rasch et al., Science (2007)

cards.hook: Unfinished stuff nags at you. But the famous memory claim? Shaky.
cards.title: Open Loops Pull You Back

game.prompt: In 1927, Bluma Zeigarnik stopped people halfway through small puzzles and tasks. A century of follow-up studies later, which claim holds up best?
choices: We feel an urge to go back and finish them
game.reveal: The urge to finish. Zeigarnik's memory boost often failed to show up again; a 2025 meta-analysis found the pull to resume (first shown by Maria Ovsiankina, 1928) is the sturdier finding. If you picked memory, you picked the textbook version.

cards.insight: Think of a half-read book, a half-done essay or a half-fixed shelf: they tug at you. The tug is real. The idea that it sharpens memory is contested.
cards.model: An open task doesn't just sit there; it pulls you back. Close it or park it on purpose.
cards.try_today: Pick one small task you left half-done (a reply, a form, a drawer) and finish it in 10 minutes. Notice the relief.
cards.try_team: Each person names one 'open loop' bugging them. Pair up: finish one now, or write down when it will get done.

source.work: Zeigarnik, Psychologische Forschung (1927); Ovsiankina (1928); Ghibellini & Meier, meta-analysis (2025)

cards.hook: Lying awake replaying tomorrow? Five minutes with a pen might help.
cards.title: Park It on Paper

game.question: In a sleep lab, one group spent 5 minutes before bed writing tomorrow's to-do list. Another wrote what they had already done. How many minutes sooner did the to-do group fall asleep?
game.explain: About 9 minutes sooner, and longer, more specific lists went with faster sleep (Scullin et al., 2018). Writing down what's left seems to let the mind stop holding it.

cards.insight: It was one small study of 57 young adults, so treat it as promising, not proven. Small studies of plan-making point the same way: a written next step quiets the nag.
cards.model: Your mind keeps holding open tasks until they're parked somewhere it trusts.
cards.try_today: Tonight, before bed, write tomorrow's to-do list on paper, as specific as you can. Then put the list and the screen away.
cards.try_team: End the week or the school day with a 'parking lot': everyone writes their open tasks and next steps on one shared sheet before leaving.

source.work: Scullin et al., Journal of Experimental Psychology: General (2018); Masicampo & Baumeister, JPSP (2011)

cards.hook: Your advice was good. So why did they get more upset?
cards.title: Three Kinds of Conversation

steps.scenario: Your friend says: 'My brother corrected me in front of the whole family at dinner.' You reply…

options.text: Next time, just correct him right back.
options.feedback: Could work in a practical talk. But this one sounds like feelings first. Solutions land better after they feel heard.

options.text: In front of everyone? That sounds embarrassing.
options.feedback: Yes. This is an emotional conversation. Naming the feeling tells them you're on the same channel.

options.text: My brother does that too, it's so annoying.
options.feedback: Friendly instinct, but it moves the spotlight to you. Stay on their story a bit longer.

steps.scenario: Later they say: 'OK, I'm calmer. What should I actually say to him?' Now you…

options.text: Keep validating: 'That must have felt awful.'
options.feedback: Kind, but they just switched channels. They're asking for a plan now.

options.text: Offer two concrete options and ask which fits.
options.feedback: Right. The talk turned practical, so you turned with it. Matching is a moving target.

options.text: Ask what this says about their place in the family.
options.feedback: That's a social, who-are-we question. It may matter later, but right now they asked for a next step.

cards.insight: Most talks are practical (what do we do?), emotional (how do we feel?) or social (who are we?). Advice in an emotional talk often misses. Notice the kind, and when it switches.
cards.model: Ask: is this about solving, feeling, or identity? Then answer in that same channel.
cards.try_today: In your next real conversation, silently label it practical, emotional, or social before you reply.

source.work: Supercommunicators (2024)

cards.try_team: Read out 3 real messages (group chat, a note from school, a work email). Everyone votes: practical, emotional or social? Talk through the splits.

cards.hook: Your mate texts you a problem. Advice or a hug? Can you sort all 7?
cards.title: Fix It, or Hear Me?

game.prompt: Feelings or belonging first, or a fix first?

items.text: I got 4 out of 10 on the maths test. Again.
items.why: 'Again' carries the feeling. Name it before you suggest a tutor.

items.text: Which bus gets me to the Trafford Centre by 10?
items.why: A clear practical question. Answer it. A feelings chat here would feel odd.

items.text: Everyone got invited to the party except me.
items.why: This is about belonging, the social kind of talk. Listen before you plan.

items.text: My phone's on 2%. Have you got a charger?
items.why: Pure logistics. Hand over the cable.

items.text: I didn't get into the sixth form I wanted and now I don't know what I'm doing.
items.why: Sounds like a planning problem, but it's about who you are now. Ask before you suggest options.

items.text: How do we split the bill fairly between five of us?
items.why: A maths and fairness question. Offer a method.

items.text: My mum keeps reading my messages.
items.why: Trust and privacy: feelings first. Plans can come after they feel heard.

cards.insight: Duhigg describes three kinds of talk: practical, emotional and social. Here we fold emotional and social talks together as "hear me first". Many sentences sound practical but carry a feeling or a question of belonging underneath. Clues: 'again', 'everyone', 'except me', big changes. Not sure? Ask.
cards.model: Before you solve it, check the need: 'Do you want ideas, or just to vent?'
cards.try_today: Next time someone shares a problem, ask 'Do you want ideas, or do you just need to vent?' before you answer.
cards.try_team: Each person writes one thing they said this week. Others guess: did they want a fix, a listener, or to belong? The writer reveals.

source.work: Supercommunicators (2024)

cards.hook: Want someone to calm down? Stop trying to convince them.
cards.title: Looping for Understanding

steps.scenario: Your mum (or dad, or sibling) snaps: 'You never help with the dishes!' You did them twice this week. You say…

options.text: That's not true, I did them Tuesday and Thursday.
options.feedback: Accurate — and it will probably start a fact fight. They don't feel heard yet, so facts sound like defense.

options.text: It sounds like you feel you're carrying most of the housework. Is that right?
options.feedback: That's a loop: repeat the heart of it, then check. You can share your facts after they say 'yes, exactly.'

options.text: Let's not do this right now.
options.feedback: Taking a break can be wise. But without a loop first, it can feel like a door closing.

steps.scenario: They answer: 'Not exactly — it's that I always have to ask.' You…

options.text: Ah, so it's less the dishes and more having to be the one who notices. Right?
options.feedback: Perfect. A loop that gets corrected isn't a failure — it's the loop working. Now you know the real issue.

options.text: Well, you could just ask nicely.
options.feedback: Understandable reflex, but it skips past what they just told you. Loop once more.

cards.insight: Looping: ask, say back what you heard in your own words, then check you got it right. People soften when they're shown they were heard, not just told. Being corrected is part of it.
cards.model: Ask → say it back in your words → 'Did I get that right?' → repeat until they say yes.
cards.try_today: In one conversation today, say back what you heard and ask 'Did I get that right?' before giving your view.

source.work: Supercommunicators (2024); Rogers & Farson, Active Listening (1957)

cards.try_team: In pairs: one moans about something small for 1 minute; the other loops until they hear 'yes, exactly.' Swap.

from_source.quote: The reason why we have two ears and only one mouth is that we may listen the more and talk the less.
from_source.cite: Zeno of Citium, in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, VII.23, trans. R. D. Hicks (1925)
from_source.next_read: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VII, sections 1-38 (the life of Zeno)

cards.hook: 'I hear you' sounds kind. So why can it make things worse?
cards.title: Real Loop or Fake Loop?

game.prompt: Does this reply prove you listened?

items.text: I hear you.
items.why: It claims you listened but proves nothing. They have nothing to check.

items.text: So the worst part was that nobody even asked you. Right?
items.why: Their point in your words, plus a check. They can say yes or fix it.

items.text: I know exactly how you feel.
items.why: Often a turn to your own story. And they can't correct a guess you never said.

items.text: Let me check: it's not the money, it's that nobody told you first?
items.why: Specific and checkable. Even if you're wrong, their correction gets you closer.

items.text: Totally. Anyway, what I'd do is…
items.why: A nod, then straight to advice. The listening was just waiting.

items.text: You want more say in the plan. Did I get that right?
items.why: Short and complete: a summary plus 'Did I get that right?'

cards.insight: A real loop has two parts: their point in your words, and a check. Without the check it's still a guess. The moment they say 'yes, that's it' is often when tension drops.
cards.model: Understanding isn't what you feel — it's what the other person confirms.
cards.try_today: Pick one person today and do one full loop, ending with 'Did I get that right?'
cards.try_team: Play 'loop tennis': one person gives an opinion in 2 lines; the next loops it to a 'yes' before adding their own. Go round the circle.

source.work: Supercommunicators (2024); Rogers & Farson, Active Listening (1957)

cards.hook: After a great party, do you feel charged up or drained?
cards.title: Where You Recharge

questions.q: After a long, busy day (school, work or family), I want…

options.label: A quiet room and no talking

questions.q: When I have a hard problem, I…

options.label: Talk it out to figure it out

questions.q: A free Saturday with no plans feels…
In a loud, busy room I…

zones.label: Quiet-leaning today
zones.text: Today your answers lean toward recharging in quiet. That isn't shyness: you can be warm and bold and still refuel best alone.

zones.label: Middle zone today
zones.text: Today your answers sit near the middle, like most people's. The pull toward people or quiet can shift with sleep, stress and who's around.

zones.label: People-leaning today
zones.text: Today your answers lean toward refuelling with people and buzz. Quiet focus may go better with some structure, or company nearby.

cards.insight: Introversion isn't shyness; it's mostly how much stimulation feels good. Most people land near the middle. 'Recharge' is a handy lens, but researchers still debate what extraversion measures.
cards.model: Not shy vs. loud — notice what drains you and what refuels you, then plan around it.
cards.try_today: Look at tomorrow's schedule and add one 10-minute recharge block that fits your end of the spectrum.

source.work: Quiet (2012); Psychological Types (1921)

cards.try_team: Planning a team, class or family day? Each person marks one moment they'd want quiet and one they'd want company. Build both in.

cards.hook: If every human vanished tonight, would your cash be worth a cent?
cards.title: Shared Stories

game.prompt: Rock or agreement?

items.text: The value of a banknote
items.why: The paper stays. Its value lives in what millions of people agree to accept.

items.text: A mountain
items.why: Rock doesn't need anyone's belief. The name 'Everest' does, though.

items.text: A country's border
items.why: Rivers are real; the line on the map is an agreement people keep.

items.text: A company like Peugeot (or Google)
items.why: Harari's own example is Peugeot: the factories could burn down and the company would still exist, in law and in shared belief.

items.text: Gravity
items.why: It pulls whether anyone believes or not.

items.text: Your follower count meaning you matter
items.why: The number is real data. What it says about you is a story people agree to tell.

cards.insight: Harari argues humans cooperate in huge numbers because we believe the same stories: money, laws, nations. 'Fiction' doesn't mean fake or bad. These stories are tools, and they can be rewritten.
cards.model: Some things are rocks, some are agreements. Agreements can be questioned — and changed.
cards.try_today: Name one 'rule' you follow today and ask: is this a rock or an agreement? Who could change it?

source.work: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind (2011)

cards.try_team: List 5 rules your team, class or family follows. Sort them: rock or agreement? Pick one agreement that no longer helps and redesign it together.

cards.hook: Can you argue the other side so well they'd thank you?
cards.title: Steelmanning

steps.scenario: Your friend thinks phones should be banned in schools. You disagree. Which reply is a steelman?

options.text: So you think teens are too dumb to handle a phone?
options.feedback: That's a strawman — a weaker version that's easy to knock down. They'd likely just get annoyed.

options.text: You're worried phones pull kids' attention away from learning and from each other, and a clear rule is easier than constant fights. Fair?
options.feedback: Steelman. It's their best version, in words they'd agree with. Now your disagreement will actually be heard.

options.text: Whatever, people said the same about TV.
options.feedback: Might be a real point later, but it skips their argument instead of meeting it.

steps.scenario: They say: 'Yes, exactly.' Now you…

options.text: Say where you agree, then share your concern about emergencies and teaching phone skills.
options.feedback: Great. Agreement first, then disagreement. This is close to Rapoport's rules as Dennett describes them.

options.text: Say 'Great, but you're wrong because…'
options.feedback: You earned the floor, so don't spend it on 'you're wrong.' Start with what you share.

cards.insight: A strawman attacks the weakest version of a view. A steelman states the strongest one first. It makes you fairer, makes others listen, and sometimes shows you what you were missing.
cards.model: Before you disagree, state their view so well they say 'yes, exactly.'
cards.try_today: Pick a view you disagree with and write its strongest case in 3 sentences — as if you believed it.

source.work: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking (2013)

cards.try_team: Pick a topic people disagree on. In pairs, each states the other's view until they hear 'yes, exactly.' Only then debate. 5 minutes per pair.

from_source.quote: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
from_source.cite: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859), Chapter II
from_source.next_read: On Liberty, Chapter II, 'Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion'

cards.hook: Fair criticism has steps. Most of us jump straight to the last one.
cards.title: Rapoport's Rules

game.prompt: Order the steps for criticizing someone's view fairly
items: Restate their view so clearly they wish they'd said it that way
Name where you agree and what you learned from them
Only then, offer your criticism
game.explain: Daniel Dennett popularized these as 'Rapoport's Rules,' crediting the game theorist Anatol Rapoport. He lists agreeing and learning as two steps; here they're one. Dennett's bet: by the last step, the other person is far more ready to listen.

cards.insight: Criticism lands better once the other person feels understood and respected. These rules slow you down just enough to check you're arguing with their real view, not one you invented.
cards.model: Restate → agree and learn → then critique. Earn the right to disagree.
cards.try_today: Next time you disagree in a chat, class or meeting, do steps 1 and 2 out loud before making your point.

source.work: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking (2013)

cards.try_team: In your next group decision, nobody may criticize an idea until they've restated it and named one thing they agree with. Notice the mood.

cards.hook: You think people will say no if you ask for help. Want the real odds?
cards.title: Asking for Help Is Brave

game.prompt: People had to get 5 strangers to fill out a short form. They guessed they'd need to ask about 20. How many did it actually take?
game.reveal: About 10, half as many as they feared. If you guessed 20, you think like the askers did: we expect more no's than we get (Flynn & Lake, 2008). Bohns (formerly Lake) found the same later.

cards.insight: We underestimate how often people say yes. We focus on the cost of helping; they feel how awkward it is to say no. Asking isn't weakness. It's often how connection starts.
cards.model: Others say yes more than you predict. 'Help' is a short, brave word.
cards.try_today: Ask one person for a small, specific bit of help today, even by text. Too big? Write down who you'd ask and what you'd say.

source.work: Flynn & Lake, 'If You Need Help, Just Ask' (JPSP, 2008); Bohns, You Have More Influence Than You Think (2021)

cards.try_team: Go round: each person names one small thing they could use help with this week. Others offer only what's easy for them. Count the yeses.

cards.hook: Group chat or one person? One of these usually gets ignored.
cards.title: How to Ask for Help

steps.scenario: Your phone won't back up your photos and you're stuck. You…

options.text: Post 'Can anyone help with phones?' in the big group chat.
options.feedback: Feels safer, but in a crowd everyone can assume someone else will answer. That is the diffusion of responsibility first seen in emergencies (Darley & Latané, 1968) and later in online chat rooms.

options.text: Message one person who knows phones: 'Could you look at my photo backup for 10 minutes?'
options.feedback: Yes. One named person, one clear task, a small size. That's the easiest kind of ask to say yes to.

options.text: Keep trying alone. You don't want to bother anyone.
options.feedback: Very human. But we tend to overestimate how much asking bothers people. You may be skipping an easy yes.

steps.scenario: Next, a bigger favour: a lift to an appointment next week. You can text or ask in person. You…

options.text: Send a long text full of apologies.
options.feedback: Texts are easy to put off, and all the sorry makes the favour sound heavier than it is.

options.text: Ask in person or by phone, simply and warmly.
options.feedback: In one study, people asked strangers in person to fill in a short survey got about 34 times more yeses than people who asked by email (Roghanizad & Bohns, 2017). With friends the gap is likely smaller, but in-person asks are harder to overlook.

steps.scenario: They said yes and drove you. Afterwards you…

options.text: Apologize again for being such a bother.
options.feedback: Kind instinct, but it frames help as a burden. Helpers often feel better than askers expect (Zhao & Epley, 2022).

options.text: Thank them and say exactly how it helped.
options.feedback: Yes. Seeing the difference they made is the helper's reward, and it makes the next ask easier for you both.

cards.insight: Askers misjudge three things: how often people say yes, how much the way you ask matters, and how good helping feels. Ask one person, be specific, ask face to face, thank well.
cards.model: One person, one clear ask, face to face, then a real thank-you.
cards.try_today: Pick one small thing you're stuck on. Ask one person today: 'Could you help me with this for 10 minutes?'
cards.try_team: Go round the room: each person names one thing they're stuck on, in one sentence. Anyone who can help in under 10 minutes says so.

source.work: Roghanizad & Bohns, JESP (2017); Zhao & Epley, Psychological Science (2022); Bohns, You Have More Influence Than You Think (2021)

cards.hook: The teams you'd trust most looked worst on paper.
cards.title: Fear Hides Mistakes

game.prompt: A researcher tracked drug errors on hospital wards. Wards with better teamwork and leadership had…
game.reveal: More. In Amy Edmondson's 1996 study of 8 hospital units, the better-led teams recorded more errors. Her conclusion: they weren't making more, they were more willing to report them. A small study, but it launched her research on psychological safety.

cards.insight: Silence can look like success. When owning up feels safe, problems surface early, while they're small and fixable.
cards.model: Fear doesn't stop mistakes. It hides them.
cards.try_today: Admit one small mistake out loud today, at home, school or work, and say what you'll do next. Notice who relaxes.
cards.try_team: Start your next meeting, class or family dinner with each person naming one thing that went wrong this week and what it taught them. Leader goes first.

source.work: Edmondson, 'Learning from Mistakes Is Easier Said Than Done' (J. Applied Behavioral Science, 1996); The Fearless Organization (2018)

cards.hook: Your next sentence decides whether they ever tell you again.
cards.title: Make It Safe to Speak Up

steps.scenario: Group project, two days to the deadline. A classmate admits they forgot to save last night's work. You say…

options.text: "Seriously? That was your one job."
options.feedback: Fair to be frustrated. But what they learn is 'next time, hide it', and you find out later, when it's worse.

options.text: "Thanks for telling us now. What do we rebuild first?"
options.feedback: Yes. Thank the telling, then turn to the fix. That's how you get warned early next time.

options.text: Say nothing and quietly redo it yourself tonight.
options.feedback: Generous, but nobody learns what went wrong, and you carry it alone. Fixing it together works better.

steps.scenario: Your teenager tells you they scraped the car pulling out of the driveway. You say…

options.text: "How many times have I told you to be careful?"
options.feedback: Understandable. But the message heard is 'telling me costs you'. The next scrape may stay secret.

options.text: "I'm glad you told me. Are you OK? Let's look at it together."
options.feedback: Yes. Safety isn't zero standards: you can still agree how they help pay for it. You're rewarding honesty, not the scrape.

steps.scenario: You lead a meeting and want honest input on your plan. You close with…

options.text: "Any questions? No? Great."
options.feedback: A quick yes/no question invites silence. Silence isn't agreement.

options.text: "What am I missing? I'm sure there's something."
options.feedback: Yes. Edmondson's advice for leaders: admit you can be wrong and ask real questions. It makes speaking up the normal thing to do.

options.text: "My door is always open if you disagree."
options.feedback: Well meant, but it leaves the risk with them: they must come to you, alone. A specific question in the room works better.

cards.insight: Psychological safety isn't niceness or low standards. It's knowing you won't be punished for speaking up. Thank the telling, ask real questions, fix together.
cards.model: Thank the telling, then fix the problem. People repeat what gets rewarded.
cards.try_today: Next time someone brings you bad news, make your first words 'Thanks for telling me.' Then ask what they need.
cards.try_team: End your next meeting or class by asking 'What are we missing?' and wait a full 10 seconds of silence before anyone answers.

source.work: Edmondson, 'Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams' (ASQ, 1999); The Fearless Organization (2018)

cards.hook: Grand gestures feel big. Trust mostly notices the small stuff.
cards.title: Trust Deposits

game.prompt: What does this do to trust?

items.text: Texting 'on my way!' before you've actually left
items.why: Tiny, but people learn that your words and the clock don't match.

items.text: Telling the class whose idea won your group the project
items.why: Naming who did the work is a deposit for them, and makes you safe to work with.

items.text: Picking up your grandkid exactly when you said you would
items.why: Boring reliability is the main deposit. It shows your word means something.

items.text: Presenting a teammate's analysis to the boss as 'what I found'
items.why: Taking credit is a big withdrawal, and people remember it for a long time.

items.text: Saying 'I'll try, but I can't promise' when you're unsure
items.why: An honest maybe beats a broken yes. It keeps your real promises worth something.

items.text: Owning up fast after you've broken a promise, then fixing it
items.why: The broken promise cost you; quick honesty and a fix win much of it back.

cards.insight: Trust grows from small, plain things: words that match deeds, and credit given where it's due. Covey's 'emotional bank account' is a metaphor, not a measurement, but a handy one.
cards.model: Every kept word is a deposit. Every overpromise is a loan you may not repay.
cards.try_today: Check your last three 'I'll…' messages. Keep one you forgot, or send an honest update about it.
cards.try_team: At your next meeting or family meal, each person thanks someone else by name for one specific thing they did this week.

source.work: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989)

cards.hook: You've kept 20 promises. How much can one broken one cost?
cards.title: Trust Builds Slow, Breaks Fast

game.prompt: People read 45 bits of news about a local power plant, good and bad, and rated how each would change their trust in it. Which moved trust more?
game.reveal: The bad news, by a wide margin. Paul Slovic (1993) found negative events cut trust far more than matching positive events raised it. His study was about a power plant, not friends, but it fits a wider pattern: bad tends to weigh more than good.

cards.insight: Trust climbs in small steps and can fall in one big one. That's why kept promises matter: they're the slow savings that cushion the day you slip.
cards.model: Trust is slow to build and quick to lose. Promise small, keep it, repeat.
cards.try_today: Make one promise today small enough to keep for sure, then keep it on time.
cards.try_team: Each person lists one promise they made the group this month: kept, late or dropped. No blame; renegotiate the dropped ones out loud.

source.work: Slovic, 'Perceived Risk, Trust, and Democracy' (Risk Analysis, 1993)

cards.hook: You spent 40 minutes picking a lunch spot. Was that door locked?
cards.title: One-Way vs Two-Way Doors

game.prompt: If this goes wrong, can you walk back through the door?

items.text: Trying a new gym class this week
items.why: Hate it? Don't go next week. Cheap to undo, so decide fast.

items.text: Getting a face tattoo
items.why: Hard and painful to reverse. This one deserves slow thinking.

items.text: Picking a paint color for your room
items.why: Paint is cheap. A weekend fixes a bad call.

items.text: Lending all your savings to a friend's 'sure thing'
items.why: Money lent is hard to get back, and so is the friendship. Slow down here.

items.text: Testing a new morning routine for a week
items.why: A one-week experiment is the definition of reversible.

items.text: Saying something cruel in an argument
items.why: Words can be forgiven, but rarely unsaid. Pause before this door.

cards.insight: Most choices are two-way doors: if they go wrong, you can step back. Save your slow, careful thinking for the few doors that lock behind you.
cards.model: Ask 'Can I undo this?' Reversible: decide fast and learn. Irreversible: slow down.
cards.try_today: Pick one choice you've been stalling on. If it's reversible, decide it in the next 5 minutes and treat it as a test.

source.work: Amazon shareholder letter (2015)

cards.try_team: List 5 choices your team, class or family keeps putting off. Vote: one-way or two-way door? Decide every two-way door before you leave the room.

cards.hook: Do you treat a menu like a marriage? Let's see where you land.
cards.title: How You Weigh Small Choices

game.right: Fast on small, slow on big

questions.q: Choosing a show to watch tonight, I usually…

options.label: Scroll for 20+ minutes and feel unsure
Narrow it to two, then pick
Pick one in a couple of minutes; I can switch

questions.q: Picking a birthday card for a friend, I…

options.label: Read most of the rack and still doubt my pick
Check a few, then go with one
Grab one that feels right and write a good message

questions.q: When a small choice turns out wrong, I…

options.label: Feel annoyed for a day, then let it go

questions.q: When buying something with free returns, I…

options.label: Read a few reviews, then buy
Buy the good-enough one and test it

zones.label: Today: over-deliberating
zones.text: Today your answers give small choices big-choice energy. That's tiring. Try a deadline for reversible picks and save your care for the big ones.

zones.label: Today: mixed
zones.text: Your answers today are mixed: some small choices get sorted fast, others eat your time. Asking 'Can I undo this?' tips them the right way.

zones.label: Today: sorting doors
zones.text: Your answers today move fast where it's safe and slow where it matters. Keep checking that 'fast' never sneaks onto a one-way door.

cards.insight: Good deciders match speed to stakes. Barry Schwartz linked always hunting for the best option ('maximizing') to lower satisfaction, but later studies are mixed.
cards.model: Match your decision speed to how reversible the choice is, not how anxious it makes you.
cards.try_today: Set a 2-minute timer for your next small choice (food, show, outfit). When it rings, pick and don't look back.

source.work: Amazon shareholder letter (2015); The Paradox of Choice (2004)
