cards.try_team: Before your next group choice (a film, a trip, a project name), ask: can we undo it? If yes, set a 3-minute limit, pick, and move on.

cards.hook: You're 80, in a rocking chair. Which choice still stings?
cards.title: The 80-Year-Old Test

game.prompt: Look back from age 80. Which hurts more over the years: the risks you took that failed, or the chances you never took?
game.reveal: Over a lifetime, most people regret the chances they never took. Picked failed risks? That's true in the short run: fresh mistakes sting most. But they fade, while 'what if' stays open (Gilovich & Medvec, 1995).

cards.insight: Failed tries hurt, then fade: you learn and move on. Untaken chances stay open as 'what if'. It's a lens for close calls, not a license for reckless bets.
cards.model: From age 80, inaction usually hurts longer than a failed try. Let that tip close calls toward action.
cards.try_today: Write down one thing you'd regret never trying. Then write the smallest first step you could take this week.

source.work: The experience of regret (Psychological Review, 1995); The Power of Regret (2022)

cards.try_team: Each person finishes 'At 80, I'd regret our group never trying…' (club, class, family, team). Pick one and plan its first small step together.

cards.hook: The 80-year-old test can be hijacked. Can you spot when?
cards.title: Regret Test, Used Well

steps.scenario: An old friend you drifted from pops up on your feed. Messaging after 3 years feels awkward. Use the 80-year-old test. You…

options.text: Send one line: 'Saw this and thought of you'
options.feedback: Yes. The awkward bit lasts a minute. In Daniel Pink's big regret survey, lost friendships were one of the four most common kinds of regret.

options.text: Wait for them to message first
options.feedback: Very common, and they're probably waiting too. Looking back from 80, the unsent message is the one that tends to linger.

options.text: Leave it. If it mattered, it would have lasted
options.feedback: Friendships often fade from drift, not because they didn't matter. A short message is a cheap, two-way door.

steps.scenario: A mate says: 'Put all your savings into this new crypto coin. At 80 you'll regret missing out!' Does the test say yes?

options.text: No. That's fear of missing out using the test's name
options.feedback: Right. The test tips close calls toward trying. It can't turn a bet you can't afford to lose into a good one. All your savings is a one-way door.

options.text: Yes. Regrets about not acting last longest
options.feedback: Tempting logic, but that research is about chances people wished they'd tried, not bets that wiped them out. Losing your savings is a regret too.

options.text: Never take risks, then there's nothing to regret
options.feedback: Sounds safe, but from 80, a life with no tries is the regret people describe most. The skill is sizing the risk, not avoiding all of it.

cards.insight: Regrets about not acting tend to last longer than regrets about acting (Gilovich & Medvec). But the test is for meaningful tries you can afford, not all-in bets.
cards.model: Ask 'Will I regret not trying?' then 'Can I survive it failing?' Two yeses: go.
cards.try_today: Message one person you've drifted from. Keep it to one line, like 'Saw this and thought of you.'
cards.try_team: Everyone writes one 'I wish we'd tried…' for your group. Sort them: cheap to try, or a one-way door? Plan the cheapest one this month.

source.work: The experience of regret (Psychological Review, 1995); The Power of Regret (2022)

cards.hook: Your plan already failed. It's a year from now. Why did it?
cards.title: The Pre-Mortem

steps.scenario: Your group festival trip is in 2 months. Before you book anything, what's the smartest first move?

options.text: Picture it's after the trip and it was a disaster. List why.
options.feedback: Yes. That's a pre-mortem: 1) say the plan, 2) assume it already failed, 3) write reasons alone, 4) share, 5) fix the top risks. Step 2 is the key move.

options.text: Hype everyone up so nobody drops out
options.feedback: Energy helps, but it hides problems. Imagining the failure first brings them out while you can still fix them.

options.text: Wait and sort problems as they come
options.feedback: Common, but by then the easy fixes are gone. Naming risks now is cheaper.

steps.scenario: Your list: money ran out, someone's parents said no, tickets sold out, the tent broke. Which can you fix TODAY?

options.text: Someone's parents said no
options.feedback: One message tonight settles it. Fix the cheap, fast risks first.

options.text: Money ran out
options.feedback: Worth planning, but saving takes weeks. A budget chat is a good next step after the quick wins.

options.text: The tent broke
options.feedback: Good catch, but that's a check for the week before, not today.

cards.insight: The key move is assuming it already failed: that frees people to name risks. Imagining an event as done helps people find more reasons for it (Mitchell et al., 1989).
cards.model: Pretend it already failed, then ask why. Fix those reasons before you start.
cards.try_today: Take one plan for this week. Write 'It failed because…' three times. Fix the easiest reason now.

source.work: Back to the Future: Temporal Perspective in the Explanation of Events (1989); Performing a Project Premortem (Harvard Business Review, 2007)

cards.try_team: Next planning meeting or family trip chat: 5 minutes, everyone silently writes 'It failed because…', then read them out. Fix the top two risks first.

cards.hook: Coin flip: win 100 or lose 60. Why do so many people say no?
cards.title: Expected Value

game.question: Heads you win 100, tails you lose 60 (any currency). On average, how much is one flip worth?
game.explain: Expected value = chance × payoff, added up. 0.5 × 100 + 0.5 × (−60) = 50 − 30 = 20. Over many flips you'd average about +20 a flip.

cards.insight: Losses tend to feel about 1.5–2× bigger than equal gains, so many people refuse bets like this one even though they pay on average. Expected value shows the math under the feeling. One flip can still lose.
cards.model: Odds × payoff, added up. Take bets with positive value that you can afford to lose.
cards.try_today: Write two outcomes for one choice today, each with a rough chance and payoff. Multiply each pair and compare.

source.work: Pascal–Fermat letters (1654); Prospect Theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979); Thinking in Bets (2018)

cards.try_team: Take one real group choice (a fundraiser, a trip, a new rule). Everyone guesses the chance and payoff of the best and worst case. Compare the numbers aloud.

from_source.quote: Let us weigh the gain and the loss in wagering that God is. Let us estimate these two chances.
from_source.cite: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, §233 (trans. W. F. Trotter, 1910)
from_source.next_read: Pensées §233, where Pascal applies the arithmetic of stakes to the question of God (read it as philosophy, not betting advice); then the 1654 Pascal–Fermat letters on fairly dividing an interrupted game.

cards.hook: Bad outcome = bad decision? Your brain says yes. Here's why not.
cards.title: Judge the Decision, Not the Dice

steps.scenario: Your friend spent weeks choosing a second-hand laptop: read reviews, asked someone who knows tech, tested it in person. A month later it dies. They say: 'I'm so stupid for buying it.' You reply…

options.text: "You decided well with what you knew. The outcome was bad luck."
options.feedback: Yes. Separating decision quality from outcome is the whole skill. It keeps them learning instead of blaming.

options.text: "Yeah, you should have seen it coming."
options.feedback: Hindsight makes the future look obvious. If no info pointed to it, the decision wasn't the problem.

options.text: "Never buy second-hand again."
options.feedback: Understandable instinct, but it learns the wrong lesson from one roll of the dice.

steps.scenario: Now flip it. Someone drives home after drinking and arrives safely. Good decision?

options.text: No. A good outcome doesn't fix a bad bet.
options.feedback: Right. The risk was real; they just got lucky. Luck doesn't make the decision wise.

options.text: Yes, nothing bad happened.
options.feedback: That's 'resulting': grading a choice by how it turned out. It teaches people to repeat lucky mistakes.

cards.insight: Poker player Annie Duke calls it 'resulting': judging a choice only by how it turned out. Good choices sometimes lose; bad ones sometimes win. Judge the process.
cards.model: Decision quality = what you knew and how you weighed it. Outcome = decision + luck.
cards.try_today: Pick one past choice you regret. Ask: given what I knew then, was it reasonable? Write one sentence answering.

source.work: Thinking in Bets (2018)

cards.try_team: After a game, test or project, review one call in two columns: 'what we knew then' and 'what luck did'. Praise good process, even when it lost.

cards.hook: Every yes has a hidden price. Quick: would you buy these?
cards.title: What Is Not Seen

game.prompt: New trainers you love cost £60. Option A: buy them. Option B: keep the £60 for other things you want (tickets, food with friends, saving). Which do you pick?
game.reveal: No wrong answer. But in one study, just naming option B cut buyers from 75% to 55% (Frederick et al., 2009); later replications found a smaller effect. Bastiat's point, 1850: the cost you see is the price; the cost you don't see is everything else that money could have been.

cards.insight: Every yes is a no to something else: money, time, attention. Our minds rarely show what we give up unless someone names it. Bastiat called it 'what is not seen'.
cards.model: The real price of a yes is the best thing it pushes out. Name it before you agree.
cards.try_today: Before your next yes (a purchase, a meeting, an hour online), name what it pushes out. Then decide.

source.work: What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen (1850); Opportunity Cost Neglect (Journal of Consumer Research, 2009)

cards.try_team: Spending a shared budget or Saturday? Before voting, each person names what a yes pushes out. Decide only after the trade-offs are said aloud.

from_source.quote: the first only is immediate; it manifests itself simultaneously with its cause—it is seen. The others unfold in succession—they are not seen
from_source.cite: Frédéric Bastiat, That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen (1850), opening paragraph; 19th-century English translation
from_source.next_read: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen, introduction and ch. 1 'The Broken Window'

cards.hook: A free ticket. What did it really cost? 1 in 5 economists got it.
cards.title: The Free Ticket Puzzle

game.question: You win a free ticket to Band A (you can't sell it). Same night, Band B costs £40, and seeing them is worth £50 to you. You go to Band A. What did you give up?
game.explain: £10. Going to A means giving up B. Seeing B was worth £50 to you but would have cost £40, so you give up £50 − £40 = £10 of value. When 199 economists got this puzzle (with 0, 10, 40 or 50 as options), only about 22% picked 10 (Ferraro & Taylor, 2005).

cards.insight: Opportunity cost is the value of the best thing you give up, minus what it would have cost you. Even experts skip it. Some argue the puzzle's wording is unclear, so hold it lightly.
cards.model: 'Free' isn't free: the cost is the best option you give up, minus its own price.
cards.try_today: Pick one 'free' plan this week. Write what you'll miss to do it, and decide if it still wins.
cards.try_team: Pose the ticket puzzle to your group and compare guesses. Then ask: what 'free' thing are we doing that quietly costs us a better option?

source.work: Do Economists Recognize an Opportunity Cost When They Sense One? (Topics in Economic Analysis & Policy, 2005)

cards.hook: Pick one topic you give advice on. Are you inside your circle?
cards.title: Circle of Competence

questions.q: Think of one topic you give advice on. I've had real results in it, not just opinions.
I can explain where my knowledge on it stops.
People who know more than me would mostly agree with my advice.
I feel sure when I talk about it.
I'd make a big decision on it without asking anyone.
I often say 'I'm not sure' on this topic.

results.name: Outside both (early)
results.text: Today your dot sits outside both circles: your answers say this topic is new to you, and you know it. That's honest. Learn from people with results, and keep decisions small and reversible.

C.name: Confidence ahead of proof
C.text: Your answers put confidence ahead of track record on this topic. That's where mistakes live. Before big calls, ask someone with results to check you.

K.name: Proof ahead of confidence
K.text: Your answers show more track record than you claim on this topic. Humility is good, but your knowledge could help others. Share it, and say where it ends.

CK.name: Inside the circle
CK.text: Your answers line up confidence and proof on this topic. Your job now is guarding the border: notice when a question drifts past what you've tested.

cards.insight: Warren Buffett's rule: the size of your circle matters less than knowing where its edge is. Socrates said wisdom starts with knowing what you don't know.
cards.model: Know the edge of what you know. Act boldly inside it; ask, test, or pass outside it.
cards.try_today: Write one topic where you're truly competent and one where you only feel confident. Ask an expert one question on the second.

source.work: Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter (1996); Plato, Apology

cards.try_team: Each person names one topic they've truly tested and one they only feel sure about. Make a 'who to ask' list from it and use it next time you're stuck.

from_source.quote: he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.
from_source.cite: Plato, Apology 21d (trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1871)
from_source.next_read: Plato, Apology 20e–23c: the oracle at Delphi and Socrates' search for a wiser man

cards.hook: You paid double for the worse weekend. Do you still go?
cards.title: The Pricier, Worse Trip

game.prompt: You booked two weekend trips by mistake, same dates, no refunds. Trip A cost twice as much. Trip B is the one you'd enjoy more. You can only go on one. Which?
choices: Trip B, the one I'd enjoy more
game.reveal: Trip B. Both payments are gone whichever you pick, so only the weekend ahead counts. Yet when Arkes & Blumer (1985) gave students this puzzle, more than half chose the pricier trip they'd enjoy less.

cards.insight: Money already spent can't be won back by suffering through the worse option. It just feels like waste if you don't 'use' it.
cards.model: Spent is spent. Choose as if you were starting fresh today.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you keep only because it cost a lot (a gadget, a course, clothes). Ask: would I choose it today for free? Act on the answer.
cards.try_team: List one project, club or plan your group keeps 'because we've put so much in'. Ask together: starting fresh today, would we pick it? Decide openly.

source.work: The Psychology of Sunk Cost (Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1985)

cards.hook: Quitting feels like wasting it all. But is the waste already done?
cards.title: Past Cost, Future Choice

steps.scenario: You're 2 years into guitar lessons your parents paid for. You've stopped enjoying it and want to try drawing instead. The thought 'all that money' stops you. You…

options.text: Ask: if I were choosing a hobby today, which would I pick?
options.feedback: Yes. The lessons are paid either way. Talk it through with your parents: the skills you built aren't lost, and the next hour is what's up for grabs.

options.text: Keep going so the money isn't wasted
options.feedback: A very human pull. But the money is spent whether you continue or not. More unhappy hours don't bring it back.

options.text: Quit everything at once, today
options.feedback: Clear-headed, but you can test it first: a month of drawing beside guitar shows what you actually prefer.

steps.scenario: At work, a project is 18 months in. New numbers say it will likely lose money even if finished. A colleague says: 'We can't stop now, look how much we've invested.' You…

options.text: Ask what it costs to finish versus what it's now likely to return
options.feedback: Right. Only future costs and gains decide. The 18 months are gone; the next 6 aren't. Name it kindly: stopping isn't the same as admitting failure.

options.text: Agree. Stopping would waste 18 months
options.feedback: Understandable, and common in organisations. But finishing a losing project adds to the loss rather than rescuing what's spent.

options.text: Blame whoever started it
options.feedback: Tempting, but blame makes people defend past choices harder. In Staw's 1976 study, people who made the first call kept funding it more.

steps.scenario: Your 15-year-old car needs a big repair, the third this year. 'I've already spent so much fixing it,' you think. You…

options.text: Compare: cost of this repair and the next few, versus replacing it
options.feedback: Yes. Past repairs don't count; they're paid. The question is which option costs less from here, for the reliability you need.

options.text: Fix it, or the earlier repairs were for nothing
options.feedback: Those repairs gave you years of driving, so they weren't for nothing. They just can't vote on today's choice.

options.text: Scrap it right away
options.feedback: Maybe, but past spending shouldn't push you out either. Sometimes one more repair really is the cheapest road ahead.

cards.insight: Past costs pull us to keep going. The pull is real but modest in studies. And staying is fine when the future says so.
cards.model: Ask 'From here, is this the best use of my next hour or next bit of money?' Ignore what's gone.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you're sticking with. Write one line: 'If I hadn't started yet, would I start today?' Act if the answer is a clear no.
cards.try_team: Before your next review of a long project, ban the phrase 'we've already invested'. Discuss only remaining cost and likely payoff.

source.work: Toward a Positive Theory of Consumer Choice (1980); Knee-deep in the Big Muddy (1976)

cards.hook: You say you feel 'bad'. Can you do anything with that word?
cards.title: Name It to Tame It

game.prompt: Could you act on this feeling-word?

items.text: "I feel bad."
items.why: Bad how? Sad, guilty, tired, scared? Each one needs a different fix.

items.text: "I'm embarrassed about what I said at dinner, and also just tired."
items.why: Two clear parts: one needs a quick repair, the other needs sleep.

items.text: "Ugh. Everything."
items.why: 'Everything' is too big to touch. Shrink it to one feeling, one cause.

items.text: "I'm anxious because I haven't opened the bill yet."
items.why: Now the next step is obvious: open the bill.

items.text: "I'm stressed."
items.why: Stressed could be overloaded, unsure, or lonely. Dig one layer down.

items.text: "I feel left out because nobody replied in the group chat."
items.why: Specific feeling plus cause. You can check the story or reach out.

cards.insight: Precise feelings come with handles; vague ones don't. People who tell emotions apart in finer detail tend to cope better with stress. Lisa Feldman Barrett calls it emotional granularity.
cards.model: A vague feeling is a fog. A named feeling is a map with a next step on it.
cards.try_today: Next time you think 'I feel bad', swap it for two exact words, like 'disappointed and hungry'. Then act on the easier one.

source.work: How Emotions Are Made (2017); Kashdan, Barrett & McKnight, 'Unpacking Emotion Differentiation' (2015)

cards.try_team: Go round the group: each person names today's mood in two exact words (not 'fine' or 'busy'). No fixing, just listening. Three minutes.

cards.hook: Saying 'I'm angry' out loud: does it fuel the anger or cool it?
cards.title: The Label Effect

game.prompt: In a brain-scan study, people looked at angry and scared faces. Some just matched the faces. Others picked a word for the emotion, like 'angry'. What happened in the alarm center of their brain?
choices: Naming it made the alarm louder
game.reveal: Naming it calmed it. Picking the emotion word lowered activity in the amygdala, the brain's alarm (Lieberman et al., 2007). Guessed 'louder'? Fair: venting can stoke anger. But a calm label isn't venting.

cards.insight: Naming a feeling gives your thinking brain a job. It won't erase the feeling, but it can take the edge off enough for you to choose what to do next.
cards.model: Words are a dimmer switch for feelings: name it and the alarm quiets down.
cards.try_today: When something stings today, finish this sentence in your head or in a note: 'Right now I feel ___ because ___.'

source.work: Lieberman et al., 'Putting Feelings Into Words', Psychological Science (2007)

cards.try_team: Open a class, meeting or family dinner with a 30-second round: 'Right now I feel ___ because ___.' Anyone can say 'pass'.

from_source.quote: An emotion, which is a passion, ceases to be a passion, as soon as we form a clear and distinct idea thereof.
from_source.cite: Spinoza, Ethics (1677), Part V, Proposition 3, trans. R. H. M. Elwes (1883)
from_source.next_read: Spinoza, Ethics, Part V, Propositions 1-10 and their proofs (Elwes translation)

cards.hook: You fired off that reply in 4 seconds. Where did your choice go?
cards.title: The Pause

game.prompt: Something just made you furious. Does this move buy you time, or keep you hot?

items.text: Three slow breaths, longer out than in
items.why: Slow exhales calm the body's alarm. Calming moves reliably lower anger in studies.

items.text: Punching a pillow to 'get it all out'
items.why: Feels like release, but in studies hitting things kept anger higher, not lower.

items.text: Saying to yourself: 'I feel disrespected'
items.why: Naming the feeling gives your thinking brain a job. That buys you seconds.

items.text: Rereading the message five more times
items.why: Each reread replays the sting. That's rumination, and it keeps the fire fed.

items.text: Typing your reply in your notes app, not the chat
items.why: You get to say it without sending it. Decide later if it should go.

items.text: Firing back fast 'to clear the air'
items.why: A fast reply comes from the alarm, not from you. The air rarely clears.

items.text: Leaving the room for ten minutes
items.why: Time and distance let the first jolt fade before you choose.

cards.insight: You can't stop the first jolt, but you can widen the gap. Calming moves help; venting tends to keep anger hot. (The famous 'gap' quote isn't actually in Viktor Frankl's books.)
cards.model: Feel it fast, act on it slow. The pause is where your choice lives.
cards.try_today: Before your next heated reply, take three slow breaths with longer exhales than inhales, then decide: now, later, or never.

source.work: Emotional Intelligence (1995); Bushman, PSPB (2002); Kjærvik & Bushman, Clinical Psychology Review (2024)

cards.try_team: Agree a team or family rule: no replies to heated messages for 10 minutes. Try it for one week, then talk about what changed.

from_source.quote: …not to be hurried away with the appearance. For if you once gain time and respite, you will more easily command yourself.
from_source.cite: Epictetus, Enchiridion, chapter 20, trans. Elizabeth Carter (1758)
from_source.next_read: Epictetus, Enchiridion, chapters 1, 5 and 20 (each under a page)

cards.hook: Four words at 11pm, and your brain writes the worst ending.
cards.title: Pause Before Send

steps.scenario: 11:04pm. A text from a close friend: 'We need to talk tomorrow.' Your stomach drops. You…

options.text: Reply right away: 'Is something wrong?? Whatever it is, I can explain.'
options.feedback: Totally human: the worry wants an answer now. But replying from panic often adds stress for both of you.

options.text: Notice the dread, name it ('I'm scared I upset them'), and breathe before doing anything.
options.feedback: Yes. You felt the jolt and didn't let it drive. Naming the fear can take a little of its edge off (affect labelling).

options.text: Lie awake replaying everything you said to them this month.
options.feedback: Your brain is trying to protect you by rehearsing threats. It rarely helps, and it costs sleep.

steps.scenario: You've paused. The worry is still there. What now?

options.text: Send a short, calm reply ('Sure, when suits you?') or decide to answer in the morning. Then put the phone down.
options.feedback: Calm, clear, done. Either way you made a choice, and you're responding to the text, not the worst story about it.

options.text: Write a long message defending everything you've done lately.
options.feedback: Understandable, but you're answering an accusation nobody made yet. Save it for the actual talk if needed.

options.text: Keep rereading the text in bed, hunting for a hidden meaning.
options.feedback: Very common. But the text holds no more information than before, so rereading mostly feeds the worry and costs sleep.

cards.insight: A vague message plus a tired brain at night breeds worst-case stories. Pause, and answer what was said. Sending one yourself? Add a line of context, or wait till morning.
cards.model: Respond to what was said, not to the scariest story your brain wrote about it.
cards.try_today: Today, before you send any message that could worry someone, add one sentence of context.

source.work: Emotional Intelligence (1995); Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011); Lieberman et al., Putting feelings into words (Psychological Science, 2007)

cards.try_team: Managers, teachers, parents: agree that no one sends a bare 'we need to talk'. Always add one line of context ('Nothing bad, just planning').

cards.hook: Would you talk to a friend the way you talked to yourself today?
cards.title: Inner Critic or Inner Coach?

questions.q: You make a silly mistake (a wrong answer, a missed bus, a typo everyone saw). Your first inner words are…

options.label: 'Oops. Anyone could do that. What's the fix?'

questions.q: You're struggling and others seem fine. You think…

options.label: 'Lots of people struggle with this, even if they don't show it.'

questions.q: When you feel low, you tend to…

options.label: Get busy so I don't dwell
Notice it, then do one small thing I need

questions.q: Being kind to yourself after failing feels like…

zones.label: Your critic was loud today
zones.text: Today your inner voice leaned tough, often because it wants to keep you safe or improving. You can keep the high standards and drop the insults: try how a good coach would say it. That voice learned to be harsh for a reason. You can retrain it one sentence at a time.

zones.label: Mixed
zones.text: Today's answers swing between harsh and fair. Notice which situations switch the critic on, so you can catch it sooner.

zones.label: Coach-leaning
zones.text: Today's answers lean kind: setbacks met with warmth and a plan. That's a skill, not softness. It's worth keeping on bad days too.

cards.insight: Kristin Neff's self-compassion: kindness to yourself, remembering everyone struggles, seeing pain clearly. It isn't going soft: in one study it led people to study longer after failing.
cards.model: High standards, kind voice. Coaches correct mistakes without insulting the player.
cards.try_today: Write one sentence to yourself about a recent mistake, exactly as you'd write it to a friend who made the same one.

source.work: Neff, 'Self-Compassion' (2003); Breines & Chen, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin (2012)

cards.try_team: In a class, team or family review, each person names one recent mistake and what a kind coach would say about it. The leader goes first.

cards.hook: Is being kind to yourself just a nicer word for making excuses?
cards.title: Kind, Not Soft

game.prompt: You just failed at something. Is this real self-compassion, or a look-alike?

items.text: "I failed the test. That hurts, and lots of people fail it the first time."
items.why: Kind and honest: it names the pain and remembers you're not the only one.

items.text: "The test was stupid anyway. I'm too smart for it."
items.why: That's ego protection. It dodges the pain, so there's nothing left to learn from.

items.text: "Why does this always happen to me? Nobody has it this bad."
items.why: Self-pity cuts you off from others. Self-compassion says: other people struggle too.

items.text: "I messed up. What would help me do better next time?"
items.why: Kindness plus a plan. Good coaches comfort and correct in the same breath.

items.text: "I'll skip practice for the rest of the month. I deserve it."
items.why: Feels kind today. Real kindness asks what helps you in the long run.

items.text: "I'm worn out. A short rest, then I'll try again."
items.why: Meeting a real need without dropping the goal. That's the balance.

cards.insight: Neff separates self-compassion from self-pity, excuses and ego-boosting: it faces the mistake and stays kind. Studies link it to better well-being, though most are correlational.
cards.model: Self-compassion isn't lowering the bar. It's being on your own side while you climb.
cards.try_today: Next time you mess up, say one sentence that names the pain and one that names a next step, out loud or in your notes.
cards.try_team: After a loss or mistake, go round: each person says one honest 'that stung' and one 'next time we'll…'. No blame, no pretending it was fine.

source.work: Neff, 'Self-Compassion: An Alternative Conceptualization', Self and Identity (2003); MacBeth & Gumley, Clinical Psychology Review (2012)

from_source.quote: What progress, you ask, have I made? I have begun to be a friend to myself.
from_source.cite: Seneca (quoting Hecato), Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 6 'On Sharing Knowledge', trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
from_source.next_read: Seneca, Moral Letters, Letter 6 'On Sharing Knowledge' (two pages)

cards.hook: You put it off again. Guilt or forgiveness: which gets it done?
cards.title: Procrastination Is a Feeling Problem

game.prompt: Students who procrastinated studying for a first exam were later asked how much they had forgiven themselves for it. Before the next exam, who procrastinated less?
choices: Those who stayed hard on themselves
game.reveal: The forgivers procrastinated less before the next exam (Wohl, Pychyl & Bennett, 2010). Picked 'hard on themselves'? Guilt feels like it should push us. It's one correlational study of 119 students, but it fits a wider pattern: guilt keeps the task tied to a bad feeling.

cards.insight: We rarely avoid the task itself; we avoid the feeling it gives us. Delay is a quick mood fix that costs later. Beating yourself up adds more bad feeling, so it often backfires.
cards.model: Often you're avoiding a feeling, not the task. Shrink the feeling and the task gets easier to start.
cards.try_today: Name the feeling the task gives you, forgive yesterday's delay in one sentence, then work on it for just 5 minutes.

source.work: Wohl, Pychyl & Bennett, Personality and Individual Differences (2010); Sirois & Pychyl (2013)

cards.try_team: Each person names one task they're avoiding and the feeling it brings, in one word. Then everyone picks a 5-minute first step and does it now.

from_source.quote: Lay hold of to-day's task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow's.
from_source.cite: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 1 'On Saving Time', trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
from_source.next_read: Seneca, Moral Letters, Letter 1 'On Saving Time' (one page)

cards.hook: The task opens. Your thumb finds your phone. What just happened?
cards.title: Who Gets the Yucky Stuff?

steps.scenario: You finally open the thing you've been dodging: an essay, a tax form, a tricky message. 'Ugh, where do I even start?' Your thumb drifts to your phone. Best move?

options.text: Wait until you're in the mood for it.
options.feedback: A very common hope. But the mood usually turns up after you start, not before. Waiting lets the 'ugh' decide.

options.text: Name the feeling ('confused'), then shrink the step: write down the one question you're stuck on.
options.feedback: Yes. Confusion is the feeling; a tiny, clear step is the fix. You repair the mood by starting, not by escaping.

options.text: Tell yourself off: 'You always do this.'
options.feedback: Understandable, but it piles guilt on top of the 'ugh'. More bad feeling makes the task even easier to avoid.

options.text: Promise to do all of it tomorrow at 6am.
options.feedback: Future-you always seems tougher. But they'll meet the same 'ugh', with less time. That's the next question.

steps.scenario: Real study: people chose how much of a disgusting drink (ketchup mixed with soy sauce) to drink 'for science'. Who did they sign up for the biggest dose?

options.text: Themselves, right now
options.feedback: Good guess, but no: today-you got the smallest dose. We shield our present self from bad feelings.

options.text: Their future self, weeks later
options.feedback: Right. Future-you got about as much as a stranger would (Pronin et al., 2008). We hand future selves the yucky stuff, and our tasks too.

options.text: No difference
options.feedback: Fair guess, but there was one: the present self got the smallest dose, future selves got about as much as strangers.

cards.insight: Delay is mood repair: it swaps a bad feeling now for a bigger one later, and hands it to future-you. Starting tiny fixes the feeling; waiting for motivation rarely does.
cards.model: Don't wait to feel ready. Start small, and the feeling follows.
cards.try_today: Pick one task you're dodging. Name its feeling in one word, then do 5 minutes of the first step. You may stop after 5.
cards.try_team: Each person writes the task they're dodging and its feeling ('boring', 'scary'). Pairs agree a 5-minute first step for each. Check in tomorrow.

source.work: Sirois & Pychyl, Social and Personality Psychology Compass (2013); Pronin, Olivola & Kennedy, PSPB (2008)

cards.hook: A week of sadder posts. How much sadder did people write?
cards.title: Moods Are Contagious

game.question: In 2012, Facebook ran a one-week experiment on 689,003 users. For one group, it hid some of the positive posts in their feeds. By how much did the share of positive words in that group's own posts drop?
game.explain: About 0.1 percentage points (Kramer, Guillory & Hancock, 2014). Real, but tiny, and measured in words, not felt mood. Users never agreed to take part.

cards.insight: Moods can spread, but in this famous study the effect was tiny: big crowds make tiny effects detectable, not important. If a feed leaves you heavier, that's information, not weakness. Notice the mood you bring, without blaming yourself.
cards.model: Moods are weather. Notice what front you walked into, and what front you bring with you.
cards.try_today: Mute or unfollow one account that reliably drags your mood, then notice how your next scroll feels.

source.work: Hatfield, Cacioppo & Rapson, Emotional Contagion (1994); Kramer et al., PNAS (2014)

cards.try_team: Before a meeting or class, everyone names their mood in one word. Leaders: your mood in the first 2 minutes is the weather. Check it first.

cards.hook: You owe someone a thank-you. Why is it still unsent?
cards.title: Thanks Land Better Than You Think

game.prompt: In experiments, people wrote a short thank-you letter to someone who had mattered to them: a teacher, a friend, a colleague. They guessed how the reader would feel. Then the readers were asked. What did the writers get wrong?
choices: They overrated how happy it would make the reader
They underrated the reader's joy and overrated the awkwardness
game.reveal: Writers lowballed how happy and surprised readers felt, and overrated how awkward it would be (Kumar & Epley, 2018). Picked 'overrated'? Many of us fear thanks will seem over the top. Readers mostly just felt good.

cards.insight: Writers fret about finding the right words; readers mostly notice the warmth. That gap keeps many thank-yous unsent.
cards.model: Your thanks is worth more to them than it feels to you. Send it imperfect.
cards.try_today: Write three sentences to someone who helped you: what they did, when, and what changed for you. Send it today.
cards.try_team: Each person spends 5 minutes writing a specific thank-you to someone outside the room: a teacher, ex-colleague, neighbour. Send before you leave.

source.work: Kumar & Epley, 'Undervaluing Gratitude', Psychological Science (2018)

cards.hook: A gratitude list can quietly go stale. Is yours on autopilot?
cards.title: Three Good Things, Done Right

steps.scenario: For three weeks you've written three good things each night: a test that went well, a meeting that ran smoothly, a call with your sister. Lately it's 'food, bed, phone' and it feels like homework. Best move?

options.text: Push on: every night, no excuses.
options.feedback: Not quite. A list on autopilot stops making you notice anything. In one small study, counting blessings once a week beat three times a week (Lyubomirsky et al., 2005).

options.text: Write less often, but get specific: one fresh good thing and why it happened.
options.feedback: Yes. Fresh and specific beats long and routine. The original exercise also asks why each good thing happened (Seligman et al., 2005), which makes you look closer.

options.text: Quit: it clearly doesn't work for you.
options.feedback: Fair to question it: the effects are modest. But boredom often means the format went stale, not the idea. Change the format before you drop it.

steps.scenario: A friend, a coworker or your grown-up child says they've had a miserable week. You're tempted to say: 'Look on the bright side, you have so much to be grateful for.' Best move?

options.text: Say it: gratitude helps.
options.feedback: Kind aim, poor timing. Handed over from outside, gratitude can sound like 'your feelings are wrong' and add guilt to a bad week.

options.text: Listen first and name what they seem to feel. Leave gratitude for them to choose.
options.feedback: Right. Gratitude works as a choice, not an order. Hard feelings first; good things can sit beside them later.

options.text: Share your own gratitude list as an example.
options.feedback: Well meant, but it turns their bad week into your lesson. Listening first does more.

cards.insight: Gratitude lists give many people a small lift, not a fix-all. Early big results shrank against fair comparisons, so it's contested. Keep it fresh, and keep it voluntary.
cards.model: Notice good things specifically and freshly, and never use gratitude to cancel a hard feeling.
cards.try_today: Tonight write one good thing from today in detail, plus one line on why it happened. Skip it if you're not feeling it.
cards.try_team: End a class, shift or family dinner with each person naming one specific thing that went right this week and who made it happen.

source.work: Seligman et al., American Psychologist (2005); Lyubomirsky, Sheldon & Schkade, Review of General Psychology (2005); Davis et al., Journal of Counseling Psychology (2016)

cards.hook: When something's hard, what's the first sentence in your head?
cards.title: Fixed vs Growth Mindset

questions.q: Your first try at something new (a tool, a skill, a subject) goes badly. Your first thought is…

options.label: I'm just bad at this kind of thing.
Ugh. Maybe I'm not cut out for this.
My method didn't work. Time for a new one.

questions.q: A friend is way better than you at something you care about.

options.label: They're a natural. I'll never catch up.
Some of it is talent, some is practice.
It stings, but I'm curious how they got there.

questions.q: Someone gives you blunt feedback on something you made (an essay, a drawing, a dish).

options.label: It feels like a verdict on me.
I get defensive first, then think.
It's free information about the work.

questions.q: Picking between an easy task and a stretch task (a game level, a recipe, a project), you usually…

options.label: Easy when I'm drained, stretch when I have energy.
Take the stretch. That's where I grow.

zones.label: Leaning fixed today (on these topics)
zones.text: Today's answers treat hard things as tests of who you are. That's tiring, and very common. Next time, try treating it as a test of your method instead.

zones.label: Mixed today (like most people)
zones.text: Your answers mix both mindsets, as most people's do. Notice which topics flip you to 'fixed': that's where the work is. Fun fact: you can be growth for football and fixed for maths on the same day.

zones.label: Leaning growth today
zones.text: Today's answers treat ability as trainable. Pair that with real changes of method, not just 'try harder', and it pays off.

cards.insight: Mindset shifts by topic; it isn't one setting. Big studies find teaching it has small average effects, near zero in some, a bit larger for struggling students. A lens, not magic.
cards.model: Treat a struggle as feedback on your method, not a verdict on your worth.
cards.try_today: Pick one 'I'm just not a ___ person' belief and write one different method you haven't tried yet.

source.work: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success (2006)

cards.try_team: Each person shares one 'I'm not a ___ person' belief. The group suggests one new method to try for it. Fix methods, not people.

cards.hook: "You're so smart" or "How did you do it?" Which helps more?
cards.title: Praise the Process

steps.scenario: Your 11-year-old cousin aces a tricky maths quiz and shows you, beaming. You say…

options.text: "Wow, you're so smart!"
options.feedback: Totally natural and kind. The catch: if 'smart' is the reason, a future hard problem can feel like proof they aren't.

options.text: "Nice! What did you do to crack the hard ones?"
options.feedback: This points at what they did, something they can repeat next time. It also gets them talking.

options.text: "Cool, but was it an easy quiz?"
options.feedback: Probably meant as a joke, but it shrinks the win. Celebrate first, calibrate later.

steps.scenario: Next week they fail a quiz and say, "I'm just bad at maths." You reply…

options.text: "No you're not, you're brilliant!"
options.feedback: Warm, but it argues with their feeling and gives them nothing to do next.

options.text: "Not everyone's a maths person, it's fine."
options.feedback: Kind intent, but it confirms the fixed story they just told themselves.

options.text: "This topic isn't clicking yet. What did you try? What could you try next?"
options.feedback: Accepts the feeling, adds 'yet', and turns it into a plan. That's the growth move.

cards.insight: A famous 1998 study found kids praised for being smart later picked easier tasks. A large 2019 replication (Li & Bates) didn't find that effect. Praising what someone did is still low-risk and gives them something to repeat.
cards.model: Praise what someone did (strategy, effort, choices), not what they are.
cards.try_today: Give one person a compliment today that names a specific thing they did, not a trait they have.

source.work: Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance (1998); Li & Bates, JEP: General (2019)

cards.try_team: At dinner, in class or at work (say, in a code review), go round once: each person names one specific thing someone else did well this week, and how.

cards.hook: "I can't do this." One small word changes the whole sentence.
cards.title: The Power of 'Yet'

steps.scenario: Your friend sighs, "I can't code." Which reply helps most?

options.text: "Yeah, it's hard."
options.feedback: Honest and kind, but it agrees with the stop sign and leaves no next step.

options.text: "You can't code yet. What's the first tiny thing you'd learn?"
options.feedback: Same facts, new story: 'yet' puts them on a path, and the question gives them a first step.

options.text: "Sure you can!"
options.feedback: Warm, but it argues with how they feel and gives them nothing to do next.

steps.scenario: You catch yourself thinking, "I'm bad at public speaking." Rewrite it:

options.text: "I'm bad at it, full stop."
options.feedback: Very common, and it turns one rough moment into a permanent label. Try adding a time word.

options.text: "I'm not good at it yet. Next step: a 2-minute talk to a friend."
options.feedback: Honest about today, open about tomorrow, and it ends in something you can actually do.

options.text: "Speaking doesn't matter anyway."
options.feedback: Understandable armour, but it shuts the door instead of finding a first step.

cards.insight: No lab study here, just a story: Carol Dweck describes a Chicago school that graded unfinished courses 'Not Yet' instead of 'Fail'. 'Yet' doesn't change your skill; it changes the story about time, so the next try feels worth making.
cards.model: Add 'yet': it turns a verdict into a stage on a path.
cards.try_today: Catch one 'I can't…' you say today and finish it out loud with '…yet, and my next step is ___'.

source.work: The Power of Believing That You Can Improve, TED talk (2014)

cards.try_team: For one week, when anyone in your family, class or team says 'I can't', the others add a friendly '…yet?' and ask for the next step.

from_source.quote: Men become builders by building and lyre-players by playing the lyre.
from_source.cite: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1, trans. W. D. Ross (1908)
from_source.next_read: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapters 1-4 (on how virtues are acquired by practice)

cards.hook: Talent or not giving up: who survived the army's hardest summer?
cards.title: Grit vs Talent

game.prompt: New cadets at West Point, the US army academy, face 'Beast Barracks', a brutal first summer. Which better predicted who stayed?
game.reveal: The grit survey, in that one 2007 study, beat the academy's own score at predicting who finished. But dropouts were rare, and later reviews found the effect smaller than the hype: it's mostly the 'keep going' part that matters.

cards.insight: Sticking with a goal through boredom matters, but grit is contested: a 2017 review of 88 samples found modest links to success, mostly from the perseverance part. One ingredient, not the recipe.
cards.model: Keep going on the boring bits. That part of grit holds up; the rest is oversold.
cards.try_today: Name one long-term goal and write the single smallest action that keeps it alive this week.

source.work: Grit: Perseverance and passion for long-term goals (2007); Much ado about grit (2017)

cards.try_team: Each person names one long goal and the boring part they keep skipping. Pair up and agree one 10-minute step on that part this week.

cards.hook: Sprinting, wandering, or building for the long haul: which is you now?
cards.title: Your Grit Map

questions.q: I've cared about the same big goal for over a year.
New ideas often pull me away from old projects.
I know what I'm working toward in the next few years.
Setbacks don't knock me off course for long.
Lately, my energy for projects fades after a few weeks.
Lately, I've been able to finish what I start, even the boring parts.

results.name: Explore mode
results.text: Today's answers show you're still sampling, and that's valid: interests are often found by trying things. Pick one thread to follow for a month. Low staying power often reflects energy and circumstances, not character.

P.name: Spark mode
P.text: Your answers show a clear interest, with effort that comes in bursts. Shrink the daily step so small you can't skip it.

S.name: Steady mode
S.text: Your answers show real staying power. Check that it's aimed at something you actually chose, not just what's in front of you.

PS.name: Long-haul mode
PS.text: Today's answers show stable interest plus staying power. Protect it by also knowing when a path stops serving you: grit includes smart quitting.

cards.insight: Duckworth splits grit in two: keeping an interest over time, and pushing through setbacks. How much grit predicts success is debated, so use this as a mirror, not a score.
cards.model: Grit = a direction you keep + effort you sustain. Build the weaker half.
cards.try_today: Write your one-sentence 'top goal' on a sticky note and put it where you'll see it tomorrow morning.

source.work: Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance (2016)

cards.try_team: Everyone writes one goal for this term on a card and swaps with a partner, who checks in weekly: 'Still your goal? What's the next step?'

cards.hook: Played guitar for 10 years? Why might you be no better than year 2?
cards.title: Deliberate Practice

game.prompt: You've got 10 minutes with your guitar. What order levels you up?
items: Pick the bit you always mess up
Do just that bit, slightly too hard
Check what went wrong, then go again
game.explain: Playing songs you know = staying still. Drilling the bit you fumble = getting better.

cards.insight: Hours alone don't make experts; focused work on weak spots helps far more. The '10,000-hour rule' oversimplifies Ericsson, and a 2014 meta-analysis found practice explains only part of skill gaps.
cards.model: Not more practice: harder, narrower practice with feedback.
cards.try_today: Pick a skill you use often, name its weakest sub-part, and drill only that for 10 focused minutes.

source.work: Peak (2016); Deliberate practice and performance: a meta-analysis (2014)

cards.try_team: Pick one thing your team, class or family does often (a pitch, a dish, a match). Name its weakest part and run 3 quick rounds on just that, with feedback.

cards.hook: You've played one game for 500 hours. Are you actually getting better?
cards.title: Practice or Just Repetition?

game.prompt: Does this grow the skill, or just keep it where it is?

items.text: Playing ranked matches every night without ever watching your replays.
items.why: Hours on autopilot keep your rank where it is. Replays show the exact mistake.

items.text: Replaying the 3 bars you always fumble, slowly, until they're clean.
items.why: One weak spot, just past your level, with instant feedback from your own ears. Textbook.

items.text: Driving to work every day for 20 years.
items.why: Keeps you fluent, but rarely sharpens skills like skid control. That needs targeted practice.

items.text: Going back over a chess game you lost to find the move where it went wrong.
items.why: Finding the exact error and fixing it is the heart of deliberate practice.

items.text: A 400-day streak on a language app, always on the easy setting.
items.why: Streaks build habit, which matters. But if it never stretches you, it's mostly upkeep.

items.text: Rewriting a great article from your notes, then comparing it to the original.
items.why: Ben Franklin's own trick: the original shows exactly where your version falls short.

items.text: Cooking a new dish, then asking someone for one thing to change.
items.why: A stretch plus honest feedback. Asking for just one thing keeps it usable.

cards.insight: Ericsson argued that once a skill feels automatic, more hours add little; growth comes from narrow, slightly-too-hard work with feedback. Later reviews found practice matters but explains less than he claimed (Macnamara et al., 2014).
cards.model: Hours keep a skill. Feedback on your weakest part grows it.
cards.try_today: Pick a hobby where you've stopped improving. Find the one moment you always get wrong and practise only that for 10 minutes.
cards.try_team: Pick one thing your class, team or family does on repeat. Ask: where are we just repeating? Choose one weak spot to practise, with feedback.

source.work: Peak (2016); The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (1791); Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald, Psychological Science (2014)

from_source.quote: without looking at the book, try'd to compleat the papers again
from_source.cite: Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography, Part One (written 1771), on rewriting Spectator essays
from_source.next_read: Franklin's Autobiography, Part One: the passage where he teaches himself to write from The Spectator

cards.hook: You just messed up in front of people. What you do next matters.
cards.title: Mistakes as Data

steps.scenario: You posted the wrong date for a friend's party in the group chat. Two people already planned around it. Someone points it out. Your first move…

options.text: Quietly delete the message and hope nobody noticed.
options.feedback: Very human. But the lesson stays hidden, and people may still plan around the wrong date.

options.text: Post a short correction: what was wrong, the right date, sorry for the hassle.
options.feedback: Clean and calm. Owning it fast builds trust and stops the error spreading.

options.text: Apologise at length about how useless you are.
options.feedback: Harsh self-talk feels responsible but uses energy you need for the fix. Be kind to yourself and precise about the error.

steps.scenario: That evening the mistake is still on your mind. What do you do with it?

options.text: Replay it and feel bad until it fades.
options.feedback: Understandable, but feeling bad isn't the same as learning. The pain is a signal, not the lesson.

options.text: Write 3 lines: what happened, why, what I'll change.
options.feedback: This is the alchemy: a mistake turned into a rule you keep, like 'check the date before I post'.

options.text: Decide you're just hopeless at organising things.
options.feedback: One slip is one data point, not a verdict on you. Look for the cause you can change.

cards.insight: A mistake shows exactly where your method breaks. Ray Dalio sums it up as pain plus reflection equals progress. The trick is to study the cause, not punish yourself.
cards.model: Mistake → cause → new rule. Keep the lesson, drop the shame.
cards.try_today: Write down one recent mistake in 3 lines: what happened, why, and one rule you'll follow next time.

source.work: Principles: Life and Work (2017)

cards.try_team: After a slip at work, school or home, hold a 5-minute no-blame review: what happened, why, and one rule you add. Talk about the process, not the person.

from_source.quote: To have faults and not to reform them, this, indeed, should be pronounced having faults.
from_source.cite: Confucius, Analects XV.29 (trans. James Legge, 1861)
from_source.next_read: Analects, Book I.8 ('When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them') and Book XV

cards.hook: What makes a good day at work or study? Bosses guessed wrong.
cards.title: The Progress Principle

game.prompt: 669 managers ranked five things that motivate people: praise, rewards, clear goals, support, and making progress. Where did 'making progress' land?
game.reveal: Dead last. Yet in nearly 12,000 diary entries from 238 workers, making progress on meaningful work was the strongest booster of their best days. Same goes for school: a tiny visible win beats a big vague goal.

cards.insight: We underrate small steps, yet in 12,000 diary entries visible progress lifted motivation most. Keeping a record of your wins gives you evidence to reach for on hard days.
cards.model: Progress you can see is the strongest fuel. Keep evidence of it.
cards.try_today: Start a 'wins' note: list 3 hard things you've already handled. Add one small win every evening.

source.work: The Progress Principle (2011)

cards.try_team: End a meeting, class or family dinner with one quick round: 'One small step forward I made this week.' 30 seconds each, no ranking.

cards.hook: One step forward, one step back. Which does your brain count louder?
cards.title: Setbacks Shout, Wins Whisper

game.prompt: In a diary study, 238 people wrote about their workday, every day, for months. What moved their mood more: a step forward, or a step back?
game.reveal: A step back. In Amabile and Kramer's diaries, a setback's power to sink happiness was more than twice as strong as progress's power to lift it. If you picked 'forward', that's the hopeful guess, and progress did matter a lot. It just whispers while setbacks shout.

cards.insight: Bad events tend to weigh more than good ones (Baumeister and colleagues, 2001). So a day with one step forward and one back can feel like a loss. Writing wins down gives them a fair vote.
cards.model: Setbacks shout, progress whispers. Write the wins down so they get a vote.
cards.try_today: Tonight, write one step back and two steps forward from today, however small. Read the forward ones twice.
cards.try_team: End the week with each person naming one setback and one bit of progress. Write the progress where everyone can see it.

source.work: The Progress Principle (2011); Bad is stronger than good (2001)

cards.hook: Is this the dip you push through, or the sign to walk away?
cards.title: Quitting Wisely

game.prompt: Is this a real quit signal, or not (yet)?

items.text: It's hard, but you're measurably better than a month ago.
items.why: Hard plus progress is the classic dip. The reward usually lies on the other side.

items.text: You keep going mainly because of what you've already spent.
items.why: That's the sunk cost trap. Past costs are gone either way; judge only the road ahead.

items.text: Knowing what you know now, you'd never start this today.
items.why: Annie Duke's test: if you wouldn't choose it fresh, staying is often just inertia.

items.text: You had a terrible week and feel like giving up tonight.
items.why: A bad night is a feeling, not data. Rest, set a calm review date, and decide then.

items.text: Your goal changed and this no longer leads anywhere you want.
items.why: Grit toward the wrong goal is just stubbornness. Redirect the effort.

items.text: It keeps costing you sleep, health, or key relationships.
items.why: Real harm is a stop sign, not a toughness test. Protect the base everything else is built on.

items.text: You're stuck, but you haven't tried a new method yet.
items.why: Not a quit signal yet: change the approach before the goal. Stuck is often a method problem.

cards.insight: Quitting isn't failure; it frees time for better bets. Seth Godin separates a dip worth pushing through from a dead end. Annie Duke adds: we usually quit too late, held by sunk costs.
cards.model: Quit what you wouldn't start today. Dips that still show progress aren't quit signals.
cards.try_today: Write one commitment you're unsure about and set a 'kill criterion': the one signal that would tell you to stop.

source.work: Quit (2022); The Dip (2007)

cards.try_team: Pick one shared project, club or family plan and agree its kill criteria together: 'If ___ hasn't happened by ___, we stop or change course.'

cards.hook: Kids once got around town alone. How fast did that freedom shrink?
cards.title: The Shrinking Roam

game.question: In 1971, 80% of English 7- and 8-year-olds got to school without an adult. By 1990, what share did?
game.explain: 9%. In under 20 years, going to school alone fell from 8 in 10 young kids to fewer than 1 in 10 (Hillman, Adams & Whitelegg, 1990). Busier roads and parents' fears grew; kids' chances to handle small risks on their own shrank.

cards.insight: The drop is real. Haidt and Gray argue it helped fuel rising teen anxiety; critics say that link is still mostly correlation. Small risks you choose do seem to build skill and nerve.
cards.model: Nerve grows from small risks you choose and can judge yourself, at any age.
cards.try_today: Pick one small thing you'd usually hand to someone else, a new route, a repair, a tricky call, and do it yourself today.
cards.try_team: Each person names one thing they did alone at 10 that kids rarely do now. Agree one safe-enough version to allow or try this month.

source.work: One False Move: A Study of Children's Independent Mobility (1990); Gray, The Decline of Play (2011); Haidt, The Anxious Generation (2024)

cards.hook: Is 'be careful!' keeping them safe, or teaching them to freeze?
cards.title: Keep the Risk, Fix the Hazard

steps.scenario: Your 7-year-old grandchild is climbing a sturdy tree, a little higher than you'd like. You call up…

options.text: "Do you feel steady? Where does your next foot go?"
options.feedback: Best pick. A question hands her the judgment. The height is a risk she can see and manage, the useful kind.

options.text: "Get down now, that's too high!"
options.feedback: Understandable, and it ends the danger. It also ends the lesson: she never practises judging height herself.

options.text: Nothing. You look away and let her get on with it.
options.feedback: Trust is good, but staying near and calm lets you spot what she can't, like a rotten branch.

steps.scenario: You're 16. Friends are jumping off a pier into water nobody has checked. Your move?

options.text: Check the depth first, then decide.
options.feedback: Best pick. Unknown depth is a hazard: a danger you can't see. Make it visible, then the choice is really yours.

options.text: Jump. Hesitating is for cowards.
options.feedback: Courage isn't skipping the check. Hidden rocks don't care how brave you are.

options.text: Never jump, from any pier, ever.
options.feedback: Safe tonight, but avoiding every risk builds fear, not skill. Check first, then choose.

steps.scenario: A new teammate asks to lead next week's client call alone. It feels a little early. You…

options.text: Say yes, do a 15-minute prep, and stay on standby.
options.feedback: Best pick. Real stakes, a safety net, and room to recover: that's risky play for grown-ups.

options.text: Run it yourself. Too much is at stake.
options.feedback: Safe for this call, costly for growth. Without a first try, the next one stays scary.

options.text: Let them go in cold with no briefing.
options.feedback: That's a hazard, not a stretch: missing facts they can't see. Give the map, then step back.

cards.insight: A risk is a danger you can see and judge; a hazard is one you can't. Fix hazards, keep risks. A 2015 review tied risky outdoor play to more activity and social health; most studies were weak.
cards.model: Remove the hidden hazards, keep the visible risks. That's where skill and courage grow.
cards.try_today: Swap one 'Be careful!' for a question: 'What's your plan?' or 'Do you feel steady?' Try it on a kid, a colleague or yourself.
cards.try_team: List 3 things your team, class or family shields people from. Sort each: hidden hazard (fix it) or visible risk (allow it).

source.work: Brussoni et al., Risky Play and Children's Safety (2012); Brussoni et al., risky outdoor play and health: a systematic review (2015)

cards.hook: New project, new mistakes. Clues or roadblocks?
cards.title: Mistakes are Data Points

game.prompt: Imagine your project is like baking a cake: What's more helpful – finding the recipe wrong OR having it burn in the oven?

choices.text: The recipe being wrong (I'd fix that first)
The cake burning (it tells me what NOT to do next time)

game.reveal: Many people jump to fixing the 'recipe' - their plans. But a mistake, like burnt cake, is real-time feedback. It tells you *what actually happened* so you can adjust your process. Carol Dweck calls this 'growth mindset': seeing mistakes as data, not failures.

cards.insight: Mistakes aren't the opposite of success, they're part of the journey. They highlight what works and what doesn't.
cards.model: Every mistake is a data point guiding you towards success. Learn from it, adjust, and keep going!
cards.try_today: Think of your last 'failed' attempt at something. What did you learn that you wouldn't have known otherwise?

source.work: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success (2006)

cards.try_team: Share a recent 'failed' project with your team. Focus on ONE thing you learned from it that helped you improve.

cards.hook: Presentation ace? Bask or level up?
cards.title: The Loop of Growth

steps.scenario: You just delivered a successful presentation. How do you feel?

options.text: Relief! I nailed it, time to celebrate.
options.feedback: Totally deserved! But the best learners keep going. Celebrating is great, but so is learning from the win.

options.text: Proud and excited, but also wanting to know what worked well and what could be even better next time.
options.feedback: Yes! That's the loop: enjoy the success, then analyze it. Your future self will thank you.

steps.scenario: You want to learn from your presentation. What do you focus on?

options.text: My awesome slides and witty jokes! They were the stars, right?
options.feedback: Humor is good, but remember what helped YOU deliver it: clear structure, confident voice? Those are the real wins.

options.text: How I managed my nerves, how the audience responded, and where I could have explained things more clearly.
options.feedback: Spot on! Focus on your delivery, audience engagement, and content clarity. You're building a system for success, not just one-off wins.

cards.insight: The self-reflection loop is powerful: learn from successes AND failures. Analyze what worked, what didn't, and use that to improve next time.
cards.model: Learn, adjust, repeat. The self-reflection loop fuels continuous growth.
cards.try_today: After a challenging task today, take 5 minutes to reflect: What went well? What could you do differently next time?

source.work: Resonant Leadership (2014)

cards.hook: You swear you'll stop scrolling in bed. Why does it never stick?
cards.title: The Habit Loop

steps.scenario: Every night your phone lies on your pillow, and you scroll until 1am. Which change is most likely to break the loop?

options.text: Promise yourself: lights off at 11 tonight.
options.feedback: Worth a try, but it fights the craving head-on, late at night, when you're tired. That's the hardest link to win.

options.text: Charge the phone across the room or outside the bedroom.
options.feedback: Yes. No phone in reach, no cue. You broke the loop at its first link, before willpower was even needed.

options.text: Feel bad about it the next morning.
options.feedback: Guilt arrives after the loop is done, so it changes no link. Be kind to yourself and move the cue instead.

steps.scenario: Whenever a meeting gets tense, a colleague grabs their phone and starts scrolling. The tension (the cue) won't vanish. What helps most?

options.text: Tell them to just stop.
options.feedback: Kindly meant, but 'just stop' leaves the urge with nowhere to go.

options.text: When the urge comes, pick up a pen and write down the next question to ask.
options.feedback: Yes. Same cue, new response. Swapping in a competing action is the core of habit reversal training, a well-tested method.

options.text: Wait until the project calms down.
options.feedback: Understandable, but the loop keeps practising in the meantime. A swap can start today.

cards.insight: Most people pick willpower first. The trick is the cue. Best move: charge your phone across the room, so there's no cue and no fight. Clear's loop has four links (Duhigg's had three): remove the cue or swap the response.
cards.model: Cue, craving, response, reward. Change one link and the habit starts to change.
cards.try_today: Pick one habit you want to change and write down its cue. Then move that cue out of sight or out of reach.
cards.try_team: Each person names one group habit (late starts, phones at dinner). Together, name its cue and pick one link to change for a week.

from_source.quote: Could the young but realize how soon they will become mere walking bundles of habits, they would give more heed to their conduct...
from_source.cite: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), vol. 1, ch. IV 'Habit'
from_source.next_read: The Principles of Psychology, ch. IV 'Habit' (the closing pages, with his practical maxims)

source.work: The Power of Habit (2012); Atomic Habits (2018); Habit reversal (Behaviour Research and Therapy, 1973)

cards.hook: Everyone quotes a number for building a habit. It's way off.
cards.title: How Long a Habit Really Takes

game.question: In a UK study, people built one new daily habit. How many days did it take, on median, to feel automatic?
game.explain: Lally and colleagues (2010) followed 96 people for 12 weeks. For the 39 whose data were clear enough to model, the median was 66 days, and the projected range ran from 18 to 254 days. The popular '21 days' has no solid research behind it.

cards.insight: Still effortful after three weeks? That's normal, not failure. Simple habits (a glass of water) automate faster than hard ones (50 sit-ups). Small study, wide range: patience is part of the method.
cards.model: A typical habit took around two months in one small study, and the range is huge. Plan for the long middle.
cards.try_today: Pick one tiny habit and mark a date 66 days from today in your calendar as its check-in day.
cards.try_team: Choose one shared habit (a 5pm tidy-up, a 1-minute check-in). Put a review date 66 days out on the shared calendar and judge it then, not before.

source.work: How are habits formed (European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010)

cards.hook: Same habit, two ways to talk about it. Which one sounds like you?
cards.title: Outcome vs Identity Habits

questions.q: Someone offers you something you're cutting back on (a snack, an energy drink, one more episode). You'd most likely say...

options.label: No thanks, I'm trying to cut down.
No thanks, that's not really me anymore.

questions.q: Your main aim for fitness, study or a hobby sounds most like...

options.label: Hit a number by a date (a grade, 5 km, a weight).
Be someone who does it most days.

questions.q: After a good session, your first thought is usually...

options.label: One step closer to the target.
That's the kind of person I am.

questions.q: On a slow week, what keeps you going?

options.label: Not wanting to stop being who I've become.

zones.label: Leaning outcome today
zones.text: Today's answers aim at results. Great for direction, but results arrive slowly and can feel stuck before they show. Try adding one 'who am I becoming' line.

zones.label: A mix today
zones.text: Today's answers use both. Goals set the direction; identity can keep you going while results are slow.

zones.label: Leaning identity today
zones.text: Today's answers tie actions to who you're becoming. That can make habits sticky. Keep the identity flexible, so one slip never feels like a verdict.

cards.insight: Goals say where to go; identity can help you keep going. Each small action is a vote for a type of person, and you need a majority, not every vote. Clear argues identity outlasts goals; it is a useful lens with little direct testing. Aristotle said it first: we become what we repeatedly do.
cards.model: Every action is a vote for the person you're becoming. Win the majority, not every vote.
cards.try_today: Finish this sentence on paper: 'I am the kind of person who...' Then do one 2-minute action that proves it.
cards.try_team: Each person finishes 'We're the kind of team (or family) that...' Pick the line you like most and one 2-minute action that proves it this week.

from_source.quote: We become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.
from_source.cite: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 1 (W. D. Ross trans., 1908)
from_source.next_read: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapters 1-4 (how character is built by repeated action)

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); Nicomachean Ethics (c. 340 BCE)

cards.hook: Can't vote yet? One tiny word might still change what you actually do.
cards.title: The Voter Study That Didn't Hold

game.prompt: Before an election, researchers asked people one of two questions. Which did the FIRST study (2011) report worked better?
choices: How important is it to you to vote?
How important is it to you to be a voter?
game.reveal: The first study (Bryan et al., 2011) said 'be a voter'. Then a bigger study (Gerber et al., 2016) found no effect. The real lesson: one exciting study isn't proof.

cards.insight: Describing an action as part of who you are ('a voter', 'a reader') may make it feel more meaningful. But the original finding did not reliably replicate, so hold it loosely.
cards.model: A catchy finding is a hypothesis until it replicates. Identity labels may help some; test it on yourself.
cards.try_today: Swap "I should revise" for "I'm someone who revises", then revise for 10 minutes. Your own small experiment: does it feel different?
cards.try_team: Rewrite one group rule as a noun: 'be on time' becomes 'we're people who start on time'. Try it for a week, then ask if it felt any different.

source.work: Motivating voter turnout by invoking the self (PNAS, 2011)

cards.hook: 1% a day sounds like nothing. Guess what it compounds to in a year.
cards.title: 1% Compounding

game.question: Something grows 1% a day, compounding, for 365 days. How many times bigger is it at the end?
game.explain: 1.01 to the power of 365 is about 37.8; 1% worse daily (0.99^365) leaves about 0.03. People aren't bank accounts: skills plateau and rest days are part of it. The point is direction, not 37x.

cards.insight: We expect straight-line progress, so small daily gains feel pointless. Real skills plateau and days vary, so this is an illustration, not a forecast. Small choices still add up, both ways.
cards.model: Tiny gains compound. Judge your habits by their direction, not by today's result.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you do daily and make it 1% better today: one more page, one less scroll, one extra glass of water.
cards.try_team: Each person names one 1% fix for how you live or work together (a tidier shared shelf, a shorter meeting). Pick one and do it daily this week.

from_source.quote: Every smallest stroke of virtue or of vice leaves its never so little scar.
from_source.cite: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), vol. 1, ch. IV 'Habit'
from_source.next_read: The Principles of Psychology, ch. IV 'Habit' (the Rip Van Winkle passage near the end)

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); The Principles of Psychology (1890)

cards.hook: Most brains trip on one kind of maths. See how yours handles it?
cards.title: The Doubling Pile

game.prompt: Pick a pile. Pile A: you get 1,000 coins every day for 30 days. Pile B: you get 1 coin on day 1, 2 on day 2, 4 on day 3, doubling each day until day 30. Which ends bigger?
game.reveal: Pile B, by a mile: over 1 billion coins vs 30,000. If you picked A, you're in good company, and here's why: A is ahead for the first 13 days. Doubling looks like nothing, then like everything.

cards.insight: People reliably underestimate compound growth (Stango & Zinman, 2009). Habits don't compound like this. In one study, automaticity grew fast at first and then levelled off over about 66 days (Lally et al., 2010). The shared lesson: early days look unimpressive.
cards.model: Don't judge a slow start by week one. Give it about two months.
cards.try_today: Draw 30 boxes on paper. Tick one each day you do your tiny habit. Judge it at box 30, not box 3.
cards.try_team: Everyone secretly picks Pile A or B, then reveal together. Then choose one small daily habit for the group and review it in 30 days.

source.work: Exponential growth bias and household finance (Journal of Finance, 2009); How are habits formed (European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010); Atomic Habits (2018)

cards.hook: The habit isn't too hard. The start is too big. Can you shrink it?
cards.title: The Two-Minute Rule

game.prompt: Is this a good two-minute starting version?

items.text: Read one page of a book
items.why: Tiny, clear, and it often turns into more pages.

items.text: Read 30 pages every night
items.why: Great goal, hard start. Shrink it to one page first.

items.text: Put on your trainers
items.why: Starting is the hard part. Shoes on makes the walk or run likely.

items.text: Run 5 km every morning
items.why: Make the first step the shoes, not the whole run.

items.text: Play one scale on the guitar
items.why: Instrument out, one scale done. Often you keep going.

items.text: Clean your whole room
items.why: Try 'put away one thing' instead. Momentum does the rest.

cards.insight: For many people, starting is the hardest part. Shrink the habit until it's almost silly and the start stops being a battle. A practical rule of thumb, not a lab finding.
cards.model: Make the start so small you can't say no. Master showing up before you improve.
cards.try_today: Take one habit you keep postponing and do only its two-minute version right now. Stopping after is allowed.
cards.try_team: Pick one stalled group task. Shrink it to a 2-minute start (open the doc, list three names, clear one shelf) and do it together right now.

from_source.quote: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; ... the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
from_source.cite: Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 64 (James Legge trans., 1891)
from_source.next_read: Tao Te Ching, ch. 63-64 (on doing great things while they are small)

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); Getting Things Done (2001); Tiny Habits (2019)

cards.hook: People with 'great willpower' may just face fewer temptations. You?
cards.title: Design the Room, Not the Will

questions.q: The things I want to do more (book, water, guitar) are in plain sight.
Starting a good habit takes me under 20 seconds of setup.
Temptations (snacks, games) take effort to reach.
My phone is out of reach when I need to focus or sleep.
The easiest option in front of me (food, apps, plans) is usually a good one.
The people I spend time with do the habits I want.

advice.0: Today's lowest score: visible cues. Put the book on your pillow or the water bottle where you'll see it first.
advice.1: Today's lowest score: friction. Make good habits easier and temptations harder: lay out tomorrow's clothes tonight.
advice.2: Today's lowest score: phone distance. Charge your phone outside the bedroom tonight, or in another room while you focus.
advice.3: Today's lowest score: defaults. Change one: move social apps off your home screen, or put fruit at eye level.
advice.4: Today's lowest score: people. Find one person or group who already does the habit you want, and spend a little time there.

cards.insight: People who rated their self-control highly reported meeting fewer temptations, not resisting more (Hofmann et al., 2012, a correlational diary study). Resisting in the moment is unreliable; your surroundings work every day for free.
cards.model: Make good habits obvious and easy; make bad ones invisible and hard.
cards.try_today: Move one temptation out of sight and put one good cue in plain view. It takes two minutes.
cards.try_team: Walk your shared space (home, classroom, office) for 5 minutes. Each person hides one distraction and puts one good cue in sight.

from_source.quote: Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve.
from_source.cite: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 7 'On Crowds' (R. M. Gummere trans., 1917)
from_source.next_read: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 7 'On Crowds'

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); Everyday temptations (J. Personality & Social Psychology, 2012); Good Habits, Bad Habits (2019)

cards.hook: Two neighbouring countries. One tiny box. A gap you won't believe.
cards.title: The Power of Defaults

game.question: In Germany you ticked a box to become an organ donor: about 12% did. In Austria next door, you were a donor unless you ticked a box to opt out. What % were donors there?
game.explain: About 99.98%, effectively everyone (Johnson & Goldstein, 2003). Same kind of choice, different starting setting, and almost nobody changed it. Actual donations differed far less than sign-ups, but opt-out countries still did better.
