cards.insight: Most of us keep whatever option is already set, because choosing takes effort. So set your own defaults on purpose: your home screen, your plate, your bedside table. Defaults can be used on you as well as by you: ask who set this one, and for whose benefit.
cards.model: Whatever is already set tends to win. Choose your defaults before they choose for you.
cards.try_today: Change one default now: move one app off your home screen, or leave a book where your phone usually sits.
cards.try_team: List your group's defaults (meeting length, who speaks first, what's in the fridge). Change one this week and see what shifts.

source.work: Do defaults save lives? (Science, 2003); Nudge (2008)

cards.hook: You broke your streak yesterday. What you do next matters more.
cards.title: Come Back Small

steps.scenario: You've walked every evening for 12 days. Yesterday you were exhausted and skipped. Tonight you...

options.text: Do a 5-minute walk, even if it's short.
options.feedback: Yes. A small rep tonight keeps the habit alive. Getting back quickly matters more than the perfect streak.

options.text: Wait until Monday to restart properly.
options.feedback: Understandable, but waiting can turn one miss into a new pattern. A small walk tonight works better.

options.text: Decide you're just not a walking person.
options.feedback: That's a big verdict from one tired day. One miss says nothing about who you are.

steps.scenario: A friend says: 'I missed my practice, so the week is ruined.' You reply...

options.text: Missing once barely matters. What's the smallest bit you could do today?
options.feedback: Kind and practical. You lowered the shame and the bar at the same time.

options.text: You need more discipline.
options.feedback: Well meant, but shame tends to make restarting harder, not easier.

options.text: Yeah, just start fresh next week.
options.feedback: Supportive, but it delays the comeback. Today is a fine day to restart.

cards.insight: William James warned: 'Never suffer an exception to occur' till a habit is rooted. Lally's 2010 data was gentler: one missed day barely slowed habit formation. Treat a miss as an accident, not a collapse.
cards.model: Missing once is an accident. Clear's rule of thumb: come back soon and small, even after two misses or ten.
cards.try_today: If you missed something this week, do a tiny version of it today and tell yourself: 'One miss doesn't define me.'
cards.try_team: Agree on a 'come back small' version of your shared habit (a one-line update instead of the full check-in) for days that fall apart.

from_source.quote: Seize the very first possible opportunity to act on every resolution you make.
from_source.cite: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), vol. 1, ch. IV 'Habit' (third maxim)
from_source.next_read: The Principles of Psychology, ch. IV 'Habit': compare his first three maxims with Lally (2010).

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); How are habits formed (2010); The Principles of Psychology (1890)

cards.hook: You left school or work hours ago. Has your head left yet?
cards.title: Close the Day on Purpose

steps.scenario: It's 10 pm. The class, team or family chat is still buzzing about tomorrow, and nothing can be done about it tonight. You...

options.text: Mute it until morning and pick a set time to catch up.
options.feedback: Best move. Nothing changes overnight, and a set catch-up time tells your brain the topic has a place to land.

options.text: Keep checking so you don't miss anything.
options.feedback: Very human, but each check reopens the topic right when you can't act on it. Muting usually costs you nothing.

options.text: Reply to every message so it's all done.
options.feedback: Tidy in theory, but replies invite more replies. The chat rarely ends because you answered it.

steps.scenario: You have an hour before bed and feel drained. Which evening is most likely to leave you rested tomorrow?

options.text: Something absorbing and unrelated: cooking, a walk, a novel, a game with someone.
options.feedback: Right. Studies of mentally 'switching off' after work or study link it to less fatigue the next day.

options.text: Catching up on the news so you're up to date.
options.feedback: Understandable, but news is designed to grab attention, which keeps the mind alert, not settled.

options.text: Going over tomorrow in your head in bed.
options.feedback: Planning is useful, just earlier and on paper. In bed it often turns into replaying, which keeps you awake.

cards.insight: Rest isn't only time off. It's your mind leaving the task too. People who switch off in the evening report less fatigue, though most of this evidence is correlational.
cards.model: An evening only rests you if your mind gets to leave the day too.
cards.try_today: Pick one closing signal for tonight, like muting chats at 9 pm or saying 'done for today' as you shut the bag or laptop.
cards.try_team: Agree on a quiet hour for the group chat (say 9 pm to 7 am), with a clear rule for what counts as truly urgent.

source.work: Sonnentag & Fritz, Journal of Occupational Health Psychology (2007); Wendsche & Lohmann-Haislah, Frontiers in Psychology (2017); Deep Work (2016)

cards.hook: Some 'relaxing' habits wake your brain right up. Spot which.
cards.title: Wind Down or Rev Up?

game.prompt: What does this do to your brain before bed?

items.text: Laying out tomorrow's clothes or bag
items.why: One fewer thing waiting for you in the morning, so one fewer thing to hold in mind.

items.text: One last message check in bed
items.why: It opens new topics at the one moment you can't act on them.

items.text: Replaying an argument to win it this time
items.why: Going over it again keeps the body on alert. Writing it down earlier works better.

items.text: A warm shower or bath an hour or two before bed
items.why: A 2019 review found it helped people fall asleep about 10 minutes sooner.

items.text: Binge-watching a gripping finale until late
items.why: The excitement and the lost sleep time matter as much as the screen's light.

items.text: The same short routine in the same order each night
items.why: Repeated steps become cues: after a while the routine itself signals sleep.

cards.insight: Calm and familiar winds you down. New and exciting revs you up. Sleep helps lock in what you learned (strong evidence). The idea that it also softens bad moods is promising but still debated.
cards.model: Before bed, swap new and exciting for calm and familiar.
cards.try_today: Pick two calm steps (shower, lay out clothes, one page of a book) and do them in the same order tonight.
cards.try_team: As a family or team, swap ideas: each person shares one thing that winds them down and one that secretly revs them up.

source.work: Haghayegh et al., Sleep Medicine Reviews (2019); Walker, Why We Sleep (2017)

cards.hook: You missed your workout today. Is it a setback or a chance to reset?
cards.title: Turning Missed Chances into Power

game.prompt:
You missed your planned workout today. Which thought feels truer?
1. 'I'm falling behind, I'll never get back on track!'
2. 'This is a chance to start fresh tomorrow, with even more energy.'

choices.text: 1. 'I'm falling behind, I'll never get back on track!'
2. 'This is a chance to start fresh tomorrow, with even more energy.'

game.reveal: Choice 2 unlocks the power of reframing. James Clear says missing once is an accident, but missing twice becomes a habit. Reframing your miss as a new start can break that cycle. It's about choosing intention over inertia.

cards.insight: Missing something doesn't have to derail you. Reframing it as a chance to begin anew empowers you to get back on track.
cards.model: Reframing missed opportunities as fresh starts helps build resilience and avoid the trap of habitual setbacks.
cards.try_today: Small setbacks?  💪 Pause & reframe: 'Chance to learn & improve!'}

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018)

cards.hook: Your group chat is dead on Fridays. What's your first message?
cards.title: Lead With the Why

steps.scenario: You want your friends to start a Friday-night five-a-side (or a study group). In the group chat, your first message is…

options.text: "Pitch at 6, bring £3."
options.feedback: Useful details, but they answer a question nobody has asked yet. Logistics land better once people care.

options.text: "I'm sick of us just scrolling on Fridays, let's actually do something."
options.feedback: You gave a reason they can feel. Now the time and the £3 sound like a way in, not a chore.

options.text: "It'll be the best thing anyone's doing this term."
options.feedback: Hype can grab attention, but it doesn't say why it matters to them. A real reason travels further.

steps.scenario: A friend replies: "Sounds good but I'm busy." You reply…

options.text: "Even one week, come for the first half."
options.feedback: You kept the why alive and made the ask smaller. Easy yes, no pressure.

options.text: "Everyone's busy. It's only an hour."
options.feedback: Understandable, but it brushes off their reason. People dig in when they feel unheard.

options.text: "No worries." and leave it there.
options.feedback: Kind and respectful. You could also leave a door open with a smaller, clear option.

cards.insight: Opening with the reason made the details sound like an invitation. Sinek calls it the Golden Circle: why, then how, then what. A handy habit, but his brain-science story isn't backed by research.
cards.model: Say why it matters before what it is. Purpose first, logistics second.
cards.try_today: Before your next request or pitch, write one sentence that starts with "This matters because…" and say that first.

source.work: Start With Why (2009)

cards.try_team: Open your next meeting, class project or family plan with one line each: 'This matters to me because…'. Only then talk times and tasks.

cards.hook: Can a reason that says nothing still get strangers to say yes?
cards.title: The Power of 'Because'

game.prompt: 1978 experiment: someone asks people at a library copier, "May I go first, because I have to make copies?" (An empty reason: everyone in line has to make copies.) How many say yes?
choices: About as many as for a real reason
game.reveal: About as many: 93% said yes, vs 94% for a real reason ("I'm in a rush") and 60% for no reason. But for a bigger ask (20 pages, not 5), the empty 'because' did nothing (24%, same as no reason). Only the real reason helped (42%).

cards.insight: Langer's point was mindlessness: on small asks we react to the word 'because', not the reason. On bigger asks we wake up and weigh it. That's a tool and a warning: notice when an empty 'because' works on you. One classic study, small groups.
cards.model: On autopilot we hear 'because'; awake, we weigh the reason. Give a real one, and listen for real ones.
cards.try_today: Next time you ask someone for something, add 'because…' with your honest reason. Notice how they respond.
cards.try_team: Each person rewrites one request they'll make this week as 'Could we…, because…' with a real reason. Read them aloud: which ones make you want to say yes?

source.work: Langer, Blank & Chanowitz, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1978); Start With Why (2009)

cards.hook: Which week would you call more meaningful: easy or heavy?
cards.title: Meaning Lives in the Load

game.prompt: Week A: lie-ins, good food, nothing asked of you. Week B: tiring, but you helped your mate revise for their resit and finished the group project everyone was counting on. Which one would you call more meaningful?
game.reveal: Many people pick B as more meaningful, even when A felt happier. Research says: happy = getting, meaningful = giving. Both count.

cards.insight: In a 2013 survey of about 400 US adults, Baumeister and colleagues linked happiness to getting what you want, and meaning to giving and caring. Frankl argued similar from his own life. Meaning grows where you carry something worth it, not where you pile on until you break.
cards.model: Happiness is often about receiving; meaning is often about carrying something worth it.
cards.try_today: Pick one small thing someone relies on you for and do it with care today. Afterwards, notice how it felt.

source.work: Man's Search for Meaning (1946); Baumeister et al., Journal of Positive Psychology (2013)

cards.try_team: Go round the table: each person names one thing others rely on them for that felt heavy but worth it. Notice how often effort and meaning show up together.

cards.hook: Not every weight is yours. Can you tell which ones are?
cards.title: Pick Up the Right Load

game.prompt: Is this a load you can pick up today?

items.text: How you show up for the people who count on you
items.why: Your reliability is fully yours. It's where meaning starts.

items.text: Making everyone like you
items.why: Their feelings aren't yours to control. Your fairness and effort are.

items.text: The mess in your room that's been bugging you
items.why: Peterson's famous starting point: put your own house in order before you try to fix the world. Start small, then take on more.

items.text: Fixing a friend's life for them
items.why: You can support them. Taking over their choices is a weight that crushes both of you.

items.text: Learning the skill your goal actually needs
items.why: Closing your own skill gap is a load that pays you back.

items.text: Every bad thing in the news today
items.why: Caring is good. Carrying it all is not. Pick one thing you can act on instead.

cards.insight: Peterson argues meaning is found in the responsibility you choose to shoulder: pick up the heaviest load you can actually carry. Epictetus adds the filter: carry what is in your power, not what isn't. Sort first, then lift as much of your own as you can.
cards.model: Put down what isn't yours, then pick up as much of what is yours as you can bear.
cards.try_today: Write down three things weighing on you. Circle the one you can act on, and take one 5-minute step on it.

source.work: 12 Rules for Life (2018); Enchiridion (c. 125 AD)

cards.try_team: Everyone writes three worries on sticky notes. Sort them together: 'ours to act on' vs 'not ours'. Pick one 'ours' and agree a first step.

from_source.quote: Some things are in our control and others not.
from_source.cite: Epictetus, Enchiridion, ch. 1 (trans. Elizabeth Carter, 1758)
from_source.next_read: Enchiridion, chapters 1-5 (short; about 10 minutes)

cards.hook: Is your life a cage or a flood right now? Find your spot.
cards.title: The Border of Order & Chaos

questions.q: My typical week is…

options.label: Different every day, hard to plan

questions.q: How much of my week is new to me (new tasks, places, people)?

options.label: Lots is new, and it's exciting but a lot

questions.q: This week, how many surprises did you have to absorb?

options.label: More than I can keep up with

questions.q: My daily routines (sleep, work or homework, phone time) are…
The big things in my life right now (home, work or school, people) feel…

options.label: Several things up in the air at once

zones.label: Leaning Order
zones.text: Today your answers lean toward order: steady, maybe a bit tight. Add one small unknown: a new route, a new skill, a new person. (Keeping away from the unknown can feel safe without being stable.)

zones.label: On the Border
zones.text: Today your answers sit on the border: enough structure to stand on, enough new to grow. If some answers sat at opposite ends, pick the one area that feels most out of balance.

zones.label: Leaning Chaos
zones.text: Today your answers lean toward chaos: lots is moving. One fixed anchor helps: same wake time, a daily walk, or a fixed time your phone goes on charge.

cards.insight: Peterson (Maps of Meaning) pictures life on a border between order, the known, and chaos, the unknown, an idea he links to the Taoist yin and yang. Too much order goes stale; too much chaos overwhelms. Grow by facing the unknown voluntarily.
cards.model: Stand on order, step willingly into chaos. Growth happens at the edge you choose to face.
cards.try_today: If you lean Order, try one new thing today. If you lean Chaos, fix one anchor: same bedtime tonight.

source.work: Tao Te Ching, ch. 42; Peterson, Maps of Meaning (1999); 12 Rules for Life (2018), Rule 2

cards.try_team: Ask the group: which routine keeps us steady, and what one new thing could we try this month? Keep one of each and check back in a week.

cards.hook: A clown on a unicycle rides past you. Would you even notice?
cards.title: Your Aim Decides What You See

game.prompt: You're crossing a campus square, talking on your phone. A clown in a bright costume rides past on a unicycle. Would you notice?
game.reveal: Probably not. In Hyman and colleagues' 2010 study, only about 25% of people on a phone call said they saw the clown, even when asked directly. About half of people walking alone without a phone (51%) did. Their aim, the call, decided what got through.

cards.insight: The missed clown is solid science. The life lesson is a lens, not a law: your aims steer what you notice. Aristotle's mark was the good life itself; small targets serve it, they don't replace it.
cards.model: What you aim at shapes what you see. Choose the aim on purpose.
cards.try_today: Write one aim for this week in a single line. Tonight, list three things you noticed today that could help it.

source.work: Hyman et al., Did you see the unicycling clown?, Applied Cognitive Psychology (2010); Nicomachean Ethics; 12 Rules for Life (2018)

cards.try_team: Everyone writes this week's one aim and swaps papers. For a day, watch out for one thing that could help your partner's aim, then share it.

from_source.quote: Shall we not, like archers who have a mark to aim at, be more likely to hit upon what is right?
from_source.cite: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, ch. 2 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1908)
from_source.next_read: Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, chapters 1-2: the chief good as the target of a life

cards.hook: 'Just do your best' sounds kind. Does it actually help you?
cards.title: Aim at a Clear Target

steps.scenario: You want to get fitter this month. Which aim do you write in your phone?

options.text: "Do my best and see how it goes."
options.feedback: Kind and low-pressure. But in many studies, 'do your best' led to less progress than a clear, stretching target. Vague aims are easy to quietly lower.

options.text: "Run 5 km without stopping by the 30th."
options.feedback: Specific, stretching, still reachable. That's the kind of aim goal research keeps backing: you know exactly what you're working toward.

options.text: "Run a marathon by the 30th."
options.feedback: Love the ambition! But goals far beyond reach tend to get dropped, or cause injuries. Stretch, don't snap.

steps.scenario: Plot twist: you've just started chess and know almost nothing. What's your aim for month one?

options.text: "Win 20 online games."
options.feedback: Clear, but on a new, complex skill, chasing results early can backfire: you rush instead of learning. Result targets work better once you know the basics.

options.text: "Learn 3 opening ideas and try them every game."
options.feedback: Smart. When a skill is new and complex, a learning goal (figure out how) tends to beat a result goal. The wins come later.

options.text: "No aim, just play."
options.feedback: Playing for joy is great. If you want to improve, though, one small learning aim gives your practice a direction.

cards.insight: Clear, stretching aims beat 'do your best' in hundreds of studies. Two catches: for new, complex skills, aim to learn first; and over-tight targets can push people to cut corners.
cards.model: Aim specific and a little stretching. If the skill is new, aim to learn first.
cards.try_today: Rewrite one vague aim ('get better at X') as a clear target with a number and a date. Put it where you'll see it.
cards.try_team: Swap 'let's do our best' for one shared target: your team, class or family picks a clear, stretching goal, a date, and how you'll check progress.

from_source.quote: When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.
from_source.cite: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 71 (trans. R. M. Gummere, 1917)
from_source.next_read: Seneca, Letter 71, opening paragraphs

source.work: Locke & Latham, American Psychologist (2002); Seijts & Latham, Academy of Management Executive (2005); Seneca, Moral Letters, 71

cards.hook: Bored, stressed, or lost in it? Watch your dot find the zone.
cards.title: Find Your Flow Channel

questions.q: It stretches me.
I could do it half-asleep.
It asks more of me than my usual tasks.
I know how to do most of it well.
I'd need to learn new things to do it well.
I've done tasks like this well before.

results.name: Apathy Zone
results.text: Today this task looks low on both challenge and skill: easy to drift and scroll. Pick one tiny goal that stretches you a bit, and start there.

C.name: Anxiety Zone
C.text: Today the task feels bigger than your skill. Shrink it: do one piece you can manage, or get a quick lesson first.

S.name: Boredom Zone
S.text: Today your skill is ahead of the task. Raise the bar: add a time limit, a quality goal, or a harder version.

CS.name: Flow Channel
CS.text: Today high challenge meets high skill. This is where time disappears. Protect it: phone away, one clear goal.

mid.name: On the Fence
mid.text: Today this task sits in the middle on both challenge and skill: not clearly dull, stressful or absorbing. Nudge one side: make it a bit harder, or learn one small piece first.

game.prompt: Think of your main task this week (school, work, a hobby). Answer every line for that task.

cards.insight: People get most absorbed when a high challenge meets matching skill and a clear goal. Too easy is dull; too hard is stressful. Later studies back this, but find the link weaker.
cards.model: Flow = challenge slightly above skill + clear goal + quick feedback.
cards.try_today: Pick one task and tweak it: a bit harder if bored, smaller if stressed. Then do 10 minutes with your phone away.

source.work: Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience (1990)

cards.try_team: Before a group task, each person rates their part 'too easy', 'just right' or 'too hard'. Swap or split parts until most say 'just right'.

cards.hook: Your last focus session flopped. Which flow ingredient was missing?
cards.title: The Four Flow Ingredients

questions.q: In my last focus session, I knew exactly what 'done' looked like.
In my last focus session, I could tell within minutes if I was on track.
In my last focus session, the task felt neither too easy nor too hard.
In my last focus session, I went 25 minutes without checking my phone.

advice.0: Clear goal scored lowest today. Before you start, write one line: 'Done means…'. Vague goals are a top flow-killer.
advice.1: Quick feedback scored lowest today. Build a check: a practice test, a word count, a friend's quick look. Flow needs to see progress.
advice.2: Right difficulty scored lowest today. Adjust the task: add a challenge if it's dull, split it if it's overwhelming.
advice.3: Interruptions scored lowest today. Put your phone in another room for one 25-minute block. Switching leaves part of your mind elsewhere.

cards.insight: Csikszentmihalyi found flow is more likely with a clear goal, fast feedback and a task just above your skill. Protecting focus from interruptions helps all three. Fix the weakest one first.
cards.model: Don't chase flow. Set up its conditions and let it arrive.
cards.try_today: Fix your weakest ingredient, then work for 10 focused minutes and notice how it felt.

source.work: Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience (1990)

cards.try_team: For one 25-minute group work block: agree what 'done' looks like, put all phones away, and check progress together at the end.

cards.hook: Hope is supposed to keep you going. Does it always?
cards.title: Faith Without a Deadline

game.prompt: James Stockdale, a US pilot, was held prisoner in Vietnam for over 7 years. He was asked which fellow prisoners struggled most to hold on. Who did he name?
game.reveal: The optimists. In his telling, they kept picking dates: 'out by Christmas', then Easter. Each missed date hit them harder. Stockdale held two things at once: total faith he'd get home, and zero denial about how bad it was.

cards.insight: This is one man's account to Jim Collins, not a study. Its lesson: hope tied to a date you don't control can break you. Keep faith in the ending; face today's facts.
cards.model: Never doubt the ending. Never deny the facts. Drop the deadline you don't control.
cards.try_today: Pick one hard thing you're waiting out. Write one line of brutal fact, then one line of faith. Cross out any date you can't control.

source.work: Good to Great (2001), Jim Collins, ch. 4

cards.try_team: Facing a long slog together? List three brutal facts on one side and one shared belief about the ending on the other. No promised dates.

cards.hook: Picturing success feels great. That might be the problem.
cards.title: Dream It, Then Find the Wall

steps.scenario: Your big exam is in three weeks and you're behind. What's the best thing to tell yourself tonight?

options.text: "I'll ace it. Just picture the grade and stay positive."
options.feedback: Feels good, but research suggests pure daydreams can relax you before you've done the work.

options.text: "I want a good grade. My biggest obstacle is my phone at night, so if it's 8pm, it goes in the kitchen."
options.feedback: Best. A clear wish, the real obstacle, and an if-then plan: hope plus facts.

options.text: "I'm too far behind. It's hopeless."
options.feedback: Honest about the facts, but it drops the faith. Without it, there's no reason to start.

steps.scenario: You lead a project that's slipping. Your boss asks for an update. What do you say?

options.text: "We'll catch up, the team is great."
options.feedback: Upbeat, but it hides the facts. Collins found strong leaders faced bad news head-on.

options.text: "We're two weeks behind because of X. Here's the plan to recover, and I'm confident we'll deliver."
options.feedback: Best. Brutal fact first, then a plan, then confidence: the Stockdale mix.

steps.scenario: You're relearning to walk well after a knee operation. Progress is slow. Which thought helps most?

options.text: "I'll be hiking by next month."
options.feedback: A hopeful date, but if it slips, the letdown can sap your effort. Hope for the ending, not the date.

options.text: "This will be slow and some days will hurt. I'll do my exercises daily, and I will get there."
options.feedback: Best. You name the hard part and still expect to get there. That keeps you doing the exercises.

options.text: "At my age, why bother?"
options.feedback: Understandable on a bad day, but it turns a slow fact into a final verdict.

cards.insight: In Gabriele Oettingen's studies, people who only daydreamed about success often put in less effort than those who also pictured the obstacle. Pairing the wish with the wall helps, with modest but replicated effects.
cards.model: Wish, then obstacle, then if-then plan. Hope gives the why; facts give the how.
cards.try_today: Name one goal, the biggest inner obstacle, and write one plan: 'If [obstacle], then I will [action].'

source.work: Rethinking Positive Thinking (2014), Gabriele Oettingen

cards.try_team: Each person writes the group's goal, the single biggest obstacle, and one 'If..., then we...' plan. Pick the most common obstacle and adopt its plan.

cards.hook: You're lost in London. Want the satellite photo or the tube map?
cards.title: The Map Is Not the Territory

game.prompt: You need to get across London fast. You can take one: a perfect satellite photo of every street, or the famous tube map that bends rivers and squashes distances. Which gets you there?
game.reveal: For most trips, the tube map wins. It bends geography on purpose so you can act fast. If you picked the photo, you spotted the catch: studies of London riders found the map's distortions push some people onto slower routes, even riding between stops that are quicker to walk. A map is only good for the trip it was built for.

cards.insight: A more accurate map isn't always a better one. Your beliefs about people, money and yourself are maps too: simplified, useful for some trips, misleading on others.
cards.model: Every belief is a map. Ask 'useful for what?' before asking 'true or false?'
cards.try_today: Pick one firm belief about yourself. Write one situation where that map works and one where it would get you lost.

source.work: Korzybski, Science and Sanity (1933); Box, Science and Statistics (1976) and Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building (1979)

cards.try_team: Each person names one rule your group runs on ('homework before screens', 'we always reply fast'). Ask together: useful for which trip? Where does it mislead?

from_source.quote: All models are wrong but some are useful.
from_source.cite: George E. P. Box, 'Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building' (1979)
from_source.next_read: Box, 'Science and Statistics', Journal of the American Statistical Association 71 (1976), sections 'Parsimony' and 'Worrying Selectively'

cards.hook: Your bathroom scale tells the truth, right? Swipe and see.
cards.title: Map or Territory?

game.prompt: Is this the thing itself, or a description of it?

items.text: The number on your bathroom scale
items.why: A reading of your body, not your body. It ignores muscle, water, and how you feel.

items.text: The rain falling on you right now
items.why: As close to the thing itself as you get. You can't argue with it, only respond.

items.text: A friend's 5-star restaurant review
items.why: Their compressed experience. Your night there may differ.

items.text: Your 'I'm bad at maths' story
items.why: A summary of some past moments, not a fact about every future one.

items.text: The taste of the coffee in your mouth
items.why: Closer to the thing than any menu. Korzybski: even taste is your nerves' summary.

items.text: Your exam grade or step count
items.why: A useful number that leaves out most of what you actually did.

cards.insight: Most of what we react to is a map: numbers, labels, stories, reviews. Handy, but they leave things out. When a map upsets you, check the territory before you act.
cards.model: When a label stings, ask: is this the thing, or a description of the thing?
cards.try_today: Next time a number or label bothers you today, name one important thing it leaves out.

source.work: Science and Sanity (1933)

cards.try_team: Put one number your group watches on the table (grades, likes, sales, steps). Everyone names one important thing it leaves out. Five minutes, no debate.

cards.hook: Expert doctors scanned for one thing. Guess how many missed a gorilla.
cards.title: You See What You Aim At

game.question: Radiologists searched lung scans for nodules. Researchers pasted in a gorilla 48 times the size of a typical nodule. What % of the radiologists missed it?
game.explain: Drew, Vo & Wolfe (2013): 20 of 24 expert radiologists (83%) missed it, even though eye-tracking showed most of those who missed it looked right at it. Their aim was 'find nodules'.

cards.insight: Attention follows aims. Even experts hunting for one thing filter out much of the rest, a gorilla included. That's how focus works, but it means your goals quietly shape what you see.
cards.model: Your aim is a filter. Change what you're looking for and the world rearranges.
cards.try_today: Before your next walk or meeting, set a new aim: 'notice three things that are going well.' Then count them.

source.work: Drew, Vo & Wolfe, The invisible gorilla strikes again, Psychological Science (2013); Peterson, Maps of Meaning (1999)

cards.try_team: Before a class, practice or meeting, give everyone a different 'look for' job: one good idea, one risk, one person who's quiet. Compare notes at the end.

from_source.quote: My experience is what I agree to attend to. Only those items which I notice shape my mind.
from_source.cite: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), vol. 1, ch. XI 'Attention'
from_source.next_read: The Principles of Psychology, vol. 1, ch. XI 'Attention', opening pages (free online)

cards.hook: A stranger swaps into someone else mid-chat. Surely you'd notice?
cards.title: The Person Swap

game.prompt: A stranger with a map asks you for directions. As you explain, two workers carry a door between you. Behind it, the stranger is replaced by a different person with different clothes and voice. Would you notice?
game.reveal: If you said yes, you're in good company: almost everyone does. But in Simons and Levin's 1998 street study, about half of the people kept giving directions to the new person without noticing. One likely reason: people stored a rough label ('a stranger with a map'), not the face. In a follow-up, students noticed a swap more often when the stranger looked like a fellow student.

cards.insight: We often store a rough label, not the details. A small study (15 people), but this 'change blindness' has been found many times.
cards.model: We often store a label, not the person. Aim to notice the person and you'll see more of them.
cards.try_today: In your next chat, set a tiny aim: notice one thing about the person (their mood, their eyes, what they care about today).
cards.try_team: Pair up for 60 seconds of chat, then turn back to back. Each changes one small thing (glasses, sleeve, hair). Turn round: who spots it? Then swap.

source.work: Simons & Levin, Failure to detect changes to people during a real-world interaction, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (1998)

cards.hook: 11pm. A text: 'We need to talk.' What does your gut say?
cards.title: Reframing

steps.scenario: 11pm. Your manager (or a close friend, or your partner) texts: 'We need to talk. Tomorrow?' No context. Your heart speeds up. What do you tell yourself?

options.text: 'I've done something wrong. I should prepare for the worst.'
options.feedback: A very normal first reaction, especially if you're already on edge. It's just one story out of many, and you don't have to settle it tonight.

options.text: 'I don't know what this is yet. Could be news, a favour, a plan. I'll find out tomorrow.'
options.feedback: That's reappraisal: same facts, wider frame. You haven't lied to yourself, you've just stopped writing the ending early.

options.text: 'Whatever, I don't care.'
options.feedback: Pushing the feeling down often keeps it buzzing underneath. Research suggests suppression tends to work worse than reframing.

steps.scenario: Next morning, still a bit nervous. What's a useful move?

options.text: Reply: 'Sure. Anything I should prepare? What time works?'
options.feedback: Turns a vague threat into a concrete plan. Often you'll get the context you were missing.

options.text: Replay worst cases until you meet
options.feedback: Understandable, but going round in circles rarely adds information. One small action usually helps more.

cards.insight: Events arrive inside a frame. Changing the frame, not the facts, can change your body's reaction and your next move. Studies find reappraisal usually beats pushing feelings down.
cards.model: Same facts, new frame: 'What else could this mean?' is the cheapest stress tool you own.
cards.try_today: When something stings today, write two other honest explanations for it before you react.

source.work: Gross & John, Individual differences in two emotion regulation processes (2003); Epictetus, Enchiridion; Seneca, Moral Letters 13

cards.try_team: If you lead a team or class: before sending 'Can we talk?', add one line of context ('Nothing bad, want to plan next week'). Agree this as a group rule.

from_source.quote: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
from_source.cite: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 13 'On Groundless Fears', trans. R. M. Gummere (1917)
from_source.next_read: Seneca, Moral Letters, Letter 13 'On Groundless Fears' (about 4 pages)

cards.hook: Some 'positive thinking' makes you feel worse. Can you spot which?
cards.title: Reframe, Not Spin

game.prompt: Something went wrong. Is this thought an honest reframe, or spin?

items.text: Failed your driving test: 'Now I know exactly which two things to practise.'
items.why: True, useful, and it points to a next step. That's a reframe.

items.text: Failed your driving test: 'Who cares, I never wanted to drive anyway.'
items.why: Sour grapes. If part of you doesn't believe it, it won't calm you.

items.text: Friend hasn't replied all day: 'She might just be busy. I'll check in tomorrow.'
items.why: A believable other explanation, plus an action. You stay open, not certain.

items.text: Low mark on an essay: 'Grades are meaningless, so it doesn't matter.'
items.why: Denial. Grades leave things out, but this one still has information for you.

items.text: Bus cancelled, 25-minute wait: 'Good time to call Grandma.'
items.why: Same facts, better use of them. Nothing here is pretend.

items.text: Feeling low: repeating 'I am totally happy and loved' ten times.
items.why: In one study, statements like this made people with low self-esteem feel worse.

cards.insight: Reframing works when you believe the new frame. Spin and forced positivity can backfire: in one study, 'I am a lovable person' made people with low self-esteem feel worse.
cards.model: A good reframe is true, believable and points to a next step. If it's not true, it's spin.
cards.try_today: When something stings today, write one reframe. Then ask: do I actually believe this? If not, find a truer one.
cards.try_team: Someone shares a small setback. Everyone offers one reframe; the group votes each 'honest' or 'spin', and says why. Keep it light and kind.

source.work: Gross & John (2003); Wood, Perunovic & Lee, Positive self-statements: Power for some, peril for others, Psychological Science (2009); Epictetus, Enchiridion

from_source.quote: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things.
from_source.cite: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5, trans. George Long
from_source.next_read: Epictetus, Enchiridion, sections 1-5 (about two pages)

cards.hook: Your heart's pounding before a big talk. Enemy or fuel?
cards.title: Stress Mindset

questions.q: Before an exam or big moment, my racing heart means…
When a stressful task looms (a deadline, an exam, a big job), I mostly see it as…
Looking back, stressful times in my life…
Feeling stressed is a sign that…

zones.label: Leaning 'stress harms'
zones.text: Today your answers read stress mostly as danger, and if you've had a hard time, that makes sense. For everyday nerves (a talk, an exam), try one more reading: my body is getting me ready. If stress feels constant or heavy, that's a reason to get support, not a mindset failure.

zones.label: A mixed lens
zones.text: Today your answers see both sides. Next time, notice which story you pick in the moment. Sometimes you can pick which story to lean on.

zones.label: Leaning 'stress can fuel'
zones.text: Today your answers read stress as energy. Keep that, and still watch for real overload: rest is part of the deal.

cards.insight: In Alia Crum's studies, people shown stress as enhancing reported somewhat better performance and fewer stress symptoms. Jeremy Jamieson found reading a racing heart as 'gearing up' helped too. Effects are modest; heavy or constant stress needs real support.
cards.model: Some stress is your body gearing up, not breaking. Reframe the everyday kind; get support for the heavy kind.
cards.try_today: Before your next nervous moment, take one slow breath and tell yourself: 'This is energy for something I care about.'

source.work: Crum, Salovey & Achor, Rethinking stress (2013); Jamieson et al., Journal of Experimental Psychology: General (2012); McGonigal, The Upside of Stress (2015)

cards.try_team: Before a match, exam or big deadline, everyone says one thing they care about in it. Then together: 'This buzz is energy for that.' One slow breath.
cards.notes: Q3 is deliberately downweighted (values ±1) so a hard past isn't scored as harshly as present-day appraisals.

cards.hook: 'I'm just not a people person.' How would you prove that?
cards.title: Pragmatic Truth

game.prompt: You believe 'I'm not a people person.' William James would ask: what difference does this belief make in practice? Which test adds something reflection alone can't?
choices: Reflecting, then living one week as if it might be false
game.reveal: Reflection matters; it is where the question starts. But James and Peirce held that an idea's meaning shows in its practical consequences, so the test has to leave the armchair too. Beliefs like this can quietly keep themselves alive, because they steer us away from the very moments that could test them. A small, low-stakes test is kinder and more informative than reflection alone.

cards.insight: Pragmatism asks: what happens when you act on this idea? A philosophical lens, not a lab finding, and facts still matter. James's view of truth was hotly disputed (Russell among others); take it as a method, not the last word.
cards.model: Judge a belief by its consequences: run the experiment, then decide.
cards.try_today: Pick one limiting belief. Try one small, low-stakes action that only makes sense if it's false. Note what happened, no grading.

source.work: James, Pragmatism (1907); Peirce, How to Make Our Ideas Clear (1878)

cards.try_team: Each person names one 'we're just not the kind of group that…' belief. Pick one, design a one-week test that could prove it false, and agree when to check.

from_source.quote: The truth of an idea is not a stagnant property inherent in it. Truth happens to an idea.
from_source.cite: William James, Pragmatism (1907), Lecture VI 'Pragmatism's Conception of Truth'
from_source.next_read: James, Pragmatism, Lecture II 'What Pragmatism Means', then Lecture VI (free online)

cards.hook: Your lens might be fogged in one spot. Find which in 30 seconds.
cards.title: Your Perception Loop

questions.q: I notice details others miss, including small signs things are changing.
I often realise later that I missed something obvious.
When something goes wrong, I can come up with more than one explanation.
My first read of a situation usually feels like the only one.
When I'm proven wrong, I update my view fairly quickly.
I keep doing what I've always done, even when results disappoint.

results.name: All three dimmed today
results.text: Today no step stands out, which often happens when we're tired or busy. A starting point, not a verdict. Begin with Perceive: one minute a day noticing three new things.

P.name: Noticing leads today
P.text: Today your answers show strong noticing, with less room for second readings or changing course. Try asking 'what else could this mean?'

A.name: Interpreting leads today
A.text: Today your answers show you re-read situations well, but may be working from thin data and slow to change course. Gather one more fact before deciding.

R.name: Adjusting leads today
R.text: Today your answers show you change course readily. Check you're adjusting to real signals, not noise: notice and interpret first.

AP.name: Noticing + interpreting
AP.text: Today your answers show clear seeing and flexible thinking, but insight may not turn into change. Try Recalibrate: make one small adjustment this week.

PR.name: Noticing + adjusting
PR.text: Today your answers show you spot change and move fast, maybe on the first interpretation. Try Appraise: pause for a second explanation.

AR.name: Interpreting + adjusting
AR.text: Today your answers show you reframe and adapt well, but may be missing inputs. Try Perceive: ask someone what they see that you don't.

APR.name: All three switched on
APR.text: Today all three steps are at least switched on. Keep it honest by checking results, not just feelings. Pick the step you scored lowest and sharpen it.

cards.insight: Qlip's own framework (built on Powers's control theory, not a tested scale): perceive, appraise, recalibrate, act, repeat. Your weakest step is where your view can quietly bend.
cards.model: Perceive, appraise, recalibrate. Your weakest step is where your view of reality bends.
cards.try_today: Take one frustrating situation from this week and run it through your weakest step, on paper, in five minutes.

source.work: Original QUMNI Perceptual Control Framework (house model), drawing on Powers, Behavior: The Control of Perception (1973)

cards.try_team: Take one recent hiccup (a lost match, a missed deadline, a row). Spend 90 seconds each on: what did we see, what did it mean, what will we adjust?

cards.hook: A thermostat is smarter than most New Year's resolutions. Why?
cards.title: Perceive, Adjust, Repeat

steps.scenario: You promised yourself 20 minutes of guitar (or running, or a language app) a day. Two weeks in, you've done it 3 times. What would a thermostat do?

options.text: Try harder tomorrow. More willpower.
options.feedback: Very common, and it rarely changes the result. A thermostat doesn't try harder; it checks the reading and adjusts.

options.text: Admit it's just not for me and stop.
options.feedback: Maybe, one day. But you'd be quitting on 3 data points without asking why. Check first, then decide.

options.text: Look at what actually happened on the missed days, change one thing, try again.
options.feedback: That's the loop: perceive, appraise, recalibrate, act, check. Small corrections beat big resolutions.

options.text: Write a bigger, more perfect plan.
options.feedback: Tempting, but a new plan without new information repeats the old one. Measure first.

steps.scenario: You check: the missed days were all when you got home after 8pm. Best adjustment?

options.text: Move practice to before dinner, and make it 10 minutes on late days.
options.feedback: Adjust to the real signal, keep it small, then check again next week.

options.text: Promise to do 40 minutes on the good days to make up.
options.feedback: Ambitious, but it ignores the signal. The late days will still break the loop.

cards.insight: Good controllers don't need a perfect plan. They need a fast loop: notice, compare, adjust, act, check. Habits and goals improve the same way: small corrections, often.
cards.model: Don't aim for a perfect plan. Aim for a fast, honest feedback loop.
cards.try_today: Pick one goal. Set a 2-minute check-in tonight: what happened, what does it mean, what will I adjust tomorrow?
cards.try_team: End a practice, lesson or week with 3 questions, one minute each: What happened? What does it mean for our goal? What one thing do we change next time?

source.work: Powers, Behavior: The Control of Perception (1973); adapted as the original QUMNI Perceptual Control Framework

cards.hook: You walk in wearing something cringe. How many people clock it?
cards.title: Fewer People Notice Than You Think

game.question: Students put on a T-shirt with a big, uncool singer's face and walked into a room of peers. What % of the room later noticed who was on the shirt?
game.explain: About 23%. The shirt-wearers guessed close to half would notice (Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, 2000). Guessed high? So did they: you feel your own shirt all day; others mostly don't.

cards.insight: We sit at the centre of our own story, so we guess others are watching us about twice as closely as they are. Small studies, but the pattern has held up.
cards.model: You're the star of your show, an extra in everyone else's. Halve your guess of who noticed.
cards.try_today: Next time you feel everyone saw your slip, ask one person if they noticed. Write down the guess first, then the answer.

source.work: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, 'The Spotlight Effect in Social Judgment', JPSP (2000)

cards.try_team: Everyone writes one moment this week they felt watched (a wrong answer, a typo, a stumble). Others say if they even noticed. Usually: barely.

cards.hook: One awkward moment. How long will people remember it?
cards.title: The Slip Is Smaller Outside Your Head

steps.scenario: In class you answer a question confidently, and it's wrong. A couple of people laugh. Next lesson, you…

options.text: Say 'oops, mixed that up' if it comes up, and put your hand up again
options.feedback: Best move. A light, quick fix tells people it's no big deal, and it usually isn't to them.

options.text: Stay silent for the rest of term so it can't happen again
options.feedback: Understandable, it stung. But the silence costs you more than the slip did; most classmates likely moved on that day.

options.text: Explain at length why your answer was nearly right
options.feedback: Natural urge, but a long defence keeps the moment alive. Short and light lets it fade.

steps.scenario: You lose your words mid-sentence while speaking to a group at work or in a club meeting. Afterwards you…

options.text: Replay it all evening and plan to avoid speaking up
options.feedback: Very common. But people judge our public mishaps less harshly than we expect (Savitsky, Epley & Gilovich, 2001).

options.text: Note one thing to tweak next time, then let it go
options.feedback: Yes. Others mostly remember your point, not the pause. One fix, then move on.

options.text: Send everyone a message apologising for the stumble
options.feedback: Kind instinct, but it puts a spotlight on something few people noticed.

steps.scenario: At a family get-together you call a relative's partner by the wrong name. You…

options.text: Smile, say 'sorry, got my names muddled', and carry on
options.feedback: Right. A warm one-line fix is what most people hope for, and then they move on.

options.text: Avoid them for the rest of the day
options.feedback: Easy to feel that pull. But steering clear makes the moment bigger than the slip was.

options.text: Bring it up again later to apologise once more
options.feedback: Caring, but one apology is enough; repeating it keeps the spotlight on.

cards.insight: Your slip feels huge because you see it from the inside. Others are busy with their own day, and judge it more gently than you predict. A quick, light fix is usually enough.
cards.model: A quick, light fix ends the moment for them; replaying it only keeps it going for you.
cards.try_today: Recall one recent cringe moment. Write how you think others saw it, then a kinder guess. Which is more likely?

source.work: Savitsky, Epley & Gilovich, 'Do Others Judge Us as Harshly as We Think?', JPSP (2001)

cards.try_team: Before a talk or meeting, agree a light line for slips ('let me try that again'). Use it once on purpose so it feels normal for everyone.

cards.hook: A huge win would change everything. For how long, though?
cards.title: The Thrill Wears Off

game.prompt: Researchers asked big lottery winners, up to about 18 months after winning, how happy they felt day to day. Compared with their neighbours, they were…
game.reveal: About the same, in a small 1978 study of 22 winners (Brickman et al.), and they enjoyed small things like a chat or a joke a bit less. Picked 'happier'? You're partly right: a large Swedish study found big winners stayed more satisfied with life for years, though not happier from moment to moment (Lindqvist et al., 2020).

cards.insight: New things quickly become your normal, so the daily glow fades even when the gain is real. How satisfied you feel with life can shift; the day-to-day buzz mostly settles back.
cards.model: Gains turn into the new normal. Expect the glow to fade and plan for it.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you were excited to get last year. Use it today as if it were new, and notice one detail you'd stopped seeing.

source.work: Brickman, Coates & Janoff-Bulman, JPSP (1978); Lindqvist, Östling & Cesarini, Review of Economic Studies (2020)

cards.try_team: Each person names something they wanted badly that now feels ordinary. Then name one way to make it feel fresh again. Share the best idea.

cards.hook: Some changes you get used to in weeks. Others never feel normal.
cards.title: What You Get Used To

game.prompt: Does the feeling fade, or does it stick around?

items.text: The buzz of a brand-new phone
items.why: Within weeks it's just your phone. Same features, far less thrill.

items.text: The lift from a pay rise or promotion
items.why: It helps, but soon it's the new baseline and your wants rise to match.

items.text: Retiring to a sunnier place for the weather
items.why: Sun matters less day to day than we expect (Schkade & Kahneman, 1998).

items.text: The stress of a long daily commute
items.why: People don't seem to fully get used to it (Stutzer & Frey, 2008).

items.text: Varied, regular time with people you like
items.why: Changing, surprising joys fade slower than fixed ones (Lyubomirsky, 2011).

cards.insight: We adapt fast to stable gains, slowly to daily hassles and changing joys. So cutting daily friction and keeping good things varied tends to pay off longer than more stuff.
cards.model: Spend on variety and less friction. Sameness is what fades fastest.
cards.try_today: Name one daily hassle you've 'accepted'. Spend 10 minutes finding one way to shrink it this week.

source.work: Lyubomirsky, 'Hedonic Adaptation to Positive and Negative Experiences' (2011); Stutzer & Frey (2008); Schkade & Kahneman (1998)

cards.try_team: List the group's three biggest daily hassles and three recent 'upgrades'. Vote: which fix would still feel good in six months?

cards.hook: A big deadline looms. Do you brace for impact or gear up?
cards.title: Stress: A Choice, Not a Curse

steps.scenario: You're facing a tough project with a short deadline. How do you approach it?

options.text: Focus on avoiding mistakes and staying calm, hoping for the best.
options.feedback: It's natural to want things to go smoothly, but this mindset can make stress feel heavier. You might miss opportunities to push yourself.

options.text: Embrace the challenge! See it as a chance to learn and grow, even if it gets intense.
options.feedback: That's the power of a stress mindset! Viewing stress as fuel can actually help you perform better. You're more likely to be engaged and creative.

steps.scenario: Your project hits a snag. How do you react?

options.text: Panic sets in, and you feel overwhelmed. It's going to fail.
options.feedback: This mindset can create a self-fulfilling prophecy. Remember, setbacks are part of the process.

options.text: You see this as a problem to solve. You brainstorm solutions and adjust your approach.
options.feedback: That's resilience! Viewing challenges as opportunities for growth helps you stay focused and find creative solutions.

cards.insight: Changing how you view stress can change its effect on you. A 'stress mindset' sees it as fuel, not a foe, leading to greater engagement and resilience.
cards.model: See stress as growth fuel! Learn from setbacks and unleash your inner drive.
cards.try_today: Next time you feel stressed, pause and ask yourself: What can I learn from this? How can I use this energy to my advantage?

source.work: The Upside of Stress (2019)

cards.try_team: Team challenges: 'What's the most stressful part of this project? How can we turn that into a growth opportunity?'

cards.hook: Snowball or thermostat? Sort 6 everyday loops.
cards.title: Snowball or Thermostat?

game.prompt: Does this settle back like a thermostat (←) or keep growing like a snowball (→)?

items.text: Short on sleep, you scroll late to unwind, then sleep even less
items.why: Tired leads to scrolling leads to more tired. Vicious circles are reinforcing too.

items.text: Money in savings earns interest, which earns more interest
items.why: Growth feeds more growth. Classic reinforcing loop.

items.text: You feel hungry, eat, and the hunger goes away
items.why: Your body pulls you back toward a set point. That's balancing.

items.text: A rumor spreads: the more people know, the more people tell
items.why: Each new teller makes more tellers, whether the rumor is true or false.

items.text: You speed up when late, slow down once you're on time
items.why: The gap to a goal drives the action, and the action closes the gap.

items.text: Practicing makes it easier, so you practice more
items.why: Virtuous circle: skill makes practice pleasant, practice builds skill.

cards.insight: Most things that change over time run on two loops. Reinforcing loops (snowballs) amplify, good or bad. Balancing loops (thermostats) pull back to a target. It's a thinking tool from systems science, not a lab finding. Know which loop you're in before you push.
cards.model: Reinforcing loops snowball; balancing loops hold a set point. Ask which one is running.
cards.try_today: Write one habit you want as a loop: 'A makes B, B makes more A.' Find the arrow you can strengthen today.

source.work: Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008)

cards.try_team: With your team, class or family: each person names one loop in your shared life. Vote: snowball or thermostat? Pick one to feed or break this week.

cards.hook: One skipped walk can turn into a lost month. Where would you cut it?
cards.title: Cut the Vicious Circle

steps.scenario: The loop: low energy, so you skip your walk. Moving less, you sleep a bit worse. Worse sleep, even less energy. Which link is easiest to cut today?

options.text: Fix my energy first, then start walking again
options.feedback: Waiting to feel ready is how the loop keeps running. Energy often follows movement, not the other way round.

options.text: A 5-minute walk, even feeling flat
options.feedback: Yes. Tiny and doable on a bad day. One small action can turn the same circle the other way.

options.text: Plan a full new fitness routine for Monday
options.feedback: Big plans feel good, but they start later and ask for energy you don't have yet.

steps.scenario: A week later the loop is turning the good way, then you miss two days. You think…

options.text: "Ruined. Back to square one."
options.feedback: Understandable, but loops don't reset to zero. Calling it ruined is what restarts the downward lap.

options.text: "Two days off. Short walk today and the loop keeps turning."
options.feedback: Right. A loop is about direction, not a perfect streak. Nudge it back the good way.

cards.insight: Spirals can feel like bad luck or a flaw in you, but often they're just a loop. Draw the circle and you see each link. You don't fix it all, just one arrow.
cards.model: If it keeps getting worse (or better) on its own, look for the circle, then cut or feed one link.
cards.try_today: Sketch one loop in your life as 4 boxes and arrows. Circle the easiest link and change just that one today.
cards.try_team: Draw a loop your group keeps falling into (late starts, messy kitchen, missed homework). Everyone marks the easiest link. Change that one for a week.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990)

cards.hook: Why do you always end up scalding, then freezing, in a new shower?
cards.title: The Shower Problem

steps.scenario: Hotel shower. Water is cold. You turn the knob toward hot. Five seconds later it's still cold. You…

options.text: Crank it much hotter. It clearly isn't working.
options.feedback: Very human, and exactly how you get scalded. The hot water was already in the pipe, on its way.

options.text: Wait a few more seconds before touching it again
options.feedback: Yes. The pipe adds a delay. Give your last action time to show its result.

options.text: Give up and take a cold shower
options.feedback: Brave, but the system was working. It was just slow to report back.

steps.scenario: Three weeks into a new workout plan, you don't feel much different yet. You…

options.text: Double the intensity to force results
options.feedback: That's the shower move again. Overcorrecting raises the risk of injury or burnout.

options.text: Keep the plan and judge it again after 8 weeks
options.feedback: Bodies, skills, and relationships all respond with a lag. Set a fair review date.

options.text: Switch to a totally different plan
options.feedback: Switching resets the clock before the first plan could show anything.

cards.insight: When results lag behind actions, it feels like nothing works, so we push harder. Then the late results land and we overshoot. Many problems are delay problems, not effort problems.
cards.model: Slow feedback plus impatience equals overshoot. Act, wait for the lag, then adjust.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you're trying to improve. Write how long it fairly takes to show results, and set a reminder for that date.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Sterman, Business Dynamics (2000)

cards.try_team: Before changing a plan, ask the group: how long should this take to show results? Agree a review date and don't touch the knob before it.

from_source.quote: Faster is slower.
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4, then ch. 5 'A Shift of Mind' on balancing loops and delays

cards.hook: Smart people, one small change, total chaos. Who's to blame?
cards.title: The Beer Game

game.prompt: A shop, a wholesaler, a distributor and a factory pass orders up a chain. Each delivery takes weeks. Customers change once: from 4 cases a week to 8, then stay at 8. What happens up the chain?
choices: Orders rise smoothly to 8 and stay there
Orders swing between huge and almost none
game.reveal: They swing wildly. Stock is slow to arrive, so players keep ordering, then drown in it and stop. If you picked 'smoothly', that's what nearly everyone expects. Afterwards, many players blamed wild customer demand. It had changed once.

cards.insight: In MIT's Beer Game, played since the 1960s, smart people make the same swings again and again. The cause isn't who plays. It's the delay built into the chain.
cards.model: When everyone overreacts, look for the delay before you look for someone to blame.
cards.try_today: Before you order, send, or ask again, check: is my last action still on its way? Wait one cycle first.
cards.try_team: When a problem in your group swings back and forth, draw the chain on paper and mark every delay. Agree to change one thing at a time.

source.work: Sterman, 'Modeling Managerial Behavior: Misperceptions of Feedback in a Dynamic Decision Making Experiment', Management Science (1989); Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990)

from_source.quote: Structure influences behavior.
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 3 'Prisoners of the System, or Prisoners of Our Own Thinking?'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 3 (the full Beer Game story and its three lessons)

cards.hook: Most people push where change is hardest. Can you find the lever?
cards.title: Where to Push

game.prompt: Rank these places to change a system, from weakest to strongest lever
items: Numbers (budgets, targets, quantities)
Feedback loops (how strongly the system self-corrects)
Information (who sees what, when)
Rules (incentives, permissions, punishments)
Goals (what the system is actually trying to do)
Mindset (the shared beliefs the whole system grows from)
game.explain: Donella Meadows ranked 12 places to intervene. Tweaking numbers is the easiest and usually the weakest. Changing goals and mindsets is harder, but it changes everything downstream.

cards.insight: Adjusting numbers rarely changes how a system behaves. Changing who sees what, the rules, or the goal moves more with less force. Meadows called her list a draft, not a law.
cards.model: Numbers are easy and weak. Information, rules, and goals are harder and strong.
cards.try_today: Pick one stuck problem. Instead of 'more' or 'less' of something, write one change to its rules, information, or goal.

source.work: Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999)

cards.try_team: At your next meeting, class council or family talk, ask 'what are we actually rewarded for?' before asking anyone to try harder.

from_source.quote: Give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth.
from_source.cite: Archimedes, as reported by Pappus of Alexandria, Collection, Book 8 (traditional English rendering)
from_source.next_read: Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 6 'Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System'

cards.hook: When stuck, do you try harder or change the game? Find out.
cards.title: Tweaker or Redesigner?

questions.q: You keep spending too much. Your first move is…

options.label: Promise to be stricter with myself
Track every purchase for a month
Make savings move automatically on payday

questions.q: Your group project keeps missing deadlines. You…

options.label: Make progress visible to everyone each week
Ask what each person is really rewarded for

questions.q: You want to read more. You…

options.label: Put a book where your phone usually sits
Just try to remember to read

questions.q: The same argument with a friend, sibling or partner keeps coming back. You…

options.label: Prepare my points better for next time
Agree a pause rule when it starts
Ask what each of you is actually trying to protect

zones.label: Tweaker
zones.text: Today's answers reach for effort and numbers first. Honest work, but tiring. Next time, ask: what rule, information, or goal is producing this?

zones.label: Switch-hitter
zones.text: Today's answers switch between pushing harder and redesigning. Notice which one you grab under stress, and try the redesign first once this week.

zones.label: Redesigner
zones.text: Today's answers look for the structure behind the problem. Keep going, and give redesigns time: their results also arrive late.

cards.insight: Meadows ranked 'numbers' (targets, budgets) among the weakest levers; we add willpower to that list. Changing what people see, what's rewarded, or the goal tends to work with less strain.
cards.model: Before pushing harder, ask what structure is producing the result.
cards.try_today: Take one 'I should try harder' and rewrite it as a change to your surroundings, rules, or reminders. Do that change now.

source.work: Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008)

cards.try_team: Next time your team or class is stuck, ban 'try harder' for 5 minutes. List changes to what people see, what's rewarded, or the goal.

from_source.quote: Small changes can produce big results
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4; then Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 6

cards.hook: A city paid people per rat tail. Guess what it got more of.
cards.title: The Rat Tail Bounty

game.prompt: Hanoi, 1902. Rats are spreading through the new sewers, so officials pay a small bounty for every rat tail handed in. What happens next?
game.reveal: It backfired. People were seen with live rats missing only their tails, so the rats kept breeding, and there were reports of rats being farmed for tails. Historian Michael Vann documented it. If you guessed 'rats disappear', that's what the officials expected too: the fix rewarded tails, not fewer rats.

cards.insight: A quick fix eases the symptom today, while its side effect quietly feeds the problem. The side effect is late, so the fix looks like it works, and we repeat it.
cards.model: Ask of every fix: what does this reward, and what will it feed in three months?
cards.try_today: Name one quick fix you use often (snacking, cramming, avoiding). Write what it might be feeding in the long run.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Vann, 'Of Rats, Rice, and Race' (2003)

cards.try_team: Pick one rule or reward your group uses (points, chores, targets). Spend 5 minutes asking: how could someone game this, and what would that feed?

from_source.quote: Today's problems come from yesterday's "solutions."
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4; Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 5 'System Traps... and Opportunities'

cards.hook: The fix worked on Monday. Why is the problem bigger by Friday?
cards.title: Spot the Backfire

steps.scenario: Mexico City, 1989. To cut smog, each car is banned from driving one weekday, based on its number plate. What did many families do?

options.text: Took the bus on their banned day
options.feedback: That was the plan. But a cheaper way round it was sitting in the used-car market.

options.text: Bought a second car, often an older one
options.feedback: Yes. Car numbers rose, many extra cars were old and dirtier, and economist Lucas Davis found no clear drop in air pollution.

options.text: Drove less on every day of the week
options.feedback: A hopeful guess. The rule only touched one day, so it changed which car, not how much driving.

steps.scenario: You sleep until noon on Sunday to catch up after a late Saturday. What's the hidden side effect?

options.text: None, you've paid back the sleep
options.feedback: You do get rest. But your body clock also shifts later, and that bill arrives on Sunday night.

options.text: Sunday night you can't fall asleep, so Monday hurts
options.feedback: Right. The lie-in eases today's tiredness and pushes your clock later. Researchers call the mismatch 'social jet lag'.

steps.scenario: Money is tight, so you pay only the minimum on a card or loan each month. What grows?

options.text: Nothing, the minimum keeps it under control
options.feedback: It keeps the letters away, which is real relief. Underneath, interest keeps adding to the balance.

options.text: The total you owe, because interest keeps piling up
options.feedback: Yes. The minimum fixes this month and feeds the debt, so next month needs the same fix again.

cards.insight: Every fix has a main effect and a side effect. The main effect shows up fast; the side effect arrives later and often feeds the problem you were fixing.
cards.model: Before a quick fix, ask: what will this feed when no one is watching?
cards.try_today: Take one fix you used this week (lie-in, snack, cramming). Write its side effect and one tweak that keeps the relief.
cards.try_team: Before agreeing a new rule at home, school or work, take 5 minutes: each person imagines how a clever lazy person would get round it.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Davis, 'The Effect of Driving Restrictions on Air Quality in Mexico City', Journal of Political Economy (2008); Wittmann, Dinich, Merrow & Roenneberg, 'Social Jetlag', Chronobiology International (2006)

from_source.quote: Behavior grows better before it grows worse.
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: The Fifth Discipline, ch. 4, then Appendix 2 on the 'Fixes That Fail' archetype

cards.hook: What's your crutch quietly doing to the muscle underneath?
cards.title: Crutch or Muscle?

game.prompt: Does this treat the symptom, or build the real capacity?

items.text: A third coffee every afternoon to get through the slump
items.why: It works today, but it can hurt tonight's sleep, which deepens tomorrow's slump.

items.text: Moving bedtime 20 minutes earlier
items.why: If short sleep is behind the slump, this goes after the cause, not the feeling.

items.text: Always getting a parent or friend to make your awkward phone calls
items.why: Relief now, but your own skill and confidence never get the reps.

items.text: Making the awkward call yourself, with them nearby for backup
items.why: Uncomfortable, but each try builds the skill you were avoiding.

items.text: Using autocorrect for a word you never learn to spell
items.why: Harmless here. Not every crutch is bad; just know which muscle you're skipping.

items.text: Asking a teacher to explain the step you keep getting wrong
items.why: Help that teaches is the opposite of a crutch: it shrinks your need for help.

cards.insight: When a quick fix keeps solving a problem for you, your own ability can weaken, so you need the fix more. Help isn't the issue; help that replaces learning is.
cards.model: Use help that teaches. Watch for fixes you need more each month.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you always outsource or avoid. Do one small piece of it yourself today, with support nearby if you need it.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990)

cards.try_team: Each person names one task they always hand to the same helper. Pair up: the helper coaches, the other does it, once this week.

from_source.quote: The easy way out usually leads back in.
from_source.cite: Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990), ch. 4 'The Laws of the Fifth Discipline'
from_source.next_read: Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 5, the trap 'Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor'

cards.hook: A group can know more than any member. Does it use what it knows?
cards.title: The Clue Nobody Said

game.prompt: Researchers gave small groups facts about three candidates in a student election. Together each group knew enough to spot the strongest one, but the key facts were split up, a piece per person. What did most groups do?
choices: Pooled the clues and picked the best
Talked about what they all already knew
game.reveal: They mostly talked about what they all already knew. In Stasser and Titus's 1985 study, shared facts got far more airtime than facts only one person held, so few groups picked the best candidate. When everyone got all the facts up front, most did. If you guessed 'pooled the clues', so did the groups.

cards.insight: Groups drift to facts everyone already holds, so the clue only one person has can go unsaid. Being quiet isn't the fix on its own; asking for unshared facts is.
cards.model: Before a group decides, ask: what does only one of us know?
cards.try_today: In your next family, class or work chat about a decision, ask: 'Has anyone noticed something the rest of us haven't?' Then wait.
cards.try_team: Before deciding, each person writes one fact they think only they know. Read them all aloud first, then discuss. Five minutes.

source.work: Stasser & Titus, 'Pooling of Unshared Information in Group Decision Making', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1985); Cain, Quiet (2012)

cards.hook: The first voice sets the room. How do you hear the slower ones?
cards.title: Make Room for Slow Thinking

steps.scenario: A teacher asks the class a hard question. Three hands shoot up within a second. What gets more thoughtful answers from more students?

options.text: Call on the first hand to keep things moving
options.feedback: Quick and natural. But then the fastest few do the thinking, and the rest learn they needn't.

options.text: Wait about three silent seconds before calling on anyone
options.feedback: Yes. In Mary Budd Rowe's classroom studies, waiting about 3 seconds led to longer answers and more students joining in.

options.text: Give the answer so nobody feels stuck
options.feedback: Kind, but it skips the thinking. A few seconds of quiet is often all people need.

steps.scenario: Your team or club needs ideas to stop wasting time. The usual way is everyone talking at once. What tends to give more ideas?

options.text: An open brainstorm, loudest ideas first
options.feedback: Lively, but people wait their turn and drop ideas while others talk.

options.text: Everyone writes ideas alone for 5 minutes, then shares
options.feedback: Yes. Diehl and Stroebe (1987) found people working alone, then pooling, had more ideas than groups brainstorming aloud. Waiting your turn blocks ideas.

options.text: Let the most senior person decide quickly
options.feedback: Fast, but you get one view of a problem everyone sees a part of.

steps.scenario: At home, the energy bill has crept up all year. Over dinner, everyone has a quick theory. What finds the real cause?

options.text: Go with the most confident theory
options.feedback: Confidence is loud, not proof. A slow creep needs the record more than a debate.

options.text: Lay the last 12 bills side by side and look first
options.feedback: Yes. A slow trend hides in any single month and shows up in a timeline. Looking together turns an argument into a shared view.

options.text: Cut everything at once and see what happens
options.feedback: Bold, but if you change everything, you won't learn what was driving it.

cards.insight: Loud, fast rooms reward the first idea. A short pause, silent writing or a timeline lets slower clues surface. That helps everyone think, not just quiet people.
cards.model: Pause before the talk: silence, paper or a timeline lets slow patterns show.
cards.try_today: Next time you ask someone a question, count three seconds in your head before you fill the silence.
cards.try_team: Open your next meeting, class or family plan with 3 minutes of silent writing. Go round, one idea each, before open talk.

source.work: Rowe, 'Wait Time: Slowing Down May Be a Way of Speeding Up!', Journal of Teacher Education (1986); Diehl & Stroebe, 'Productivity Loss in Brainstorming Groups: Toward the Solution of a Riddle', JPSP (1987); Cain, Quiet (2012)

cards.hook: A bat and ball cost 1.10. Your gut already has an answer. Check it.
cards.title: Fast & Slow Thinking

game.question: A bat and a ball cost 1.10 together. The bat costs 1.00 more than the ball. How much is the ball, in cents?
game.explain: If the ball were 10, the bat would be 1.10 and the total 1.20. Ball 0.05 + bat 1.05 = 1.10. Most people's first answer is 10, including many students at top universities.

cards.insight: The 10-cent answer arrives instantly and feels right. That's your fast mind. The slow mind only checks when you ask it to. Clever people miss this too; a pause is what helps.
cards.model: Fast thinking proposes, slow thinking checks. When it feels obvious and matters, check once.
cards.try_today: Say your gut answer out loud before your next decision that matters, then ask: 'How would I check this?'

source.work: Cognitive Reflection and Decision Making (2005); Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)

cards.try_team: Give everyone the bat-and-ball puzzle on paper, answers written silently. Reveal, then ask: which of our choices feel this obvious but never get checked?

cards.hook: Hare or owl: who's actually making your decisions this week?
cards.title: Who's Driving: Hare or Owl?

questions.q: A message annoys you. You usually…
Buying something pricey (a phone, shoes, a gadget), you…
When a headline makes you angry, you…
Someone asks: 'Quick, what's 17 × 24?' You…

options.label: Work it out step by step

zones.label: Hare-led
zones.text: Today your answers lean fast. That's efficient for routine stuff. For the few choices that matter, add one deliberate pause.

zones.label: Shared driving
zones.text: Today your answers switch between speeds. The skill now is noticing which moments deserve the owl.

zones.label: Owl-led
zones.text: Today your answers lean slow. Great for big calls. Watch for overthinking small, reversible ones; the hare handles those well.

cards.insight: Neither speed is better. The fast mind slips on numbers, anger and new things. 'System 1 and 2' (Stanovich & West, 2000) is a metaphor, not two brain parts.
cards.model: Let the hare handle the routine; call the owl for anything costly, emotional, or new.
cards.try_today: Pick one trigger (an angry message, a pricey purchase) and make it your rule to wait 10 minutes first.

source.work: Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)

cards.try_team: Agree on one shared 'owl rule', e.g. nobody replies to a heated group message for 10 minutes. Check in after a week: did it help?

cards.hook: We'll show you a random number first. Watch it bend your guess.
cards.title: Anchoring
