game.question: What percentage of UN member countries are in Africa?
game.explain: 54 of the 193 UN members are African: about 28%. You saw 65 first. If your guess landed above 35%, that number probably pulled you up. In the 1974 study, people who saw a wheel land on 65 guessed a median of 45%; those who saw 10 guessed 25%.

cards.insight: An irrelevant number still drags your guess toward it. Price tags like 'was 199, now 99' use this. Knowing about it helps a little; bringing your own number helps more.
cards.model: The first number sets the field. Bring your own number before you hear theirs.
cards.try_today: Before your next salary talk, quote or haggle, write your own number and one reason it's fair, before you hear theirs.

source.work: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974)

cards.try_team: Before any group estimate (trip cost, deadline, budget), everyone writes a number privately, then reveal together. No one anchors the room.

cards.hook: Your brain ranks dangers by how easily they come to mind. Test it.
cards.title: Availability Bias

game.prompt: Compared to how often it feels like it happens…

items.text: Dying in a plane crash
items.why: Crashes get huge coverage. Per mile, commercial flying is far safer than driving.

items.text: Being killed by a shark
items.why: Worldwide, unprovoked shark deaths are usually in single digits per year.

items.text: Older adults dying after a fall
items.why: Falls are a leading cause of injury death for people over 65. Quiet, rarely in the news.

items.text: A child taken by a total stranger
items.why: Stranger abductions are very rare; most missing children are runaways or family cases.

items.text: Heart disease as a cause of death
items.why: It's the top cause of death worldwide (WHO), yet rarely makes headlines.

items.text: Car crashes
items.why: About 1.2 million road deaths a year worldwide (WHO). So routine they're barely news.

cards.insight: Vivid, recent, dramatic events are easy to recall, so they feel common. Slow, ordinary risks hide. Your feed is a highlight reel of rare events, not a map of risk.
cards.model: Easy to imagine is not the same as likely. Ask for the count, not the story.
cards.try_today: Look up one number the next time a scary story grabs you: how many times a year does this actually happen?

source.work: Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability (1973)

cards.try_team: Everyone names the danger they worry about most. Look up one real yearly number for each together. Which fears shrink, and which grow?

cards.hook: 2, 4, 6 follows a secret rule. Most people's first guess is wrong.
cards.title: Confirmation Bias

steps.scenario: The numbers 2-4-6 follow a hidden rule. You can test any three numbers and learn if they fit. Your hunch: 'even numbers going up by 2.' Which test teaches you the most?

options.feedback: It fits, but it would fit your hunch either way. You'd learn nothing new. This is what most people try.
Another yes, but again only a test your hunch already predicts. Confirming feels productive; it rarely is.
Yes! Your hunch says 'no'. If it fits, your hunch is wrong. That's a real test. Spoiler: it fits.

options.text: Just guess the rule now
options.feedback: Bold! But without a test that could prove you wrong, you'd be guessing blind.

steps.scenario: 1-2-3 fits. So does 3-17-90. 6-4-2 does not. What's the rule?

options.text: Any three numbers going up
options.feedback: Correct. In Wason's 1960 study, only about 1 in 5 people named it on their first try, mostly because they only tested examples they expected to fit.

options.text: Numbers with a pattern
options.feedback: Close in spirit, but 3-17-90 has no neat pattern. Simpler: they just go up.

options.text: Even numbers only
options.feedback: 1-2-3 fit, so odd numbers are allowed. The rule is broader: any rising sequence.

cards.insight: We often test ideas in ways that can only say 'yes'. It feels like proof but isn't. Researchers debate how irrational this is; the fix is clear: seek what could prove you wrong.
cards.model: Don't ask 'what fits my idea?' Ask 'what would I see if I were wrong?'
cards.try_today: Pick one belief you hold firmly. Write down one thing that, if you saw it, would change your mind. Go look for it.

source.work: On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task (1960)

cards.try_team: Play 2-4-6: one person holds a secret rule, others test triples aloud. Afterwards count how many tests could have gotten a 'no'.

from_source.quote: The human understanding when it has once adopted an opinion ... draws all things else to support and agree with it.
from_source.cite: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum (1620), Book I, Aphorism 46 (trans. Spedding, Ellis & Heath)
from_source.next_read: Novum Organum, Book I, Aphorisms 45–52 (the 'Idols of the Tribe')

cards.hook: In an argument, are you defending a fort or drawing a map?
cards.title: Soldier or Scout?

questions.q: Someone shares a study that disagrees with you. First thought:

options.label: Look for what's wrong with it, but not what's right
Check its methods, the same way I'd check one I agreed with
Read what they found before judging

questions.q: When did you last change your mind on something you cared about?
Your feed mostly shows people who…

options.label: I follow some smart critics on purpose

questions.q: Being proven wrong feels like…

zones.label: Soldier mode
zones.text: Today's answers lean toward defending, which is very human. Try treating one belief as a draft, not a fort.

zones.label: Switching
zones.text: Today's answers mix scouting and defending. Notice which topics made you defensive; that's where your map is least checked.

zones.label: Scout mode
zones.text: Today's answers lean curious about being wrong. Keep it kind: scouts share maps, they don't sneer at others' wrong turns.

cards.insight: Everyone slips into defending. Scouting isn't caring less; it's wanting an accurate map more than wanting to be right. Your answers are a snapshot, not a verdict.
cards.model: A soldier asks 'Can I believe this?' or 'Must I believe this?' A scout asks 'Is it true?'
cards.try_today: In your next disagreement, ask one honest question: 'What would change your mind?' Then answer it yourself too.

source.work: The Scout Mindset (2021)

cards.try_team: In your next group debate, each side must state the other side's best argument first, until the other side says 'yes, that's it'.

cards.hook: Heads you win 150, tails you lose 100. Do you flip?
cards.title: Loss Aversion

game.prompt: One fair coin flip, real money in your own currency. Heads: you win 150. Tails: you lose 100. On average this bet pays you 25. Do you take it?
game.reveal: No wrong answer here: it's your money. But notice the pull. In Kahneman's studies most people refuse, wanting a win of about 200 before risking 100. Losses tend to feel roughly 1.5–2.5× as strong as equal gains.

cards.insight: Saying no is fine when the loss would really hurt. But we often skip small, smart risks just because losing stings. Some research finds the effect smaller than claimed for small amounts.
cards.model: Losses shout, gains whisper. For small, repeatable bets, judge the average, not the sting.
cards.try_today: Name one small risk you've avoided (asking, applying, trying). Write the realistic worst case. Is it really that bad?

source.work: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk (1979)

cards.try_team: Each person writes one small risk they've avoided. Swap papers and estimate the realistic worst case for each other. Is it as bad as it felt?

from_source.quote: We suffer more ... when we fall from a better to a worse situation, than we ever enjoy when we rise ...
from_source.cite: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), Part VI, Section I
from_source.next_read: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part VI, Section I, 'Of the Character of the Individual, so far as it affects his own Happiness'

cards.hook: Same mug, same room. Owning it for 5 minutes changes its price.
cards.title: The Endowment Effect

game.question: Students got a free mug. Those who got one named a selling price; those who didn't named a buying price. How many times more did owners want?
game.explain: About 2.5×. In Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler's 1990 study, owners asked a median of about $7.12 and buyers offered about $2.87. Same mug. Owning it for 5 minutes made giving it up feel like a loss.

cards.insight: Owning something makes letting go feel like losing, so we overprice our stuff. The effect is real but its size depends on the setup; some studies find it much smaller.
cards.model: Ask 'Would I buy this today, at this price?' not 'How much would losing it hurt?'
cards.try_today: Look at one thing you're selling online or keeping in your wardrobe or garage: would you buy it today at that price?
cards.try_team: Ask everyone: name one thing we keep only because we already have it (a tool, a habit, a club, a routine). Would we choose it again today?

source.work: Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect and the Coase Theorem (1990); Plott & Zeiler (2005)

cards.hook: Stuck on how to succeed? Ask how you'd fail instead.
cards.title: Inversion

steps.scenario: Your goal: be a better friend this year. Which question gets you a useful answer fastest?

options.text: How could I be the perfect friend?
options.feedback: Nice aim, but 'perfect' gives vague answers like 'be there more'. Hard to act on.

options.text: What would make sure I lose my friends?
options.feedback: Yes. Failure is easy to picture: cancel last minute, only talk about me, forget birthdays. Concrete and fixable.

options.text: What do the experts say friendship is?
options.feedback: Useful later, but it's about friendship in general, not your habits. Inversion goes straight to yours.

steps.scenario: Your list: cancel last minute, only talk about yourself, never ask questions, forget birthdays. Best next move?

options.text: Fix all four starting tomorrow
options.feedback: Big energy! But four changes at once rarely stick. Start with one.

options.text: Circle the one you already do a little, and stop it this week
options.feedback: Exactly. Small, honest, doable. Removing one quiet mistake often beats adding a big new effort.

options.text: Feel bad about the list
options.feedback: Very human, but guilt doesn't change much. The list is a map, not a verdict. Pick one item.

cards.insight: Your brain spots ways to fail faster than recipes for success. Mathematician Carl Jacobi advised 'invert, always invert'; investor Charlie Munger made it a life habit.
cards.model: Ask what would guarantee failure, then don't do that.
cards.try_today: Pick one goal. Write 3 ways to guarantee it fails. Circle the one you're closest to doing, and drop it today.

source.work: Poor Charlie's Almanack (2005)

cards.try_team: Ask the group: 'How could we make this trip, project or term a total disaster?' List ideas for 5 minutes, then pick one to prevent.

from_source.quote: Invert, always invert.
from_source.cite: Carl Jacobi, as quoted by Charlie Munger, Harvard School commencement speech (1986)
from_source.next_read: Charlie Munger's 1986 Harvard School commencement speech on prescriptions for misery, reprinted in Poor Charlie's Almanack

cards.hook: A city paid people for every dead cobra. Guess what it got more of.
cards.title: Second-Order Thinking

steps.scenario: Colonial Delhi, as the classic story goes. Cobras are a danger, so officials pay a reward for every dead cobra handed in. What happens next?

options.text: The cobra problem shrinks
options.feedback: That's the first-order guess, and it's what officials expected. The story has a twist.

options.text: People start breeding cobras to cash in
options.feedback: Yes. In the story, people farmed cobras for the reward. When officials scrapped it, breeders let the snakes go: more cobras than before.

options.text: Nobody bothers to hunt cobras
options.feedback: The opposite. Plenty of dead cobras came in, just not in the way that helped.

steps.scenario: A parent wants their kid to read more, so they plan to pay a coin for every book finished. Ask 'and then what?' twice. Best tweak?

options.text: Pay more per book
options.feedback: More pressure on the same number. Expect thinner books and skimming: the count goes up, the reading may not.

options.text: Read and chat about books together, and celebrate finishing a hard one
options.feedback: Good. You reward the real goal (enjoying and understanding) and keep a human check, so gaming it is harder.

options.text: Never reward anything
options.feedback: Understandable after the cobras! But rewards can work; just ask what the number will make people do.

cards.insight: First-order thinking asks 'what happens now?' Second-order asks 'and then what?' Rewards change behavior in ways nobody planned. The cobra tale is a classic parable with thin historical records; economist Horst Siebert named the 'cobra effect' after it.
cards.model: Every fix creates new incentives. Ask 'and then what?' at least twice.
cards.try_today: Write 'and then what?' before your next rule, rule-change, or reward (for you, your kids, or a group), and answer it twice.

source.work: The Most Important Thing (2011); Der Kobra-Effekt (2001)

cards.try_team: Before rewarding a number (bugs fixed, sales calls, chores done), ask together: 'How could someone hit this number without helping?' Then adjust.

from_source.quote: We can never do merely one thing.
from_source.cite: Garrett Hardin, 'The Cybernetics of Competition', Perspectives in Biology and Medicine (1963)
from_source.next_read: Frédéric Bastiat, That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen (1850), Chapter 1, 'The Broken Window' (public domain)

cards.hook: A test says you have a rare condition. How worried should you be?
cards.title: Base Rates

game.question: A condition affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test catches every real case but gives a false positive to 5% of healthy people. You test positive. Chance you have it?
game.explain: Of 1,000 people: 1 truly has it. About 50 healthy people also test positive. So 1 of ~51 positives is real: about 2%. In a 1978 Harvard study, 27 of 60 doctors and students answered 95%; only 11 got about 2%.

cards.insight: When something is rare, most positives are false alarms. That's why doctors confirm with a second test. This is just the math; real results need a real doctor.
cards.model: Start with how common it is, then adjust for the new evidence. Rare things stay fairly rare.
cards.try_today: Ask 'Out of 1,000 similar cases, how many usually turn out this way?' the next time a story or alarm surprises you.

source.work: Interpretation by Physicians of Clinical Laboratory Results (1978)

cards.try_team: Turn one scary claim into counts together: 'Out of 1,000 people like this, how many…?' Sketch the 1,000 as dots if it helps.

from_source.quote: A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.
from_source.cite: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section X, Part I
from_source.next_read: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, 'Of Miracles', Part I

cards.hook: One sentence about a stranger. Your gut picks a job in a second.
cards.title: The Count Beats the Story

game.prompt: Steve is a man in the USA. He's shy, tidy, loves order and small details, and is happiest with a quiet book. Is Steve more likely a librarian or a farmer?
game.reveal: Librarian is the natural pick: the story fits. But Kahneman notes the US had over 20 male farmers for every male librarian. Even if Steve fits librarians far better, farmers still win on the count.

cards.insight: A vivid description makes us forget how common each option is. Kahneman and Tversky showed this in 1973. Thinking in counts ('out of 100 men like Steve…') makes the error shrink.
cards.model: The story says who fits. The count says who's likely. Ask the count first.
cards.try_today: Next time you judge someone or something from one detail, ask: 'How common is each option in general?' before you decide.
cards.try_team: Before judging a new idea, person or rumour from one story, ask the group: 'How often does this usually happen?' Find one real number together.

source.work: On the Psychology of Prediction (1973); Judgment under Uncertainty (1974); Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), Introduction; Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995)

cards.hook: You watched for one minute. You're already sure who's smarter.
cards.title: The Quizmaster Illusion

game.prompt: A coin toss splits two people. One writes 10 hard trivia questions from their own odd knowledge. The other must answer them and gets about 4 right. Who seems more knowledgeable?
choices: Can't tell: the coin set the roles
game.reveal: The coin decided it. Asking your own questions is easy; answering someone else's is hard. Yet in Ross's 1977 study, watchers rated the questioner more knowledgeable, and so did the people answering.

cards.insight: We see the person, not the setup that made them look good or bad. Even knowing the roles were random didn't stop the bias.
cards.model: Before judging the player, look at the role they were handed.
cards.try_today: Next time someone looks clueless (a new classmate, colleague or relative), ask: 'Whose home turf is this?' before you judge them.
cards.try_team: Swap roles for 5 minutes: the newest person explains their own speciality and the expert asks questions. Notice who suddenly looks 'smart'.

source.work: Social Roles, Social Control, and Biases in Social-Perception Processes (1977)

cards.hook: Someone lets you down. Your brain writes their whole biography.
cards.title: Blaming People, Not Situations

steps.scenario: Your group project partner hasn't sent their part, and it's due tomorrow. Your first thought should be…

options.text: 'They're lazy. Typical.'
options.feedback: Understandable when you're stressed, but it's a guess about character from one moment. You don't yet know what's going on for them.

options.text: 'Something's probably in the way. I'll ask what's up and what they still need.'
options.feedback: Best pick. You stay open to the situation (illness, a shift at work, a crashed laptop) and you still chase the deadline.

options.text: 'Not my problem. I'll just do it all myself.'
options.feedback: It fixes tonight but skips finding out why. If the cause is fixable, it'll happen again.

steps.scenario: A usually reliable team member has missed two deadlines this month. As their manager, you…

options.text: Note it in their review as a commitment problem.
options.feedback: That locks in a character story before checking the setup. Two slips in a steady record often point to workload, unclear priorities or something at home.

options.text: Ask privately what changed and what's competing for their time.
options.feedback: Best pick. Look at the situation first: shifting priorities and overload often explain a sudden change better than 'they stopped caring'.

options.text: Say nothing and hope it sorts itself out.
options.feedback: Kind, but silence leaves both of you guessing. A curious question is kinder than a quiet verdict.

steps.scenario: Your grown-up son forgot to call on your birthday. Before you pick up the phone, you tell yourself…

options.text: 'He doesn't care about me anymore.'
options.feedback: A painful leap from one missed call. That turns a busy day into a story about the whole relationship.

options.text: 'His week must be chaotic. I'll call and see how he is.'
options.feedback: Best pick. A hectic job, a sick child or simple overload can explain a missed call. Calling keeps the door open either way.

options.text: 'I'll wait and see how long it takes him.'
options.feedback: A waiting game usually lets the hurt grow. A warm call answers the question faster.

cards.insight: Situations explain more than we think: in a 1973 study, hurried trainee ministers rarely stopped for a man slumped in a doorway. The flip side (excusing ourselves) is weaker than once claimed.
cards.model: Others' slips: ask 'what's in their way?' before 'what's wrong with them?'
cards.try_today: The next time someone annoys you, name two situations that could explain it before you decide what they're like.
cards.try_team: Take one recent mistake. Everyone lists three situation causes (time, information, tools) before anyone names a person. Fix one cause.

source.work: The Intuitive Psychologist and His Shortcomings (Ross, 1977); From Jerusalem to Jericho (Darley & Batson, 1973); The Actor-Observer Asymmetry in Attribution: A (Surprising) Meta-Analysis (Malle, 2006)

cards.hook: Epictetus sorted every worry into two piles. Can you?
cards.title: Up to Me, or Not?

game.prompt: Is it up to you?

items.text: Whether your train is late
items.why: Timetables, weather, signals. Real, but not in your hands.

items.text: Leaving 10 minutes earlier next time
items.why: Your choice, fully. This is where the energy should go.

items.text: What your teacher, boss or family thinks of your idea
items.why: You can shape it, but their mind is theirs. Aim at the pitch, not the verdict.

items.text: How clearly you explain your idea
items.why: Preparation and clarity are yours. That's the part worth practising.

items.text: Whether you win the match
items.why: Opponents, luck and refs get a vote. The Stoics called outcomes 'not up to us'.

items.text: How hard you train this week
items.why: Your decision to train is yours. Epictetus said even the body is only lent to us.

items.text: Your first emotional jolt when insulted
items.why: Seneca called these 'first movements': automatic, not chosen. The next minute is yours.

cards.insight: Epictetus taught that suffering grows when we pour effort into the 'not up to me' pile. The trick: almost every outcome you can't control has an action next to it that you can.
cards.model: Care about outcomes, but aim your effort at your own choices, judgments and actions.
cards.try_today: Write your biggest worry. Under it, list two actions that are fully up to you. Do one before tonight.

source.work: Epictetus, Enchiridion (c. 125 CE); Seneca, On Anger II

cards.try_team: Each person names one worry. Together sort it into 'up to us' and 'not up to us', then pick one 'up to us' action to do this week.

from_source.quote: Some things are in our control and others not.
from_source.cite: Epictetus, Enchiridion, ch. 1 (trans. Elizabeth Carter, 1758)
from_source.next_read: Enchiridion, chapters 1-5 (about two pages)

cards.hook: Your flight is cancelled. 200 angry people. What's your first move?
cards.title: The Stoic at the Gate

steps.scenario: The board flips to CANCELLED. A crowd forms at the desk. You…

options.text: Join the queue and tell everyone how unacceptable this is.
options.feedback: Totally human. But the anger costs you energy and changes nothing about the plane.

options.text: Open the airline app and rebook while you stand in line.
options.feedback: You spotted the part that's yours: options, timing, your next move. The queue stays a backup.

options.text: Sit down and wait for someone to announce a plan.
options.feedback: Calm is good. Pair it with one small action and you'll often get a better seat sooner.

steps.scenario: The agent says the next flight is tomorrow. You feel heat in your chest. You…

options.text: Breathe, then ask: 'What are my options for tonight?'
options.feedback: Same disappointment, better question. Calm, specific asks usually get more help than blame.

options.text: Tell the agent this is their fault.
options.feedback: Understandable, but they didn't cancel the plane. Blame aimed at the wrong target rarely pays.

options.text: Say nothing and walk off fuming.
options.feedback: You protected the agent, which is kind. Try naming one thing you can still do tonight.

cards.insight: You didn't stop caring about getting home. You moved your effort from the cancelled plane to your phone and your next question. That shift is the Stoic dichotomy of control.
cards.model: When something goes wrong, ask: what's the next move that is fully mine?
cards.try_today: Next time something annoys you, say out loud "What's mine here?" and do that one thing first.

source.work: Enchiridion (c. 125 CE)

cards.try_team: When a plan falls through (match rained off, trip delayed, deadline moved), go round: each person names one 'what's ours here?' move before anyone vents.

from_source.quote: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.
from_source.cite: Epictetus, Enchiridion, ch. 5 (trans. Elizabeth Carter, 1758)
from_source.next_read: Enchiridion, chapters 5 and 8

cards.hook: Do you spend your week on what you can change, or what you can't?
cards.title: Your Circle of Influence

questions.q: When the news is bad (prices, jobs, the world), I mostly…

options.label: Read more about it and feel worse
Look for one thing I can do in my own life

questions.q: When someone in my group project, team or family keeps letting things slide, I…

options.label: Ask them what's getting in the way

questions.q: My most common sentence starts with…
When I'm stuck, I first look for…

options.label: Who or what is to blame
The smallest thing I could change

zones.label: Concern-heavy today
zones.text: Today's answers put a lot of energy into things you can't move. That's tiring, not a flaw. Pick one worry and find the piece of it that is yours.

zones.label: Split today
zones.text: Today's answers switch between worrying and acting. Notice which topics pull you outward and give those one small action.

zones.label: Influence-focused today
zones.text: Today's answers aim at what you can move. Covey's claim is that this circle grows as you use it: trust and skill pile up.

cards.insight: Covey drew two circles: what you care about, and the smaller part you can affect. Acting inside the small one builds skill and trust, so it tends to grow. A lens, not a lab finding.
cards.model: Work inside what you can influence, and that circle slowly gets bigger.
cards.try_today: Swap one "If only they…" sentence today for "I can…" and finish it with a real action.

source.work: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989)

cards.try_team: Draw two circles on a board. List the group's frustrations, place each one, then pick one item inside 'influence' to act on this week.

cards.hook: Everyone's angry about it. Hardly anyone knows who decides.
cards.title: Find the Door You Can Push

steps.scenario: Your town plans to close the library (or youth club, or park café) you love. Your group chat is furious. You…

options.text: Post an angry rant and share every petition you see.
options.feedback: Caring is good, and petitions can help. But anger online rarely reaches the people who actually decide.

options.text: Find out who decides, and when, then go or write to them.
options.feedback: You found the edge of your circle: the meeting, the inbox, the vote. That's where concern turns into influence.

options.text: Shrug: 'Nothing I can do about the council.'
options.feedback: Understandable, and sometimes true. But you measured your circle before testing it. It's often bigger than it looks.

steps.scenario: You spoke up. They close it anyway. You still care. You…

options.text: Decide speaking up was pointless and stop bothering.
options.feedback: It stings. But you met people and learned how decisions get made. That influence stays with you.

options.text: Keep arguing in the chat about whose fault it is.
options.feedback: Very human. Blame keeps you in the concern circle, though, where nothing moves.

options.text: Start something in reach: a book swap, a reading group at a café.
options.feedback: This is Covey's point. One door closed, so you pushed one you could open. Accepting a loss and acting can go together.

cards.insight: Covey's circles are a lens, not a study. Research on 'locus of control' links believing your actions matter with better coping, though it's mostly correlational.
cards.model: Before you give up or blow up, find who decides, and which part of it is yours.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing that frustrates you. Spend 5 minutes finding out who actually decides it and how to reach them.
cards.try_team: Pick a shared gripe (a rule, a schedule, a chore). Find out who decides it, then draft one short, specific request together.

source.work: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989); Rotter, Psychological Monographs (1966)

cards.hook: Too timid or too reckless? Four answers will place your courage.
cards.title: The Golden Mean

questions.q: Someone in your group (class, family, team) says something you think is wrong. You…

options.label: Stay quiet, it's not worth it
Ask a calm question about it
Call it out bluntly on the spot

questions.q: A friend invites you on a hard hike you've never done. You…

options.label: Decline without even looking at the route
Say yes and check the route and weather
Go in trainers, no water, figure it out

questions.q: You want to start something of your own (a channel, a club, a small business). You…

options.label: Keep it in a notebook for 'someday'
Try a small version on weekends
Drop school, work or savings tomorrow to do it

questions.q: Someone is being mocked in a group chat. You…

options.label: Message them privately, then say 'not cool' in the chat
Post a long public rant at the mocker

zones.label: Leaning cautious today
zones.text: Today's answers lean cautious. Caution protects you, and sometimes it costs you. Try one small, safe step past your comfort line this week.

zones.label: Near the mean today
zones.text: Today's answers sit near the mean in these cases. Aristotle would add: the real test is doing it when fear is real and the situation is new.

zones.label: Leaning bold today
zones.text: Today's answers lean bold. That energy is useful; adding one check before you leap turns boldness into courage.

cards.insight: Aristotle put courage between cowardice and rashness. The mean is 'relative to us', not the midpoint: sometimes it's bold, sometimes a quiet no. Practical wisdom (phronesis) finds it.
cards.model: Virtue is calibration: the right action, in the right amount, at the right time.
cards.try_today: Pick one choice today and ask: what would 'too little' and 'too much' look like here? Then do the in-between.

source.work: Nicomachean Ethics (c. 340 BCE)

cards.try_team: Take a real decision your group faces. Write what 'too little' and 'too much' would look like, then agree on the right amount for this case.

from_source.quote: to feel them at the right times, with reference to the right objects, towards the right people... is what is both intermediate and best
from_source.cite: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 6 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1908)
from_source.next_read: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 6-9; Book III, ch. 6-9 (on courage)

cards.hook: Are you funnier than most people your age? Most people think so.
cards.title: Knowing You Don't Know

game.question: In a classic study, what % of US student drivers rated themselves more skilful than the median driver?
game.explain: Svenson (1981) found about 93% of a small US student sample rated themselves more skilful than the median driver. At most 50% can be. The same bias shows up everywhere: most people rate themselves above average at being kind, funny and smart.

cards.insight: Most of us rate ourselves above average, which can't all be true. Socrates thought wisdom starts with knowing what you don't know. It cuts both ways: if you usually rate yourself low, that's a guess too, and worth checking against evidence.
cards.model: Treat your self-ratings, high or low, as guesses. 'I might be wrong' opens the door to learning.
cards.try_today: Pick one opinion you hold strongly. Write the best reason someone could disagree with it, in their words, not yours.

source.work: Plato, Apology (c. 399 BCE); Svenson, Acta Psychologica (1981)

cards.try_team: Each person writes one thing the group is sure of. Swap papers and write the best reason it might be wrong. Discuss the strongest one.

from_source.quote: he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.
from_source.cite: Plato, Apology 21d (trans. Benjamin Jowett)
from_source.next_read: Plato, Apology 20e-23c (the oracle story)

cards.hook: You use a zip every day. Could you explain how it works?
cards.title: The Zip Test

game.prompt: In your head, rate how well you understand how a zip works. Now explain, step by step, how the teeth lock and unlock. In studies like this, what happened to people's ratings after they tried to explain?
game.reveal: They dropped. Rozenblit and Keil (2002) called it the illusion of explanatory depth: feeling familiar with something isn't the same as understanding it. If you guessed otherwise, you've just felt the illusion yourself.

cards.insight: Familiar things feel understood until you try to explain them. Socrates found the same in Athens: people skilled at one craft assumed they knew far more. Explaining is the honesty test.
cards.model: If you can't explain it step by step, you know less than it feels. Say it out loud to find out.
cards.try_today: Pick something you feel sure about (a news story, a gadget). Explain it out loud in 5 steps and notice where you get stuck.
cards.try_team: Each person picks a familiar thing (a lock, bike gears, wifi) and explains how it works in 2 minutes. Others may ask 'how exactly?' once.

source.work: Plato, Apology (c. 399 BCE); Rozenblit & Keil, Cognitive Science (2002)

from_source.quote: because they were good workmen they thought that they also knew all sorts of high matters
from_source.cite: Plato, Apology 22d (trans. Benjamin Jowett)
from_source.next_read: Plato, Apology 21b-23b (Socrates questions politicians, poets and craftsmen)

cards.hook: A setback you got through: would you delete it from your story?
cards.title: Amor Fati: Love Your Fate

game.prompt: Pick a real setback from your past: a rejection, a failure, a loss you've recovered from. If a button could erase it, and everything it led to, would you press it?
game.reveal: There's no wrong answer, and some pain is never 'worth it'. But many people find a setback also taught them a skill, a friend, or a direction. Nietzsche called embracing your whole story, hard parts included, amor fati.

cards.insight: Amor fati isn't pretending bad things were good. Nietzsche wanted nothing to be different; you can start smaller, by asking what a hard chapter gave you.
cards.model: You can't change what happened. You can choose what it becomes part of.
cards.try_today: Write one setback and finish this line: "Because of it, I can now…". Keep it to one sentence.

cards.hook: What were you worried about on this date three years ago?
cards.title: This Too Shall Pass

game.prompt: Try it now: what was keeping you up at night roughly three years ago? Can you name it clearly?
game.reveal: Many people can't. Research on 'affective forecasting' shows we tend to overestimate how long bad events will hurt. Feelings are weather: real, sometimes heavy, but they move. If a heavy mood isn't lifting for weeks, talk to someone you trust.

cards.insight: We tend to overestimate how long bad events will hurt (Wilson & Gilbert). The Buddha and Heraclitus taught that everything changes. Today's pain is real; it just isn't permanent.
cards.model: Feelings and fortunes are weather, not climate. Ask how much this will matter in a year.
cards.try_today: When something stings today, write it down with the date. Set a reminder to reread it in 3 months.

source.work: Wilson & Gilbert, 'Affective Forecasting' (2005)

cards.hook: Would your weekly calendar match the speech at your 80th birthday?
cards.title: Begin With the End in Mind

questions.q: This week I gave real, undistracted time to people I love.
The people closest to me would say I show up for them.
This week I moved, slept and ate like someone I'd want to be at 80.
I spent time on work, study or a hobby I'm proud of, not just busy with.
People rely on the quality of what I make.
I did something this week that helped someone beyond my circle.
This month I taught or unblocked someone without being asked.
I learned or practised something that's stretching me.
I did something this week I was not good at yet.

advice.0: Want a small next step for Relationships? Book 20 phone-free minutes with one person this week.
advice.1: Want a small next step for Health? Pick one: a 15-minute walk, or lights out 30 minutes earlier tonight.
advice.2: Want a small next step for Craft? Block one focused hour on the work you'd want to be remembered for.
advice.3: Want a small next step for Contribution? Do one small useful thing for someone who can't repay you.
advice.4: Want a small next step for Growth? Choose one skill and practise it for 10 minutes today.

game.advice_even: Even shape. No single gap stands out. Ask which of the five you'd most regret neglecting at 80, and give it one 20-minute block this week.

cards.insight: Covey pictured the speeches at your funeral; here it's your 80th birthday. Your shape shows one week, not your life: where to put attention next, not what you've failed at.
cards.model: Decide what you want said about you at the end, then plan this week backwards from it.
cards.try_today: Write three words you'd want people to use about you at 80. Put one action for each in this week's calendar.

cards.hook: How many weeks are in an 80-year life? Guess before you scroll.
cards.title: Your Life in Weeks

game.question: How many weeks are there in an 80-year life?
game.explain: 80 years × about 52.18 weeks ≈ 4,174. Oliver Burkeman built a whole book around this small number.

cards.insight: Many people guess far higher. About 4,000 weeks feels short, and that's the point: not to scare you, but to sharpen you. Seneca said life is long enough if used well.
cards.model: Time is finite and countable. Spend weeks the way you'd spend something precious.
cards.try_today: Pick this week's one most important thing, the one you'd regret skipping, and schedule it before anything else.

source.work: Four Thousand Weeks (2021); On the Shortness of Life (c. 49 CE)

cards.hook: That petty argument: would it survive one honest question?
cards.title: The Grudge-Shrinking Question

steps.scenario: You and your best friend argued. Then they posted a group photo you weren't in. They leave tomorrow for two weeks away. You…

options.text: Leave their messages on read until they apologise.
options.feedback: Not the best move. Fair to be hurt, but two weeks of silence usually makes the hurt grow, not shrink.

options.text: Text: 'Still a bit annoyed, but have a great trip. Talk when you're back?'
options.feedback: Best move. You stayed honest and kept the door open. If time felt short, this is the message you'd want sent.

options.text: Post a story about fake friends.
options.feedback: Not the best move. It feels good for a minute, then becomes one more thing to repair.

steps.scenario: In a meeting, a teammate presents part of your idea as their own. You'll work together all next month. You…

options.text: Say nothing, and quietly hold it against them for months.
options.feedback: Not the best move. Swallowed grudges leak out later and cost you months of easy teamwork.

options.text: Call it out in front of everyone at the next meeting.
options.feedback: Not the best move. You're right to want credit, but public blame tends to start a feud.

options.text: Tell them privately, calmly, and agree how you'll credit each other's work.
options.feedback: Best move. Memento mori doesn't mean swallowing it. It means fixing it without letting it eat your month.

steps.scenario: Your sister rings on your birthday. You haven't really spoken since a falling-out over a family holiday last year. You…

options.text: Thank her warmly and suggest lunch soon.
options.feedback: Best move. She reached out; you met her. The old topic can wait for a calmer day, face to face.

options.text: Keep it short and cool. She knows what she did.
options.feedback: Not the best move. Understandable, but a cool reply can turn one more year into five.

options.text: Raise the old disagreement right away to clear the air.
options.feedback: Not the best move yet. Clearing the air matters, but a birthday call is rarely the moment.

cards.insight: Remembering time is limited didn't make you a doormat. It made the grudge smaller and the next kind, honest step clearer. That's what the Stoics used the thought for.
cards.model: Before you hold a grudge, ask: if time were short, how would I want this to end?
cards.try_today: Pick one small, stale grudge and send one warm, low-pressure message. You don't have to settle everything.

cards.hook: Why do people about to move away choose like their grandparents?
cards.title: Short Time, Clear Choices

game.prompt: Imagine you're moving far away in a few weeks. You get one free half hour. Who do you spend it with?
choices: A close friend or family member
A new acquaintance you really clicked with
The author of a book you just loved
game.reveal: The familiar face. In Fredrickson & Carstensen (1990), older adults mostly picked a close partner. Younger adults spread their picks, until they imagined an upcoming move. Then they chose the familiar face too.

cards.insight: When time feels short, through age, a move, or illness, people turn toward who matters most (Carstensen's research). It tracks felt time, not age. Memento mori borrows that clarity early.
cards.model: A sense of limited time points you toward what matters. You can borrow it without waiting for an ending.
cards.try_today: Imagine you're moving away next month. Name the one person you'd make time for, and message them today.

source.work: Fredrickson & Carstensen, 'Choosing Social Partners', Psychology and Aging (1990)

cards.try_team: Ask: 'If this were our last month together as a class, team or family, what would we stop, and what would we make time for?' Pick one of each.

cards.hook: You've been asked to give a presentation. Do you…
cards.title: Speak Your Truth, Create Impact

steps.scenario: You've been asked to give a presentation at work. You know your ideas are valuable but sharing them feels risky. Do you…

options.text: Stick to the safe, pre-approved slides. It's easier and less likely to ruffle feathers.
options.feedback: Playing it safe might get you through this time, but it stifles your creativity and prevents real impact.

options.text: Inject your unique perspective into the presentation, even if it means stepping outside the script. Start with a personal story or a surprising statistic.
options.feedback: Creative truthful courage! Sharing your authentic self builds trust and makes your ideas more memorable.

options.text: Practice the presentation until you know it word-for-word, then deliver it flawlessly but without any personal touch.
options.feedback: While preparation is key, delivering a memorized speech lacks connection. Your truth can make the difference.

cards.insight: True courage isn't just about bravery; it's about using your creativity to express your authentic self and create meaningful impact.
cards.model: Speak your truth with kindness, measure progress against yourself, not others.
cards.try_today: Share your unique view or story today! Small acts of courage build big confidence 💪

source.work: The Gifts of Imperfection (2010)
